A loss whose clip ends before either is unresolved: it says nothing about returning, and the return rate counts only the resolved ones. Every pushed start is then one of four things:

   pushed  --+-- survived      no loss within the watch (and tracking came back, or not)
             +-- lost  --+-- returned        back on the reference within five seconds, and how soon
                         +-- not returned    the five seconds ran out
                         +-- unresolved      the clip ended first

The bands and the return limit are a run's own (controls.probe): by default pushes of 1 to 5 m/s, a character that loses the reference followed five seconds.

Only starts whose push lands where the reference stands are probed. The probe asks a question about balance, and a push landing while the reference lies on the floor would count a body already down as having survived, though it had no balance to keep. So a start is kept when, at its push, the reference's head is at least 0.8 of its highest anywhere in the clip - a share of the clip's own height, the same rule for any clip and any robot - and when the clip has room left for the settle and the watch:

   the reference's head height over a get-up clip
   highest   ______                                            ___________
   0.8 x    /------\------------------------------------------/-----------   the standing line
           |        \                                        /
           |         \______________________________________/
            stand     fall               lie                 rise    stand        time ->

   a start is probed when its push lands above the line, with its settle and its watch inside the clip

A run on several clips judges and probes each on its own: every line of judge.csv and recovery.csv names its clip, the run's status.zon lists each clip's recent time to failure, and its console line gives them side by side - (dance 0.74 s, get-up 1.59 s) - so the easier clip's numbers never hide the harder one's.

A run whose actor is a flow is judged and probed through the learner itself - its flow, from its mirror, at zero noise - since the lab's policy file holds a Gaussian policy; such a run writes no policy file, and keeps its policy in its state file.

Pushes also come during training, as a run setting (pushes): at random moments at a given rate per second - each physics step a push with probability rate x dt - each with a speed drawn from a range, so that a run sees small pushes taken in stride, larger ones that need a step, and some that end in a fall. Each push begins a new segment of the replay, since nothing in the state before it saw it coming.

The pushes follow a schedule in training hours (start_hours, full_hours), the clock the trainer keeps and saves with its run, so it holds whatever the machine's speed and across a resume. Before the start there are none, and characters learn to track before anything knocks them; from the start to the full hour the random pushes' rate and the top of their speed range rise together in a straight line - the rate from nothing, the top from the gentle end; from the full hour on, full strength, for as long as the run goes. A night of eight hours, pushes starting at the first hour and full at the seventh:

   hours          0      1      2      3      4      5      6      7      8 and on
   share          0      0      1/6    2/6    3/6    4/6    5/6    1      1
   rate (1/s)     0      0      0.08   0.17   0.25   0.33   0.42   0.5    0.5      (full 0.5)
   speeds (m/s)   -      -      0.5-1.0 ...                        0.5-3.5          (full 0.5 to 3.5)

A run that goes on past the eighth hour keeps training at full strength - the schedule has no end to fall off. The fleet counts the pushes it gives and their speeds, and the log carries the schedule's share beside them, so a run shows both the perturbations it asked for and the ones its characters actually met.

The lab draws every run's learning curve from its log, whichever learner wrote it, by the columns' names rather than their places. Each learner keeps its own log - PPO a line per batch, SuperTrack a line per round - but every log has training_minutes, steps_watched and failures, and that is all a curve needs: the time to failure over a window of recent lines, steps watched per failure. The first column says what a line is, and so how many lines the window holds - 8 batches or 128 rounds, each about two minutes of character-time.

SuperTrack's log. A SuperTrack run's log has a line per round and a column for every number the learner keeps, generated from one definition (SuperTrackLog.Line): add a number there and it is a column. They fall in four groups - what happened in the round, counted as the learner's totals' differences; what the host measured at its end; how long its halves took; and the device's numbers, newest:

   the round          steps watched, failures, updates; pushes and their mean speed; planning decisions and
                      the share of steps acted from a plan; actions not finite, readbacks refused, updates
                      skipped for want of windows (the last three 0 in a healthy run)
   at its end         the planning share and the mean hazard, examples held by teachers 2 and 3, the trust
   its time           acting, training on the CPU's side, judging (milliseconds)
   the device         the world model's loss, the policy's tracking, barrier, tail and gradient length, the
                      critic's value, spread and error, the flow's teachers (the table above)

The status carries the newest of the ones checked first - the world model's loss, the critic's error, the policy's gradient length, and the run's totals of skipped updates and actions that were not finite.

Safeguards. A night is long enough for something to go wrong while nobody watches, so a run protects what it has learned. On the device a weight that stops being finite never comes back - every update after spreads it - so after every round, and before every save, the trainer asks the learner whether anything is not finite: the newest readback's weights, network by network, then every number of the device's block. The first that is not ends the run, in the state failed_nonfinite with its name in the status, before anything is saved. Every file is written beside the old one and renamed over it, so a run stopped in the middle of a write keeps the file it had. And each checkpoint keeps, besides the policy, the learner's whole state under its minute - the newest four of them - which is how a run whose policy files cannot hold its policy (a flow's) is looked at later, and how any run goes back to an earlier state:

   every round          anything not finite?   yes: stop, failed_nonfinite, name it - nothing saved
   every save           anything not finite?   yes: refuse, the last good state kept on disk
   every checkpoint     policy_m00030, supertrack_state_m00030      (the newest four states kept)

Two more things a night says without being asked. At its start, how much of each kernel buffer its learner fills - activations, their gradients, parameters - so a run near the limit is seen before it grows. And after every judgement, the collapse alarm: a clip whose policy was once judged better than the servo and has since been judged no better three times running has fallen apart, and the status names it. Below the servo before ever being above it is not a collapse - an untrained policy starts there - so the alarm stays quiet through a night's first hours and speaks only of a policy that had learned. The run goes on; a person decides.

Running a long training. A run is a folder holding its run.zon. The folder lives outside the repository, because what a run writes is large and is not source; the recipes the repository keeps are in examples/geno_lab/recipes/, each copied into a new folder as its run.zon. The trainer is started on the folder - geno_trainer --run=../geno_runs/night1_full - and left. Everything it learns and everything it measures lands in that folder, each file written whole and renamed into place, so another program can read it while it runs: the state and its checkpoints, the policy, log.csv (a line a round), judge.csv and recovery.csv (a line per clip at every judgement, the servo's first), and status.zon. An empty file named stop ends it after the round; the same command carries it on from where it was.

The question a night answers comes from runs that differ in one thing. Three runs on the minute, identical but for what is being asked about: one that ends an episode at a loss, one that lets the character return, and one that adds the flow and the planner to the returns. Read at the same minutes, the first two say what returning teaches, the last two what the flow and the search add. Each file says why every number in it is what it is.

   at the start        the buffers it fills, the clips it trains
   every few seconds   its rounds, its updates, how often each clip's reference is lost
   every round         a line of log.csv - every count, every time, every device number
   every half hour     a judgement and a probe of each clip, a checkpoint; the alarm checked
   at the end          exit 0 finished or stopped, 1 a run file refused, 2 a run that failed

The morning's question is answered by recovery.csv: for each clip and each push speed, how many pushed characters kept the reference, how many lost it, and of those how many came back within five seconds - the return rate, run against run.

  PPO        batch,training_minutes,steps,steps_watched,failures,mean_reward,...      window: 8 lines
  SuperTrack round,training_minutes,steps_watched,failures,world_updates,...        window: 128 lines
                   ^ same name, found wherever it is
RunCurve.Columns.ofHeader
/// The columns of a log whose first line is `header_text` (without its newline), or null when it is no header
/// the curve can read: the first column neither `batch` nor `round`, or a needed column missing.
pub fn ofHeader(header_text: []const u8) ?Columns {
    var names: std.mem.SplitIterator(u8, .scalar) = splitScalar(u8, header_text, ',');
    const first_name: []const u8 = names.next() orelse return null;
    const window_lines: usize = if (eql(u8, first_name, "batch"))
        RunLog.window_batches
    else if (eql(u8, first_name, "round"))
        SuperTrackLog.window_rounds
    else
        return null;
    var training_minutes_at: ?usize = null;
    var steps_watched_at: ?usize = null;
    var failures_at: ?usize = null;
    var column_count: usize = 1;
    while (names.next()) |name| {
        const column_index: usize = column_count;
        column_count += 1;
        if (eql(u8, name, "training_minutes")) {
            training_minutes_at = column_index;
        } else if (eql(u8, name, "steps_watched")) {
            steps_watched_at = column_index;
        } else if (eql(u8, name, "failures")) {
            failures_at = column_index;
        }
    }
    const columns: Columns = .{
        .column_count = column_count,
        .training_minutes_at = training_minutes_at orelse return null,
        .steps_watched_at = steps_watched_at orelse return null,
        .failures_at = failures_at orelse return null,
        .window_lines = window_lines,
    };
    return columns;
}
trainSuperTrack
/// Trains a SuperTrack run round after round until it must end (`superTrackEndState`), logging every round and
/// saving everything at its first round and every `save_minutes`; the state it ended in. Memory: each round's paths
/// and files in `arena_state`, reset every round; the log grows in `progress` with `gpa`.
fn trainSuperTrack(
    gpa: Allocator,
    io: Io,
    report_interval_ms: f64,
    arena_state: *ArenaAllocator,
    folder: []const u8,
    run: lab.GenoRun,
    settings: lab.SuperTrackLearner,
    learner: *SuperTrackLearner,
    progress: *SuperTrackProgress,
) !RunState {
    const save_minutes: f32 = run.controls.save_minutes;
    while (true) {
        _ = arena_state.reset(.retain_capacity);
        const arena: Allocator = arena_state.allocator();
        if (try superTrackEndState(arena, io, folder, run.controls, learner, progress)) |end_state| {
            return end_state;
        }
        // The round, its two halves timed apart; its counts the totals' differences.
        // The pushes' schedule follows the run's training hours (`robot_track.Pushes.scheduleShare`).
        learner.fleet.training_hours = superTrackMinutes(progress) / 60.0;
        // And the rates' schedule, when it is in hours (`robot_track_resident.Options.rate_decay_hours`).
        learner.training_hours = learner.fleet.training_hours;
        const before: RoundTotals = .of(learner);
        const round_started_ms: f64 = wgpu.nowMs();
        learner.act(learner.options.collect, 1.0);
        const acting_ended_ms: f64 = wgpu.nowMs();
        learner.train();
        const training_ended_ms: f64 = wgpu.nowMs();
        const after: RoundTotals = .of(learner);
        progress.rounds += 1;
        const steps_watched: u64 = after.steps_watched - before.steps_watched;
        const pushes: u64 = after.pushes - before.pushes;
        const push_speed_sum: f64 = after.push_speed_sum - before.push_speed_sum;
        const planned_steps: u64 = after.planned_steps - before.planned_steps;
        const returns: u64 = after.returns - before.returns;
        const return_steps: u64 = after.return_steps_sum - before.return_steps_sum;
        const round_line: lab.SuperTrackLog.Line = .{
            .round = progress.rounds,
            .training_minutes = superTrackMinutes(progress),
            .steps_watched = steps_watched,
            .failures = after.failures - before.failures,
            .world_updates = learner.world_updates,
            .policy_updates = learner.policy_updates,
            .pushes = pushes,
            .push_mean_speed = @floatCast(push_speed_sum / float64(@max(pushes, 1))),
            .push_schedule = learner.fleet.pushScheduleShare(),
            .returns = returns,
            .return_mean_seconds = float(return_steps) * learner.fleet.m.opt.timestep / float(@max(returns, 1)),
            .flagged_share = flaggedShare(learner),
            .mean_hazard = meanHazard(learner),
            .planning_decisions = after.planning_decisions - before.planning_decisions,
            .planned_step_share = float(planned_steps) / float(@max(steps_watched, 1)),
            .teacher2_examples = learner.distillation_example_count,
            .teacher3_examples = learner.fpo_example_count,
            .critic_trust = learner.criticTrust(),
            .nonfinite_actions = after.nonfinite_actions - before.nonfinite_actions,
            .mirrors_refused = after.mirrors_refused - before.mirrors_refused,
            .windows_refused = after.windows_refused - before.windows_refused,
            .acting_ms = @floatCast(acting_ended_ms - round_started_ms),
            .training_ms = @floatCast(training_ended_ms - acting_ended_ms),
            .judging_ms = progress.pending_judging_ms,
            .device = learner.device_stats,
        };
        progress.pending_judging_ms = 0;
        try lab.SuperTrackLog.appendLine(gpa, &progress.log, round_line);
        progress.recent.add(round_line.steps_watched, round_line.failures);
        // And each clip's recent rounds, from the learner's per-clip counts.
        for (0..learner.exposure_by_clip.len) |clip| {
            const clip_steps: u64 = learner.exposure_by_clip[clip] - progress.clip_exposure_seen[clip];
            const clip_failures: u64 = learner.failures_by_clip[clip] - progress.clip_failures_seen[clip];
            progress.clip_recent[clip].add(clip_steps, clip_failures);
            progress.clip_exposure_seen[clip] = learner.exposure_by_clip[clip];
            progress.clip_failures_seen[clip] = learner.failures_by_clip[clip];
        }
        const minutes_since_save: f32 = superTrackMinutes(progress) - progress.saved_at_minutes;
        const is_save_due: bool = !progress.has_saved_this_start or minutes_since_save >= save_minutes;
        if (is_save_due) {
            saveSuperTrack(arena, io, folder, learner, settings, progress, .training) catch |err| switch (err) {
                error.StateNotFinite => return .failed_nonfinite,
                else => return err,
            };
        }
        // The policy file's play check - none for a flow run, which writes no policy file.
        const has_policy_file: bool = settings.actor != .flow;
        if (progress.has_saved_this_start and !progress.has_checked_policy_this_start and has_policy_file) {
            if (!try superTrackPolicyPlaysAsTrained(arena, io, folder, learner)) {
                say(io, "the policy file does not play as the learner acts - the run fails", .{});
                return error.PolicyDoesNotPlayAsTrained;
            }
            progress.has_checked_policy_this_start = true;
        }
        const minutes: f32 = superTrackMinutes(progress);
        const checkpoint_minutes: f32 = run.controls.checkpoint_minutes;
        const minutes_since_checkpoint: f32 = minutes - progress.checkpointed_at_minutes;
        const is_checkpoint_due: bool = checkpoint_minutes > 0 and minutes_since_checkpoint >= checkpoint_minutes;
        if (is_checkpoint_due) {
            saveSuperTrackCheckpoint(arena, io, folder, learner, settings, progress) catch |err| switch (err) {
                error.StateNotFinite => return .failed_nonfinite,
                else => return err,
            };
        }
        const judge_minutes: f32 = run.controls.judge_minutes;
        const minutes_since_judgement: f32 = minutes - progress.judged_at_minutes;
        const is_judgement_due: bool = judge_minutes > 0 and minutes_since_judgement >= judge_minutes;
        if (is_judgement_due) {
            const judging_started_ms: f64 = wgpu.nowMs();
            try judgeSuperTrackPolicy(gpa, arena, io, folder, learner, settings, progress, run.controls.probe);
            progress.pending_judging_ms = @floatCast(wgpu.nowMs() - judging_started_ms);
            // Said at once as well as logged with the next round: what a judgement costs sets how often to judge.
            const judging_seconds: f32 = progress.pending_judging_ms / 1000;
            say(io, "judging and probing took {d:.1} s", .{judging_seconds});
        }
        reportSuperTrack(io, report_interval_ms, folder, learner, progress);
    }
}
Compute.discardReadback
/// Forgets what the readback holds, and the copy in flight if there is one: from here, `readLatest` returns
/// null until a copy encoded AFTER this call has landed. For a caller that has just replaced buffers by
/// upload - a learner resumed from a saved state: a copy encoded before the upload would bring back exactly
/// what the upload replaced, and anything reading the readback (a mirror of the weights) would go back to it.
///
/// On the CPU backend the buffers are the module's own and every read is current: nothing to forget. On the
/// worker backend an upload writes the readback's own mirror, so the readback holds the upload already; a job
/// still in flight would overwrite it on landing, and is not guarded here - no learner runs on that backend.
pub fn discardReadback(self: *Self) void {
    switch (self.backend) {
        .cpu, .worker => {},
        .gpu => {
            const gp: *Gpu = &self.gpu.?;
            gp.have_read = false;
            gp.discard_copy_in_flight = gp.read != .invalid;
        },
    }
}

The weights and the policy are two different things. The weights are the run's training state: for PPO, both networks - the actor and the critic - Adam's two moments for every parameter, the observation normaliser's running statistics and the counters, everything the trainer needs to carry on. The policy is only what acting needs: the function from what a character senses to what it does. The critic, the optimiser and the exploration noise are tools of learning, and a policy that is deployed - watched in the lab, judged, played in a page - needs none of them. The policies' checkpoints are kept by the minute of training, a clock every learner shares, so that two runs can be compared at the same minutes. Keeping the policy apart from the training state is worth its small cost, for five reasons:

  • Every learner is watched and judged one way. PPO, SuperTrack and EfficientTDMPC keep very different training states, but each writes a policy of the same form, so one player, one show and one judge serve them all, and a comparison between learners compares their policies rather than the code that happens to run them.
  • The normalisation travels with the network. A network trained on normalised inputs computes nonsense on raw ones, and normalised by statistics other than its own it computes something subtly wrong - a classic bug, in which a policy that trained well looks broken when it is evaluated. The normaliser is frozen into the policy when it is written, and the policy normalises with the very function that normalised every observation it trained on, so that training and deployment agree by construction.
  • The policy acts by its mean action. While it learns, PPO's policy explores by sampling around its mean; shown or judged, it acts deterministically, so that what is measured is what it learned, not its noise.
  • The controller travels with it. The action's limit, its scale in radians per unit and DReCon's filter are part of the policy, so a policy is judged under the controller it was trained under.
  • What it observes and how often it decides travel with it. Learners differ in both, so a policy names its observation and carries its decision interval, and whatever plays it builds the observation it names and decides when it says. Nothing about a learner is assumed by the player.

Two observations exist today, one per kind of learner:

                 drecon                                 supertrack_features
  learner        PPO's actor                            SuperTrack's policy
  reads          watched bodies' positions and          the goal (the reference one frame ahead),
                 velocities, the reference around       then the character's own state, each in
                 the frame, the action being applied    the root's frame
  normalised by  the actor's running normaliser,        the clip's per-feature means and spreads,
                 clamped to 5 deviations                no clamp - the goal and the state alike
  decides        every 2 physics steps (30 Hz)          every physics step (60 Hz)
  controller     limit 1, DReCon's filter beta 0.2      no limit, no filter (beta 1)

SuperTrack's normaliser has one mean and one spread per feature, and both halves of the observation are measured in the same features, so the same statistics normalise the goal and the state: a policy reading 2F inputs carries F means and F spreads, F being 16 numbers for each body but the world and 3 more (robot_track.localSize). With a feature whose mean is 0.5 and spread 2, a goal of 1.5 and a state of -0.5 reach the network as (1.5 - 0.5) / 2 = 0.5 and (-0.5 - 0.5) / 2 = -0.5.

ObservationKind
/// Which observation a policy reads (`PolicyObservation`), as a policy file names it. The values are the file's, so
/// they are written out and never renumbered.
pub const ObservationKind = enum(u32) {
    /// DReCon's observation (`robot_policy.observeFrom`): the watched bodies' positions and velocities and the
    /// reference around the character's frame, in the root's heading frame, and the action being applied - what
    /// PPO's actor reads.
    drecon = 0,
    /// SuperTrack's features (`robot_track.local`): the goal - the reference one frame ahead - then the character's
    /// own state, each in the root's frame and normalised by the clip's frozen statistics. What SuperTrack's policy
    /// reads.
    supertrack_features = 1,
};
PolicyObservation
/// What a policy reads, with what it needs to build it: nothing more for DReCon's observation (its own normaliser,
/// when it has one, is the policy's `normalization`), and for SuperTrack's features the clip's per-feature means and
/// spreads, frozen when the policy was written (`robot_latent.Normalizer`: each feature `(x - mean) / spread`, no
/// clamp). The goal and the state are both normalised by the same statistics, so the policy's observation is twice
/// as wide as the normaliser.
pub const PolicyObservation = union(ObservationKind) {
    drecon,
    supertrack_features: latent.Normalizer,
};

The policy's file is its form outside a program, laid out as the structures that write and read it:

  Header              magic, version 4, layer count, flags, observation size, limit, scale, filter,
                      the normaliser's count, clip and epsilon
  ObservationHeader   which observation, the decision interval, the feature count
  layer 1 .. n        its output count, activation, SimNorm group and norm epsilon, then W and b -
                      and, for a normed layer, the norm's gain and bias
  normaliser          means, sums of squared deviations          when the observation is normalised
  features            means, spreads                             when the observation is SuperTrack's

A layer's activation is one of four. PPO's and SuperTrack's networks use two: none, a linear layer, as an actor's last layer is, and tanh. EfficientTDMPC's networks are built of TD-MPC2's normed layer (zimrnum's NormedDense; its layer norm is zimrnum's 10.2), which adds a step between the linear part and the activation: the layer's outputs are normalised together - their mean taken away, divided by their spread - and each is then scaled by its own gain and shifted by its own bias. The activation that follows is Mish in every hidden layer, and SimNorm at the end of the encoder, where the outputs are read in groups and each group becomes a small probability vector:

  linear      p = b + x W                                one value per output
  norm        n = (p - mean(p)) / sqrt(var(p) + eps)     over the layer's outputs together
  scale       s = n * gain + norm_bias                   per output
  activation  Mish(s)                     a hidden layer
              softmax of each group of s  the encoder's last layer (SimNorm): its latent state

The player computes the norm and the activation with zimrnum's own functions - the ones the agent's graph runs - so on the same pre-activations it gives the agent's numbers exactly; only the linear part's order of summation can differ.

The reader trusts nothing in a file: a version other than its own, an observation it does not know, an interval of zero, feature statistics that cannot normalise - a count that is not half the observation, a spread that is zero or not finite - or norm settings that cannot be - an epsilon that is not positive, a SimNorm group that does not divide its layer - are each refused by name. A file written before the layout last changed is not converted: its trainer writes it again.

PolicyFile.ObservationHeader
/// What a policy reads and how often it decides, after the `Header`. `feature_count` is the
/// width of SuperTrack's feature normaliser - half the observation, which is the goal then the state - and zero for
/// DReCon's observation.
pub const ObservationHeader = extern struct {
    /// `ObservationKind`, as its backing integer.
    kind: u32,
    decimation: u32,
    feature_count: u32,
    reserved: u32 = 0,
};

A SuperTrack learner's policy as a file. The learner acts from a host copy of its policy's weights, packed as the GPU kit packs them: the first layer reads the goal and the state as one input of twice the feature count, its weights a row per input with the goal's rows first, then its biases; then the second and third layers, each its weights then its biases. That is exactly a policy layer's layout, so each layer of the file is one consecutive slice of the packed weights:

  packed weights   | W1  (2F x H) | b1 (H) | W2 (H x H) | b2 (H) | W3 (H x A) | b3 (A) |
                     \________ layer 1 ________/ \______ layer 2 ______/ \______ layer 3 ______/
                         tanh, reads [goal | state]   tanh                     linear: the action

  F features, H hidden units, A actions - one per actuated degree of freedom

The feature statistics are copied into the policy, frozen, and the policy is marked to decide at every physics step with no limit and no filter - as the learner acts. Building the features has one definition, shared by the learner and by whatever plays its file: the character's state and the reference one frame ahead, each put in the root's frame (11.5), each normalised by the same statistics. Played from its file, the policy gives the kit's own policy output bit for bit on rows the kit gathered itself - the same weights, summed in the same order, through the same tanh - and on the learner's fleet it decides as the learner's copy does, to rounding, because that copy sums the goal's and the state's contributions interleaved rather than one after the other. A policy of zero weights is judged exactly as the servo alone.

Whatever plays a policy also holds every component of its action to a finite number: a non-finite component becomes zero, the servo alone on that joint. A policy with no limit has nothing else between its output and the physics, and a single NaN target would turn a body into NaNs that no failure rule ever catches, since every comparison with NaN is false.

policyOfSuperTrack
/// The policy of a SuperTrack learner (`robot_track_resident.PolicyParts`): its three layers - tanh, tanh and linear -
/// copied out of the packed weights acting uses, reading SuperTrack's features (the goal then the state, normalised by
/// a frozen copy of the learner's feature statistics), deciding at every physics step with no limit and no filter -
/// exactly as the learner acts on the fleet, whose action scale is `action_scale`.
///
/// The packed first layer is already a dense layer over `[goal | state]` in `PolicyLayer`'s layout: a row of weights
/// per input, the goal's inputs first, then its biases. So each layer is one slice of the packed weights, in order.
/// Memory: the policy's arrays are allocated with `gpa` and are the caller's - `deinit(gpa)` frees them, or, when
/// `gpa` is an arena, the arena does.
pub fn policyOfSuperTrack(
    gpa: Allocator,
    parts: resident.PolicyParts,
    action_scale: f32,
) !GenoPolicy {
    const observation_size: usize = 2 * parts.feature_count;
    const widths: []u32 = try gpa.alloc(u32, 4);
    errdefer gpa.free(widths);
    widths[0] = @intCast(observation_size);
    widths[1] = @intCast(parts.hidden_width);
    widths[2] = @intCast(parts.hidden_width);
    widths[3] = @intCast(parts.action_count);
    const layer_activations = [3]PolicyActivation{ .tanh, .tanh, .none };
    const layers: []PolicyLayer = try gpa.alloc(PolicyLayer, 3);
    var layers_made: usize = 0;
    errdefer {
        for (layers[0..layers_made]) |layer| {
            gpa.free(layer.weights_and_biases);
        }
        gpa.free(layers);
    }
    var layer_start: usize = 0;
    for (layers, 0..) |*layer, layer_index| {
        const input_count: usize = widths[layer_index];
        const output_count: usize = widths[layer_index + 1];
        const layer_activation: PolicyActivation = layer_activations[layer_index];
        const parameter_count: usize = PolicyLayer.parameterCount(layer_activation, input_count, output_count);
        const layer_parameters: []const f32 = parts.packed_weights[layer_start..][0..parameter_count];
        const weights_and_biases: []f32 = try gpa.dupe(f32, layer_parameters);
        layer.* = .{ .activation = layer_activations[layer_index], .weights_and_biases = weights_and_biases };
        layers_made += 1;
        layer_start += parameter_count;
    }
    const every_weight_used: bool = layer_start == parts.packed_weights.len;
    assertf(every_weight_used, @src(), "policyOfSuperTrack: the layers hold {d} of {d} packed weights", .{
        layer_start,
        parts.packed_weights.len,
    });
    // The statistics copied, so that the learner's later normaliser - a resumed run measures its own - cannot move
    // the policy's.
    const frozen_means: []f32 = try gpa.dupe(f32, parts.normalizer.mean);
    errdefer gpa.free(frozen_means);
    const frozen_spreads: []f32 = try gpa.dupe(f32, parts.normalizer.spread);
    const no_limit: f32 = inf(f32);
    const every_action_unfiltered: f32 = 1.0;
    const every_physics_step: u32 = 1;
    const policy: GenoPolicy = .{
        .widths = widths,
        .layers = layers,
        .normalization = null,
        .action_limit = no_limit,
        .action_scale = action_scale,
        .filter_beta = every_action_unfiltered,
        .observation = .{ .supertrack_features = .{ .mean = frozen_means, .spread = frozen_spreads } },
        .decimation = every_physics_step,
    };
    return policy;
}
supertrackFeaturesInto
/// SuperTrack's two feature vectors for character `character` of `fleet`, normalised by `normalizer`: the STATE - the
/// character's simulated bodies in its root's frame (`robot_track.local`) - into `out_state`, and the GOAL - the
/// reference one frame ahead of the character's frame, in the same root's frame - into `out_goal`. The goal is where
/// the servo aims next, so the policy sees both where the character is and where it is meant to be a step from now,
/// each in the character's own frame of reference. Each feature becomes `(x - mean) / spread`.
///
/// One definition for every place a SuperTrack policy acts: the learner while it collects and is judged
/// (`Resident.featuresOf`), and the lab's player of its policy file (`robot_lab.PolicyDecider`). `scratch` holds the
/// intermediate states and is the caller's; nothing is allocated.
pub fn supertrackFeaturesInto(
    fleet: *track.Fleet,
    character: usize,
    normalizer: latent.Normalizer,
    scratch: FeatureScratch,
    out_goal: []f32,
    out_state: []f32,
) void {
    track.stateOf(fleet.m, &fleet.data[character], scratch.simulated);
    track.local(scratch.simulated.*, fleet.root, scratch.raw_features);
    normalizer.toNormal(scratch.raw_features, out_state);
    const clip: *const dance.Clip = fleet.clips[fleet.clip_of[character]];
    const next_frame: u32 = fleet.frame[character] + 1;
    fleet.referenceStateInto(clip, next_frame, scratch.probe, scratch.reference);
    track.local(scratch.reference.*, fleet.root, scratch.raw_features);
    normalizer.toNormal(scratch.raw_features, out_goal);
}
PolicyDecider.observeFeatures
/// SuperTrack's features of `character`, into `observation`: the goal in its first half, the state in its second
/// - the order the policy's first layer reads them in - through the learner's own definition
/// (`robot_track_resident.supertrackFeaturesInto`).
fn observeFeatures(
    decider: *PolicyDecider,
    feature_normalizer: latent.Normalizer,
    fleet: *robot_track.Fleet,
    character: usize,
) void {
    const feature_count: usize = decider.raw_features.len;
    const goal_half: []f32 = decider.observation[0..feature_count];
    const state_half: []f32 = decider.observation[feature_count..][0..feature_count];
    const feature_scratch: resident.FeatureScratch = .{
        .simulated = &decider.simulated_state,
        .reference = &decider.reference_state,
        .probe = &decider.reference_probe,
        .raw_features = decider.raw_features,
    };
    resident.supertrackFeaturesInto(fleet, character, feature_normalizer, feature_scratch, goal_half, state_half);
}

EfficientTDMPC acts by planning, but its policy network is what the planner taught it, and it is that network which becomes the policy file - the show and the judge then run it without planning. The network has two parts: the encoder, which turns DReCon's observation into the latent state, and the policy, whose head gives a raw centre and a raw spread for every action dimension. The mean action is tanh of the centre, so the file keeps the head's first half - the centres' weights and biases - and drops the spreads':

   DReCon's observation (raw)
     -> normed Mish (256)                                    the encoder
     -> normed SimNorm (latent, groups of 8)
     -> normed Mish -> normed Mish                           the policy's hidden layers
     -> linear: centres | spreads   ->   keep the centres    the head, halved
     -> tanh                                                 the mean action, inside (-1, 1)

The observation goes in as it is: the encoder's first normed layer normalises its own pre-activations, so no normaliser stands in front of it. The rest of the controller is the learner's - its decision interval, its filter, its action scale - and the file's action limit is 1, since tanh never leaves (-1, 1). Played from its file, the policy gives the agent's own mean actions to within single-precision rounding.

policyOfTdmpc
/// The policy an EfficientTDMPC agent deploys (`TdmpcAgent.Networks`), as a `GenoPolicy`. The agent acts by
/// planning; its policy network is what the planner taught, and what the show and the judge run without planning:
///
///     DReCon's observation, as it is - no normaliser in front of the encoder: its first layer's norm stands in for one
///     encoder: normed Mish layers, then a normed SimNorm layer - the latent state
///     policy:  normed Mish layers, then its HEAD - a plain linear layer of 2 x A outputs
///     the mean: tanh of the head's first A outputs
///
/// The head gives a raw centre and a raw spread for each of the A action dimensions (`zimrrl.TanhMeanGaussian`); the
/// mean action is tanh of the centre, so the file keeps the head's first A columns of weights and their biases and
/// drops the spread's - a last layer of A outputs through tanh. Everything else is the learner's controller: DReCon's
/// observation, its decision interval and filter, its action scale; the limit is 1, which tanh never reaches.
/// Memory: the policy's arrays from `gpa`, the caller's (`GenoPolicy.deinit`).
pub fn policyOfTdmpc(
    gpa: Allocator,
    networks: *const TdmpcAgent.Networks,
    learner: TdmpcLearner,
) !GenoPolicy {
    const encoder: zn.Mlp(f32) = networks.encoder;
    const policy_network: zn.Mlp(f32) = networks.policy;
    const encoder_last: zn.NormedDense(f32) = switch (encoder.last) {
        .normed => |normed| normed,
        .plain => {
            assertUnreachable(@src(), "policyOfTdmpc: an encoder without its SimNorm layer", .{});
            return error.PolicyActivationUnknown;
        },
    };
    const head: zn.Dense(f32) = switch (policy_network.last) {
        .plain => |plain| plain,
        .normed => {
            assertUnreachable(@src(), "policyOfTdmpc: a policy whose head is normed", .{});
            return error.PolicyActivationUnknown;
        },
    };
    const head_input_count: usize = head.weight.shape[0];
    const head_output_count: usize = head.weight.shape[1];
    const action_count: usize = head_output_count / 2;
    // The head gives two numbers per action dimension - the centres, then the spreads - so its width is even.
    assertf(head_output_count == 2 * action_count, @src(), "policyOfTdmpc: a head of {d} outputs", .{
        head_output_count,
    });
    // The layers in order: the encoder's hidden ones, its SimNorm layer, the policy's hidden ones, the mean.
    const layer_count: usize = encoder.hidden.len + 1 + policy_network.hidden.len + 1;
    const layers: []PolicyLayer = try gpa.alloc(PolicyLayer, layer_count);
    var layers_made: usize = 0;
    errdefer {
        for (layers[0..layers_made]) |layer| {
            gpa.free(layer.weights_and_biases);
        }
        gpa.free(layers);
    }
    const widths: []u32 = try gpa.alloc(u32, layer_count + 1);
    errdefer gpa.free(widths);
    widths[0] = @intCast(encoder.spec.input);
    const normed_layers_in_order = [_][]const zn.NormedDense(f32){
        encoder.hidden,
        &.{encoder_last},
        policy_network.hidden,
    };
    for (normed_layers_in_order) |normed_layers| {
        for (normed_layers) |normed| {
            layers[layers_made] = try normedPolicyLayer(gpa, normed);
            widths[layers_made + 1] = @intCast(normed.dense.weight.shape[1]);
            layers_made += 1;
        }
    }
    // The mean: the head's first A columns - row i of its weight keeps entries 0 .. A - and their biases, through tanh.
    const mean_values: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, PolicyLayer.parameterCount(.tanh, head_input_count, action_count));
    for (0..head_input_count) |input_index| {
        const head_row: []const f32 = head.weight.data[input_index * head_output_count ..][0..action_count];
        @memcpy(mean_values[input_index * action_count ..][0..action_count], head_row);
    }
    const mean_biases_start: usize = head_input_count * action_count;
    @memcpy(mean_values[mean_biases_start..][0..action_count], head.bias.data[0..action_count]);
    layers[layers_made] = .{ .activation = .tanh, .weights_and_biases = mean_values };
    widths[layers_made + 1] = @intCast(action_count);
    layers_made += 1;
    const policy: GenoPolicy = .{
        .widths = widths,
        .layers = layers,
        .normalization = null,
        .action_limit = 1.0,
        .action_scale = learner.action_scale,
        .filter_beta = learner.beta,
        .observation = .drecon,
        .decimation = learner.decimation,
    };
    return policy;
}

A policy applies one pipeline, from what a character senses to the targets its joints are driven to:

   observation -> normalise -> layer 1 -> layer 2 -> layer 3 -> clamp -> scale -> filter -> joint targets
                  per input    tanh       tanh       linear     to +-1   rad per  beta 0.2
                                                                         unit

   observation   the task's own units: angles, heights, velocities
   normalise     each input: its mean taken away, divided by its deviation, clamped to 5 deviations
   layers        each output its bias plus its weighted inputs, through the layer's activation
   clamp         the mean action held to the controller's range
   scale         radians of joint offset per unit of action
   filter        each decision, a joint's target moves a share beta of the way to the new action

Normalising works input by input. Suppose the learner saw a joint's velocity average 0.3 rad/s, with a deviation of 0.5. A reading of 1.8 is (1.8 - 0.3) / 0.5 = 3 deviations above the mean, and the network receives 3. A reading of 3.3 would be 6 deviations, beyond the clamp of 5, and the network receives 5: a rare extreme reading cannot push the network far from anything it saw while learning. Velocities in radians per second, heights in metres and angles in radians all become numbers of about the same size, which is what lets one network learn from all of them at once. The layers keep the GPU kit's layout and its order of arithmetic - each output's bias first, then its inputs in order - because floating-point addition is not associative: summed in another order, the same weights give slightly different numbers, and a policy played here would no longer act exactly as it acted while it trained.

policyMeanAction
/// The action `policy` takes for `observation`, written into `action` (`GenoPolicy`): the observation normalised by
/// the frozen normaliser, passed through the layers - `scratch` holding each layer's input and output - and the last
/// layer's outputs clamped to the controller's range. No randomness: the policy's mean action, as the show and the
/// judge act.
pub fn policyMeanAction(
    policy: *const GenoPolicy,
    observation: []const f32,
    scratch: PolicyScratch,
    action: []f32,
) void {
    const observation_size: usize = policy.observationSize();
    const action_size: usize = policy.actionSize();
    const widest_layer: usize = policy.widestLayer();
    const observation_fits: bool = observation.len == observation_size;
    assertf(observation_fits, @src(), "policyMeanAction: an observation of {d}, the policy takes {d}", .{
        observation.len,
        observation_size,
    });
    assertf(action.len == action_size, @src(), "policyMeanAction: an action of {d}, the policy gives {d}", .{
        action.len,
        action_size,
    });
    const scratch_fits: bool = scratch.ping.len >= widest_layer and scratch.pong.len >= widest_layer;
    assertf(scratch_fits, @src(), "policyMeanAction: scratch of {d} and {d}, the widest layer {d}", .{
        scratch.ping.len,
        scratch.pong.len,
        widest_layer,
    });
    // The observation copied into the ping buffer, and normalised there by the frozen normaliser - the function that
    // normalised every observation the policy trained on.
    const normalized_observation: []f32 = scratch.ping[0..observation_size];
    @memcpy(normalized_observation, observation);
    if (policy.normalization) |normalization| {
        normalization.applyInPlaceF32(normalized_observation) catch {
            assertUnreachable(@src(), "policyMeanAction: a normaliser of another size than the observation", .{});
        };
    }
    // The layers, ping-pong: each reads the buffer the one before it wrote. The last writes straight into `action`.
    var layer_input: []const f32 = normalized_observation;
    var input_is_in_ping: bool = true;
    for (policy.layers, 0..) |layer, layer_index| {
        const is_last_layer: bool = layer_index + 1 == policy.layers.len;
        const output_count: usize = policy.widths[layer_index + 1];
        const other_buffer: []f32 = if (input_is_in_ping) scratch.pong else scratch.ping;
        const layer_output: []f32 = if (is_last_layer) action else other_buffer[0..output_count];
        applyPolicyLayer(layer, layer_input, layer_output);
        layer_input = layer_output;
        input_is_in_ping = !input_is_in_ping;
    }
    // The mean action, held to the controller's range - and never a non-finite number into the physics: a NaN target
    // makes NaN bodies, which no failure rule ever catches (every comparison with NaN is false). A non-finite component
    // becomes zero, the servo alone on that joint, as the SuperTrack learner does with its own actions. A policy with
    // no limit (SuperTrack's, an infinite `action_limit`) is held by nothing else.
    for (action) |*component| {
        const finite_component: f32 = if (isFinite(component.*)) component.* else 0.0;
        component.* = clamp(finite_component, -policy.action_limit, policy.action_limit);
    }
}

A program that plays a policy needs nothing else. A policy show puts characters on a fleet of their own and steps them one physics step at a time, so that a viewer can draw every step. A decision lasts two physics steps - DReCon's k = 2, decisions at 30 Hz over 60 Hz physics: at its first step every character observes and the policy gives its mean action, and through both steps the controller blends that action into the joints' targets. A character whose episode ends starts another at once.

The show is also the instrument the judge is built on, and it counts the way survival analysis does. Its exposure is the time at risk: a unit per character per physics step watched, whatever happens, on one clock that runs through every episode. A failure is an event on that clock: a step at which a character lost the reference. Exposure divided by failures is the mean time to failure, in physics steps - the number this section began with. Counting this way needs no choice of where episodes begin or how long they last, and a policy that never fails simply has a time to failure longer than the show. Shown this way, a PPO policy lives exactly what PPO's own show lives, action for action and failure for failure, so the lab watches every learner's run in one way.

The same decision serves the judge. The judge runs a policy from fixed starts spread across the clip - the same starts every time, each run until the reference is lost or the clip ends, with nothing random - and counts as the show counts, so that two runs judged differently differ in their policies, not in where their starts happened to fall. A policy file is judged through an actor that decides and filters exactly as the show does, so a run is judged as it is watched; the servo alone, judged on the same starts, is the baseline every policy is measured against.

A judgement also says how sure it is. Its mean time to failure is a ratio - the steps watched over the failures, both summed over the starts - and its standard error says how far that ratio would move were the policy judged on other starts of the same kind; the delta method gives it from the spread of what each start adds beyond the ratio. Two runs whose times to failure differ by less than about twice their errors cannot be told apart, and a policy that never fails on the judge's starts has a time to failure longer than the clip, with no error to give. The trainer judges its newest policy every few minutes of training, and keeps the judgements in judge.csv beside the servo's: the raw sums of each, so that every measure and its error can be worked out from the file again.

PolicyShow.step
/// One physics step (this section's head): at the first step of a decision every character observes and the
/// policy decides; then the filtered actions step the fleet, and the show counts what the step lived.
pub fn step(show: *PolicyShow, policy: *const GenoPolicy) void {
    const fleet: *robot_track.Fleet = show.fleet;
    const decides_now: bool = show.physics_steps_until_decision == 0;
    if (decides_now) {
        show.decider.decide(policy, &show.controller, fleet, show.character_count, show.actions);
        show.physics_steps_until_decision = @max(show.decimation, 1);
    }
    // One physics step under the filtered actions.
    const filtered_actions: []const f32 = show.controller.apply(show.actions);
    _ = fleet.step(filtered_actions);
    show.physics_steps_until_decision -= 1;
    // What the step lived: a unit of exposure per character, and its failures. A character whose episode ended
    // starts the next one fresh: its controller forgets the action it was applying.
    for (0..show.character_count) |character| {
        show.exposure_steps += 1;
        if (fleet.failures[character]) {
            show.failure_count += 1;
        }
        if (fleet.dones[character]) {
            show.controller.forget(character);
        }
    }
}

The parameters, in run.zon, say three things: the task every learner shares - the motion, with Geno's failure rule, physics and servo - the learner with its recipe, and the run's own controls: when it saves, keeps checkpoints and judges itself, and when it stops. The task is held apart from the learners because two runs compare only when both learned the same task. How often a learner decides, how it smooths its actions and how far an action reaches belong to the learner: they are a controller's design, and the judge compares controllers on the task they share. PPO decides every second physics step through DReCon's filter; SuperTrack acts at every step, unfiltered. Every field has a default, so a file names only what it changes - .{ .learner = .{ .ppo = .{ .envs = 64 } }, .controls = .{ .stop_after_hours = 10 } } is a whole run - and a folder without one gets one written with every default, so that each folder says what it trains and by which learner. A value the training cannot work with - no characters, a minibatch larger than the batch, a filter weight outside (0, 1] - refuses the run before anything starts, naming the field by its path and its range, as learner.ppo.minibatch or learner.ppo.beta. Every file is written whole to a new file and renamed over the old one: a reader never sees half a file, and a run stopped mid-write keeps the previous version. The weights are saved once the GPU's copy of them has caught up with the last update, so that the parameters in the file and the counters beside them - Adam's step, the batches, the normaliser's statistics - are of the same moment, and a run carried on from the file continues exactly. Started again on the same folder, the trainer carries on from the folder's weights and log, with the assist where its schedule has it after the batches already trained. Weights that do not fit the run's network - run.zon asking for a wider one, say - are refused, and the folder is left as it was. The servo alone is measured first, with the assist off, so its number is the servo's own.

train
/// Trains until the folder's `stop` file appears or the run's limits are reached, saving as it goes; the state it
/// ended in.
fn train(
    gpa: Allocator,
    io: Io,
    report_interval_ms: f64,
    arena_state: *ArenaAllocator,
    folder: []const u8,
    parameters: lab.PpoRun,
    trainer: *Trainer,
    progress: *RunProgress,
) !RunState {
    const decisions_per_collect: u32 = 64;
    const save_minutes: f32 = parameters.save_minutes;
    const checkpoint_minutes: f32 = parameters.checkpoint_minutes;
    const judge_minutes: f32 = parameters.judge_minutes;
    while (true) {
        // Paths and texts of one batch's files are made in the arena, emptied every batch.
        _ = arena_state.reset(.retain_capacity);
        const arena: Allocator = arena_state.allocator();
        if (try endState(arena, io, folder, parameters, trainer, progress)) |end_state| {
            return end_state;
        }
        if (!trainer.collect(decisions_per_collect)) {
            continue;
        }
        const stats: ppo_track.Stats = trainer.learn();
        progress.last_stats = stats;
        progress.recent.add(stats);
        const minutes_trained: f32 = trainingMinutes(progress);
        try RunLog.appendLine(gpa, &progress.log, trainer.iterations, minutes_trained, stats);
        const minutes: f32 = trainingMinutes(progress);
        const minutes_since_save: f32 = minutes - progress.saved_at_minutes;
        const is_save_due: bool = !progress.has_saved_this_start or minutes_since_save >= save_minutes;
        if (is_save_due) {
            try saveAll(arena, io, folder, trainer, progress, .training);
        }
        if (progress.has_saved_this_start and !progress.has_checked_policy_this_start) {
            if (!try policyPlaysAsTrained(arena, io, folder, trainer)) {
                say(io, "the policy file does not play as the trainer acts - the run fails\n", .{});
                return error.PolicyDoesNotPlayAsTrained;
            }
            progress.has_checked_policy_this_start = true;
        }
        const minutes_since_checkpoint: f32 = minutes - progress.checkpointed_at_minutes;
        const is_checkpoint_due: bool = checkpoint_minutes > 0 and minutes_since_checkpoint >= checkpoint_minutes;
        if (is_checkpoint_due) {
            try saveCheckpoint(arena, io, folder, trainer, progress);
        }
        const minutes_since_judgement: f32 = minutes - progress.judged_at_minutes;
        const is_judgement_due: bool = judge_minutes > 0 and minutes_since_judgement >= judge_minutes;
        if (is_judgement_due) {
            try judgeNewestPolicy(gpa, arena, io, folder, trainer, progress);
        }
        reportProgress(io, report_interval_ms, folder, trainer, progress, stats);
    }
}

What a run has learned is watched in the training lab, examples/geno_lab. It lists the run folders in runs, beside its own executable; a run chosen there is loaded - its run.zon, for the task, then its policy file - and shown by a policy show: Geno on the floor following the dance, with the reference beside him, while the camera follows him around the room. No learner is loaded to watch a run: the lab needs the policy alone, so it watches every learner's runs the same way. While the trainer runs, reload policy puts the folder's newest policy in place of the one shown, and Geno goes on dancing, now by the newer policy.

Beside each run's name the lab shows its learner, its state, how far it has trained in its learner's own unit - PPO's batches, SuperTrack's rounds - and its latest time to failure, as its status.zon says, and under them the newest judgement with its standard error, beside the servo judged on the same starts, as its judge.csv says. The two times are different numbers on purpose: the first is training's own, measured on training's characters - early on held up by the root assist, which keeps them from falling - and the second is the judge's, with no help and on fixed starts, the one to compare runs by; under the list, every run's learning curve on one plot, read from its log every few seconds. Each curve is the time to failure over its learner's window of recent lines - eight of PPO's batches, 128 of SuperTrack's rounds, each about two minutes of character-time - against minutes of training, on a logarithmic scale from 1 s to 60 s - so that going from the servo's two seconds to twenty takes the same room as going from six to a minute. A window in which nothing failed is drawn at the top, and each run's servo, measured alone before its training, is a dashed line of its colour:

   60s |            ________________________     a run whose characters stopped failing - drawn at the top
       |           /                        \
   20s |      /\/\/                          \   the assist fading: failures come back
       |     /
    5s |    /
       | - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -   the servo alone, measured before training
    1s +-------------------------------------
       0 min                              2 min

A click on a curve shows the run at that point: the policy checkpoint nearest the clicked minute, kept by the trainer as policy_m and the minute, or the newest policy for a curve's last point - so that a policy from before a run went wrong can be watched beside what it became. A run whose status says it trains, but whose status was written longer ago than three of its save intervals, is shown as silent: its trainer died, or its machine slept, without a word. Each status carries the wall-clock time it was written, so a lab started long after can tell at once.

start new training opens a form for a new run: its folder's name, then the learner - PPO, SuperTrack or EfficientTDMPC, each with a line on what it is - then that learner's own settings, the task and the run's controls. The folder's name is made from the learner and the motion - supertrack-dance-1, ppo-dance-2 - so that runs of different learners in one list say which is which. Choosing a learner starts its settings from that learner's defaults; a form opened while a run is shown starts from that run, whichever learner it trained. What would stop the run is said under the form before it starts - a name already taken, a setting out of its range, named by its path, or a learner the trainer does not train yet - and start writes the run's run.zon and starts the trainer on its folder.

A run's log is read from where the last read stopped: only whole lines, so that a line the trainer is still writing waits for the next read; a log shorter than before - a run carried on from an earlier save - is read again from its start.

The physics keeps the step the policy was trained on, 1/60 s, and each frame advances it by whole steps: the frame's duration in steps, rounded down unless within a quarter of the next whole step, so one step a frame at 60 frames a second and two at 30. Nothing is carried from one frame to the next, so the motion stays even; a device that cannot keep up shows the dance in slight slow motion rather than in jumps.

   frames a second    steps in a frame    + a quarter    steps taken    the dance's speed
        60               1.00                1.25           1             real time
        50               1.20                1.45           1             0.83
        40               1.50                1.75           1             0.67
        30               2.00                2.25           2             real time

A shown policy acts as a judged one does: each decision the policy's mean action, without exploration, through DReCon's filter, on a fleet of its own. Judging (evaluate) lives many decisions in one call and returns only what they came to; a show lives them one physics step at a time, from frame to frame, so that every step can be drawn. On the judge's starting frames, with as many characters, the two live the same steps and lose the reference at the same ones.

   startShow    a fleet of its own, DReCon's filter, the actions        (seeded: where the characters start)
   stepShow     a decision due?  observe, normalise, the mean action, clamp
                then the filter, one physics step, and what was lived: steps watched, failures
   endShow      the fleet, the filter and the actions released
stepShow
/// One physics step of the show: when a decision is due, every character observed and the policy's mean
/// action taken (clamped to the action's range, as `evaluate` does); then DReCon's filter, the step, and the
/// count of what was lived.
pub fn stepShow(self: *Self, show: *Show) void {
    const dofs: usize = self.env.subset.dofs;
    const fleet: *track.Fleet = show.fleet;
    const steps_per_decision: u32 = @max(self.options.decimation, 1);
    if (show.held_steps_left == 0) {
        for (0..show.characters) |character| {
            const first_component: usize = character * dofs;
            const action: []f32 = show.actions[first_component..][0..dofs];
            const clip: *const dance.Clip = fleet.clips[fleet.clip_of[character]];
            const previous_action: []const f32 = show.controller.lastAction(character);
            track.stateOf(self.m, &fleet.data[character], &self.env.sim_state);
            policy.observeFrom(
                self.m,
                self.env.subset,
                fleet,
                clip,
                fleet.frame[character],
                self.env.sim_state,
                &self.env.views,
                previous_action,
                self.obs_scratch,
            );
            self.normalizeObservations(self.obs_scratch, false);
            self.ppo.actMean(self.obs_scratch, action);
            const limit: f32 = self.env.options.action_limit;
            for (action) |*component| {
                component.* = clamp(component.*, -limit, limit);
            }
        }
        show.held_steps_left = steps_per_decision;
    }
    const filtered_actions: []const f32 = show.controller.apply(show.actions);
    _ = show.fleet.step(filtered_actions);
    show.held_steps_left -= 1;
    for (0..show.characters) |character| {
        show.exposure += 1;
        if (show.fleet.failures[character]) {
            show.failures += 1;
        }
        if (show.fleet.dones[character]) {
            show.controller.forget(character);
        }
    }
}

10.8 Examples#

The humanoid gym, and one iteration of PPO on it:

test "tutorial 10a: the humanoid gym, and one iteration of PPO" {
    const options = @import("build_options");
    const slow: bool = comptime @hasDecl(options, "slow_tests") and options.slow_tests;
    if (!slow) {
        return error.SkipZigTest;
    }
    const gpa: Allocator = testing_allocator;
    const env: *gym.HumanoidEnv = try .init(gpa, flex2_xml, .{});
    defer env.deinit();
    const observation: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, env.observationSize());
    defer gpa.free(observation);
    const action: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, env.actionSize());
    defer gpa.free(action);

    // An episode starts near the reference pose. An action offsets the pose the joints are servoed
    // toward; the reward pays for staying up and moving forward.
    try env.reset(1, observation);
    @memset(action, 0.0);
    const result: gym.StepResult = try env.step(action, observation);
    try expect(!result.terminated and result.reward > 0.0);

    // PPO: fill a rollout with the current policy, then update on it one minibatch at a time -
    // the unit a frame can afford.
    const trainer: *gym.PpoTrainer = try .init(gpa, env, .{ .horizon = 256, .minibatch = 64, .epochs = 2 });
    defer trainer.deinit();
    while (!trainer.rolloutFull()) {
        _ = try trainer.collect(64);
    }
    while (!try trainer.updateSlice()) {}
    try expect(trainer.last.samples == 256);
}

SAC's loop, on the cartpole:

test "tutorial 10b: SAC - act, remember, update" {
    const options = @import("build_options");
    const slow: bool = comptime @hasDecl(options, "slow_tests") and options.slow_tests;
    if (!slow) {
        return error.SkipZigTest;
    }
    const gpa: Allocator = testing_allocator;
    const agent: *gym.SacAgent = try .init(gpa, zrl.cartpole_state_dim, zrl.cartpole_action_dim, .{
        .warmup = 64,
        .batch = 32,
    });
    defer agent.deinit();
    var obs: [4]f32 = undefined;
    var next_obs: [4]f32 = undefined;
    var action: [1]f32 = undefined;
    var episode: u32 = 0;
    var state = zrl.cartpoleTaskReset(f32, zn.Rng.init(1), episode, .hold);
    try zrl.cartpoleObserve(f32, state, &obs);
    const alpha_before: f64 = agent.temperature.alpha();

    // Every step: act with the stochastic policy, remember the transition, update from the replay.
    for (0..400) |_| {
        agent.act(&obs, &action, false);
        const stepped = zrl.cartpoleTaskStep(f32, state, 10.0 * action[0], .hold);
        try zrl.cartpoleObserve(f32, stepped.state, &next_obs);
        try agent.remember(&obs, &action, stepped.reward, &next_obs, stepped.failed);
        try agent.update();
        state = stepped.state;
        obs = next_obs;
        if (stepped.failed) {
            episode += 1;
            state = zrl.cartpoleTaskReset(f32, zn.Rng.init(1), episode, .hold);
            try zrl.cartpoleObserve(f32, state, &obs);
        }
    }
    // The squashed actions stay in [-1, 1]; after the warmup every step updated; and the
    // temperature has moved toward the entropy it targets.
    try expect(@abs(action[0]) <= 1.0);
    try expect(agent.updates == 400 - 64 + 1);
    try expect(agent.temperature.alpha() != alpha_before);
}

11. SuperTrack: a world model and a policy through it#

Reinforcement learning discovers what works by trying things and scoring them. SuperTrack takes a different route, and a much more direct one: learn a model of the simulator, then train the policy by differentiating through that model. In its original form there is no reward, no critic and no exploration bonus — only two supervised problems. This chapter builds that core first and then extends it, keeping the core exactly as it is; the first section shows the whole system the extensions make.

11.1 The system at a glance#

SuperTrack's policy tracks a clip precisely, but it has one answer for every situation and sees only a short window ahead. After a hard push a character may have several good ways back - a step to the left, a step to the right - and the right one may only show its worth well past the window. The system built here keeps SuperTrack's policy unchanged and adds four things around it: a critic that values what lies past the window, a failure barrier in the cost, a planner that searches ahead for characters in danger, and a flow that learns to correct the policy with one of several answers. One world model, one cost and one critic serve all of them.

Choosing an action. Every character, at every step, starts from the policy's action and adds a correction to it - the flow's, or, for a character in danger whose plan has arrived, the plan's:

A correction is a small change to what the policy would do. The flow draws it from noise, and different noises give different corrections, so the flow can hold several ways back from the same situation where the policy, with one answer, would average them. A plan is a sequence of such corrections, found by searching ahead in the world model; it is applied to the policy's reaction to the state the character is actually in, so it stays meaningful even when the character drifts from where the plan expected it to be.

Learning. All of it learns from one stream of experience and one world model:

The policy learns exactly as SuperTrack's does: windows from the replay are rolled through the world model and the distance from the clip is differentiated back into the policy, now with the critic's value added at the window's end so that what happens after the window counts too. The flow learns from two teachers at once: the same rollouts give it the cost's gradient at each of its corrections, and the planner's corrections, from the steps characters took from their plans, give it examples to imitate - by flow matching, which keeps different ways back apart instead of averaging them. The planner scores its candidates with the same world model, the same cost and the same critic the policy learns from, so a plan it prefers is one the policy would prefer if it could see as far.

How it differs. Each of the methods it draws on solves part of the problem:

The policy learns fromA world model is used forPlanningSeveral ways backFalling
DReConrewards, by PPO--no: one Gaussianends the episode
SuperTrackthe world model's gradient over a short windowtraining the policy-noends the episode; the loss sees only the window
TD-MPC2a value learned from rewardsplanning and learning, in a latent spaceat every step, over sequences of actionsin the search, not the policythrough the value
diffusion and flow policies (DPPO, FPO)rewards, by policy gradients adapted to them--yesends the episode
this systemSuperTrack's gradient with a critic past the window; the flow also from the planner and from real returnstraining the policy and the flow, and planningfor characters in danger, over corrections around the policyyes: the flow's correctiona barrier in the cost and a pessimistic critic

Six choices set this system apart from each of them.

The tracker is kept. Everything added is a correction on top of SuperTrack's policy, which is trained exactly as before. A flow at rest with no noise adds nothing, and the rollout is then SuperTrack's own, number for number - so the extensions can only add to what tracking already does.

Plans are corrections around the policy. TD-MPC2's planner searches sequences of actions. Here a candidate is a sequence of corrections, and its rollout is the policy reacting to every state the model reaches, with the correction added. The search starts where the policy already is - the plan of zeros - and a plan joined late still applies to the state the character is actually in.

Planning only where it matters. Most of the time tracking needs no search. The planner runs for a few characters at once, those whose hazard - how far they are toward a fall - is high or rising, and stops when they have been calm for a while.

Several ways back. The policy has one answer per situation. The flow's correction comes from noise, so it can learn several and keep them apart. It learns them from three teachers whose mistakes are different: the model's gradient, the planner's corrections, and what really happened when it acted - the one no error of the world model can fool.

Falling has a price. SuperTrack's loss only sees the window, so a fall just past it costs nothing. Here the cost rises steeply near a fall - the failure barrier - and the critic's pessimistic estimate of the cost after the window is part of every rollout and every plan.

One model, one cost, one critic. The policy, the flow and the planner all judge a future the same way. What the planner prefers, the policy would prefer too if it could see as far; what the flow learns from the planner is what the policy's own objective asks for.

11.2 The idea#

The simulator is not differentiable, so a policy's effect on the future cannot be traced back to its weights through it. A neural network can be. Train one — the world model — to predict what the simulator does next from a state and an action. Then unroll the policy and the world model together for a window of frames, measure how far the predicted motion is from the target, and backpropagate that distance through every predicted frame into the policy's weights. The world model stands in for the simulator only in the backward pass: the policy still acts in the real simulator, and every transition it produces is data for the world model.

The world model predicts accelerations, not next states. Its output, scaled by acc_scale, is integrated into the next state on the tape, semi-implicitly — velocity first, then position — exactly as the simulator steps. That keeps the network's job small and smooth, and makes long predictions stable. It is trained on windows of real frames by rolling out its own predictions across the window and matching the real frames: a model trained on single steps is accurate for one step and drifts over many, and the policy's training depends on many.

The policy is trained by unrolling it through the world model over a longer window. Each frame, it chooses an action from the predicted state, the world model predicts the next state, and the loss accumulates the distance from the target — for the cartpole, upright — plus a small charge for the action. One backward pass through the whole window gives the policy's gradient. Because the gradient knows how the dynamics respond to the action, it points straight at a better policy, where RL has to estimate that direction from many noisy tries.

11.3 Data: rings and segments#

Training windows must be real stretches of motion. Each environment records into its own ring, so a window never stitches together two different cartpoles; and every push and every reset starts a new segment, so a window never spans a discontinuity the world model could not have predicted. Pushes are part of the training: a policy only learns to recover from what it has seen.

State4
/// A cartpole state: cart position, cart rate, pole angle (0 = upright), pole rate.
pub const State4 = [4]f32;
acc_scale
/// The world model's outputs are the two accelerations DIVIDED by this: the graph's one-hot pick
/// columns and the kit's `acc_scale` both multiply it back, so the two stay one model.
pub const acc_scale: f32 = 10.0;
fromCartpole
pub fn fromCartpole(s: zrl.CartpoleState(f32)) State4 {
    return .{ s.cart, s.cart_rate, s.pole_rad, s.pole_rate_rad };
}
Options
pub const Options = struct {
    hidden: usize = 32,
    batch: usize = 32,
    /// The paper's windows: 8 for the world model, 32 for the policy.
    wm_window: usize = 8,
    policy_window: usize = 32,
    wm_rate: f64 = 1.0e-3,
    policy_rate: f64 = 1.0e-3,
    /// Exploration noise on the policy's pre-squash output (the paper's sigma).
    sigma: f32 = 0.1,
    /// The tracking weights on (cart, cart rate, pole angle, pole rate), and the action penalty.
    w_cart: f32 = 1.0,
    w_cart_rate: f32 = 0.1,
    w_pole: f32 = 10.0,
    w_pole_rate: f32 = 0.1,
    w_action: f32 = 0.01,
    capacity: usize = 50_000,
    /// The simulator's step (s) - the world model integrates with it, semi-implicitly, as the
    /// simulator does - and the force limit (N): the policy's output goes through tanh, times it.
    /// zimrnum's cartpole: 0.02 s and 10 N; the page's robot.zig cartpole: 0.01 s and 6 N.
    dt: f32 = 0.02,
    max_force: f32 = 10.0,
    /// The gym's parallel cartpoles: each gets its OWN ring, so a window is one cartpole's
    /// consecutive frames.
    envs: usize = 8,
    seed: u64 = 1,
};
SuperTrack
pub const SuperTrack = struct {
    arena_state: ArenaAllocator,
    gpa: Allocator,
    options: Options,
    policy: Net,
    world: Net,
    /// `envs` rings of `per_env` records each, back to back.
    ///
    /// * ONE SHARED RING WAS THE FIRST VERSION'S BUG: the cartpoles take turns recording, so
    /// consecutive records were different cartpoles - a world-model "window" was nine states of
    /// nine cartpoles (its end check passed because record +8 is the same one a tick later), and
    /// a policy start's 1-step window never matched a segment, so the policy never trained.
    records: []Record,
    per_env: usize,
    heads: []usize,
    lens: []usize,
    rng: Random.DefaultPrng,
    // -- The world model's graph: a window of real states and forces, rolled out. --
    wm_graph: Graph,
    wm_states: [][4]Var,
    wm_forces: []Var,
    wm_loss: Var,
    wm_vars: [6]Var,
    wm_adam: gym.AdamSet,
    // -- The policy's graph: a start state and noise, rolled out through the world model. --
    pi_graph: Graph,
    pi_start: Columns,
    pi_noise: []Var,
    pi_loss: Var,
    pi_vars: [6]Var,
    pi_adam: gym.AdamSet,
    /// A drawn batch, for `trainWorldWith` / `trainPolicyWith` (which a check calls with its own).
    stage_states: []f32,
    stage_forces: []f32,
    stage_starts: []f32,
    stage_noise: []f32,
    // acting scratch
    t1: []f32,
    t2: []f32,
    out: [1]f32 = .{0},

    pub fn init(gpa: Allocator, options: Options) !*SuperTrack {
        const st: *SuperTrack = try gpa.create(SuperTrack);
        errdefer gpa.destroy(st);
        // whole-init-first: the whole struct first - defaults applied, every field named.
        st.* = .{
            .arena_state = undefined,
            .gpa = undefined,
            .options = undefined,
            .policy = undefined,
            .world = undefined,
            .records = undefined,
            .per_env = undefined,
            .heads = undefined,
            .lens = undefined,
            .rng = undefined,
            .wm_graph = undefined,
            .wm_states = undefined,
            .wm_forces = undefined,
            .wm_loss = undefined,
            .wm_vars = undefined,
            .wm_adam = undefined,
            .pi_graph = undefined,
            .pi_start = undefined,
            .pi_noise = undefined,
            .pi_loss = undefined,
            .pi_vars = undefined,
            .pi_adam = undefined,
            .stage_states = undefined,
            .stage_forces = undefined,
            .stage_starts = undefined,
            .stage_noise = undefined,
            .t1 = undefined,
            .t2 = undefined,
        };
        st.arena_state = ArenaAllocator.init(gpa);
        errdefer st.arena_state.deinit();
        const arena: Allocator = st.arena_state.allocator();
        st.gpa = gpa;
        st.options = options;
        st.out = .{0};
        st.rng = Random.DefaultPrng.init(options.seed);
        const random: Random = st.rng.random();
        const h: usize = options.hidden;
        const b: usize = options.batch;
        st.policy = try Net.init(arena, random, 4, h, 1, 0.01);
        // In: cart rate, pole angle, pole rate, force / max_force. Out: the two accelerations / 10.
        st.world = try Net.init(arena, random, 4, h, 2, 1.0);
        st.per_env = options.capacity / options.envs;
        st.records = try arena.alloc(Record, st.per_env * options.envs);
        st.heads = try arena.alloc(usize, options.envs);
        st.lens = try arena.alloc(usize, options.envs);
        @memset(st.heads, 0);
        @memset(st.lens, 0);
        st.t1 = try arena.alloc(f32, h);
        st.t2 = try arena.alloc(f32, h);
        st.stage_states = try arena.alloc(f32, b * (options.wm_window + 1) * 4);
        st.stage_forces = try arena.alloc(f32, b * options.wm_window);
        st.stage_starts = try arena.alloc(f32, b * 4);
        st.stage_noise = try arena.alloc(f32, options.policy_window * b);

        const ones_t: Tensor = try filled(arena, &.{ b, 1 }, 1.0);
        // One-hot columns that pick an acceleration out of the world model's [rows, 2] output.
        const pick_cart: Tensor = try .alloc(arena, &.{ 2, 1 });
        pick_cart.data[0] = acc_scale;
        pick_cart.data[1] = 0.0;
        const pick_pole: Tensor = try .alloc(arena, &.{ 2, 1 });
