        pick_pole.data[0] = 0.0;
        pick_pole.data[1] = acc_scale;
        const zero_col: Tensor = try filled(arena, &.{ b, 1 }, 0.0);

        // -- The world model's graph. --
        st.wm_graph = Graph.init(arena);
        st.wm_graph.useScratchAllocator(gpa);
        const wg: *Graph = &st.wm_graph;
        st.wm_vars = try st.world.vars(wg);
        const w_ones: Var = try wg.constant(ones_t);
        const w_pick_cart: Var = try wg.constant(pick_cart);
        const w_pick_pole: Var = try wg.constant(pick_pole);
        st.wm_states = try arena.alloc([4]Var, options.wm_window + 1);
        st.wm_forces = try arena.alloc(Var, options.wm_window);
        for (st.wm_states) |*cols| {
            for (cols) |*c| {
                c.* = try wg.constant(try filled(arena, &.{ b, 1 }, 0.0));
            }
        }
        for (st.wm_forces) |*f| {
            f.* = try wg.constant(try filled(arena, &.{ b, 1 }, 0.0));
        }
        var p: Columns = st.wm_states[0];
        var loss: ?Var = null;
        for (0..options.wm_window) |k| {
            p = try step(wg, st.wm_vars, p, st.wm_forces[k], w_ones, w_pick_cart, w_pick_pole, options.dt);
            const term: Var = try weightedDistance(wg, options, p, st.wm_states[k + 1]);
            loss = if (loss) |l| try wg.add(l, term) else term;
        }
        st.wm_loss = loss.?;
        st.wm_adam = try gym.AdamSet.init(arena, &st.world.tensors());

        // -- The policy's graph: rolled out through the SAME world model weights. --
        st.pi_graph = Graph.init(arena);
        st.pi_graph.useScratchAllocator(gpa);
        const pg: *Graph = &st.pi_graph;
        st.pi_vars = try st.policy.vars(pg);
        const world_in_pi: [6]Var = try st.world.vars(pg);
        const p_ones: Var = try pg.constant(ones_t);
        const p_pick_cart: Var = try pg.constant(pick_cart);
        const p_pick_pole: Var = try pg.constant(pick_pole);
        const p_zero: Var = try pg.constant(zero_col);
        const upright: Columns = .{ p_zero, p_zero, p_zero, p_zero };
        for (&st.pi_start) |*c| {
            c.* = try pg.constant(try filled(arena, &.{ b, 1 }, 0.0));
        }
        st.pi_noise = try arena.alloc(Var, options.policy_window);
        var q: Columns = st.pi_start;
        var pi_loss: ?Var = null;
        for (0..options.policy_window) |k| {
            const x: Var = try concat4(pg, q);
            const o: Var = try Net.apply(pg, st.pi_vars, x, p_ones);
            st.pi_noise[k] = try pg.constant(try filled(arena, &.{ b, 1 }, 0.0));
            // The force the world model sees: tanh(o + sigma eps), i.e. force / max_force.
            const squashed: Var = try pg.tanh(try pg.add(o, try pg.scale(st.pi_noise[k], options.sigma)));
            q = try step(pg, world_in_pi, q, squashed, p_ones, p_pick_cart, p_pick_pole, options.dt);
            var term: Var = try weightedDistance(pg, options, q, upright);
            term = try pg.add(term, try pg.scale(try pg.mseLoss(o, p_zero), options.w_action));
            pi_loss = if (pi_loss) |l| try pg.add(l, term) else term;
        }
        st.pi_loss = pi_loss.?;
        st.pi_adam = try gym.AdamSet.init(arena, &st.policy.tensors());
        return st;
    }

    pub fn deinit(st: *SuperTrack) void {
        st.wm_graph.deinitScratch();
        st.pi_graph.deinitScratch();
        st.arena_state.deinit();
        st.gpa.destroy(st);
    }

    fn filled(arena: Allocator, shape: []const usize, value: f32) !Tensor {
        const t: Tensor = try .alloc(arena, shape);
        @memset(t.data, value);
        return t;
    }

    fn concat4(g: *Graph, c: Columns) !Var {
        return g.concat(try g.concat(try g.concat(c[0], c[1], 1), c[2], 1), c[3], 1);
    }

    /// One step ON THE TAPE: the world model's accelerations from (cart rate, pole angle, pole
    /// rate, force / max_force), integrated exactly as the simulator integrates - velocities
    /// first, positions from the new velocities.
    fn step(
        g: *Graph,
        w: [6]Var,
        s: Columns,
        force_unit: Var,
        ones: Var,
        pick_cart: Var,
        pick_pole: Var,
        dt: f32,
    ) !Columns {
        const in: Var = try concat4(g, .{ s[1], s[2], s[3], force_unit });
        const acc: Var = try Net.apply(g, w, in, ones);
        const cart_rate: Var = try g.add(s[1], try g.scale(try g.matmul(acc, pick_cart), dt));
        const pole_rate: Var = try g.add(s[3], try g.scale(try g.matmul(acc, pick_pole), dt));
        return .{
            try g.add(s[0], try g.scale(cart_rate, dt)),
            cart_rate,
            try g.add(s[2], try g.scale(pole_rate, dt)),
            pole_rate,
        };
    }

    /// The tracking loss between two states: weighted mean squares per component.
    fn weightedDistance(g: *Graph, o: Options, a: Columns, b: Columns) !Var {
        const weights = [4]f32{ o.w_cart, o.w_cart_rate, o.w_pole, o.w_pole_rate };
        var total: ?Var = null;
        for (a, b, weights) |x, y, w| {
            const term: Var = try g.scale(try g.mseLoss(x, y), w);
            total = if (total) |t| try g.add(t, term) else term;
        }
        return total.?;
    }

    /// The policy's force for one state (N), with or without its exploration noise.
    pub fn act(st: *SuperTrack, state: State4, noisy: bool) f32 {
        st.policy.forwardRow(&state, st.t1, st.t2, &st.out);
        const noise: f32 = if (noisy) st.options.sigma * st.rng.random().floatNorm(f32) else 0.0;
        return st.options.max_force * tanh(st.out[0] + noise);
    }

    pub fn remember(
        st: *SuperTrack,
        env: usize,
        state: State4,
        force: f32,
        segment: u32,
    ) void {
        const ring: []Record = st.records[env * st.per_env ..][0..st.per_env];
        ring[st.heads[env]] = .{
            .state = state,
            .force = force,
            .segment = segment,
        };
        st.heads[env] = (st.heads[env] + 1) % st.per_env;
        st.lens[env] = @min(st.lens[env] + 1, st.per_env);
    }

    /// A window of `n` consecutive transitions (n + 1 states) of ONE cartpole inside one
    /// segment: the ring it is in, and the index of its oldest record; null if none was found.
    const Window = struct { ring: []const Record, first: usize };

    fn sampleWindow(st: *SuperTrack, n: usize) ?Window {
        for (0..64) |_| {
            const env: usize = st.rng.random().uintLessThan(usize, st.options.envs);
            const len: usize = st.lens[env];
            if (len < n + 2) {
                continue;
            }
            const ring: []const Record = st.records[env * st.per_env ..][0..st.per_env];
            const oldest: usize = (st.heads[env] + st.per_env - len) % st.per_env;
            const offset: usize = st.rng.random().uintLessThan(usize, len - n);
            const first: usize = (oldest + offset) % st.per_env;
            const last: usize = (first + n) % st.per_env;
            if (ring[first].segment == ring[last].segment) {
                return .{ .ring = ring, .first = first };
            }
        }
        return null;
    }

    fn setColumn(g: *Graph, v: Var, row: usize, value: f32) void {
        g.valueOf(v).data[row] = value;
    }

    /// One world-model step on a batch of sampled windows: supervised, on real transitions.
    pub fn trainWorld(st: *SuperTrack) !?f32 {
        if (!st.sampleWorldBatch()) {
            return null;
        }
        return try st.trainWorldWith(st.stage_states, st.stage_forces);
    }

    /// Draw a world-model batch into `stage_states` / `stage_forces`; false if the buffer cannot
    /// supply one yet. Either trainer (this graph, or the kit) can then take it.
    pub fn sampleWorldBatch(st: *SuperTrack) bool {
        const n: usize = st.options.wm_window;
        for (0..st.options.batch) |row| {
            const w: Window = st.sampleWindow(n) orelse return false;
            for (0..n + 1) |k| {
                const rec: Record = w.ring[(w.first + k) % w.ring.len];
                @memcpy(st.stage_states[(row * (n + 1) + k) * 4 ..][0..4], &rec.state);
                if (k < n) {
                    st.stage_forces[row * n + k] = rec.force / st.options.max_force;
                }
            }
        }
        return true;
    }

    /// One world-model step on GIVEN windows: states [batch][window + 1][4], forces (already
    /// divided by the force limit) [batch][window].
    pub fn trainWorldWith(
        st: *SuperTrack,
        states: []const f32,
        forces_unit: []const f32,
    ) !f32 {
        const g: *Graph = &st.wm_graph;
        const n: usize = st.options.wm_window;
        for (0..st.options.batch) |row| {
            for (0..n + 1) |k| {
                for (0..4) |c| {
                    setColumn(g, st.wm_states[k][c], row, states[(row * (n + 1) + k) * 4 + c]);
                }
                if (k < n) {
                    setColumn(g, st.wm_forces[k], row, forces_unit[row * n + k]);
                }
            }
        }
        try g.recompute();
        try g.backward(st.wm_loss);
        try st.wm_adam.apply(g, &st.world.tensors(), &st.wm_vars, st.options.wm_rate);
        return g.valueOf(st.wm_loss).data[0];
    }

    /// One policy step from sampled start states and fresh noise.
    pub fn trainPolicy(st: *SuperTrack) !?f32 {
        if (!st.samplePolicyBatch()) {
            return null;
        }
        return try st.trainPolicyWith(st.stage_starts, st.stage_noise);
    }

    /// Draw start states and noise into `stage_starts` / `stage_noise`; false if not yet.
    pub fn samplePolicyBatch(st: *SuperTrack) bool {
        for (0..st.options.batch) |row| {
            const w: Window = st.sampleWindow(1) orelse return false;
            @memcpy(st.stage_starts[row * 4 ..][0..4], &w.ring[w.first].state);
        }
        for (st.stage_noise) |*e| {
            e.* = st.rng.random().floatNorm(f32);
        }
        return true;
    }

    /// Take a policy's weights (in the kit's layout, from `offsets`) - so a kit-trained policy
    /// acts through this object's CPU forward.
    pub fn loadPolicy(st: *SuperTrack, params_: []const f32, offsets: [3]u32) void {
        for (st.policy.layers, offsets) |layer, off| {
            @memcpy(layer.w.data, params_[off..][0..layer.w.data.len]);
            @memcpy(layer.b.data, params_[off + layer.w.data.len ..][0..layer.b.data.len]);
        }
    }

    /// One policy step from GIVEN start states [batch][4] and noise [policy_window][batch]:
    /// rolled out through the world model, the tracking loss back-propagated into the POLICY
    /// only (the world model's gradients are not applied).
    pub fn trainPolicyWith(
        st: *SuperTrack,
        starts: []const f32,
        noise: []const f32,
    ) !f32 {
        const g: *Graph = &st.pi_graph;
        const b: usize = st.options.batch;
        for (0..b) |row| {
            for (0..4) |c| {
                setColumn(g, st.pi_start[c], row, starts[row * 4 + c]);
            }
        }
        for (st.pi_noise, 0..) |v, k| {
            @memcpy(g.valueOf(v).data, noise[k * b ..][0..b]);
        }
        try g.recompute();
        try g.backward(st.pi_loss);
        try st.pi_adam.apply(g, &st.policy.tensors(), &st.pi_vars, st.options.policy_rate);
        return g.valueOf(st.pi_loss).data[0];
    }
};

11.4 On the cartpole#

The cartpole is where the recipe is proven: eight cartpoles, a push to each pole every push_every steps, the world model on 8-frame windows, the policy on 32. With no reward anywhere, a few thousand iterations of training hold the pole upright through every push, for whole episodes. evaluate measures exactly that: episodes under the same pushes, with the policy's mean action.

push_every
/// Pushes: every `push_every` steps the pole's rate jumps by up to +-`push_size` rad/s.
pub const push_every: u32 = 40;
push_size
pub const push_size: f32 = 0.4;
episode_cap
pub const episode_cap: u32 = 500;
evaluate
/// Mean episode length of `episodes` REAL cartpole episodes under pushes: the policy without
/// noise, or no force at all (`policy` null) for the baseline.
pub fn evaluate(st: ?*SuperTrack, episodes: u32, seed: u64) f32 {
    var rng: Random.DefaultPrng = .init(seed);
    const random: Random = rng.random();
    var total: u32 = 0;
    for (0..episodes) |e| {
        var state = zrl.cartpoleTaskReset(f32, zn.Rng.init(@truncate(seed)), @intCast(e), .hold);
        var steps: u32 = 0;
        while (steps < episode_cap) : (steps += 1) {
            if (steps > 0 and steps % push_every == 0) {
                state.pole_rate_rad += push_size * (2.0 * random.float(f32) - 1.0);
            }
            const force: f32 = if (st) |s| s.act(fromCartpole(state), false) else 0.0;
            const stepped = zrl.cartpoleContinuousStep(f32, state, force);
            if (stepped.failed) {
                break;
            }
            state = stepped.state;
        }
        total += steps;
    }
    return float(total) / float(episodes);
}

11.5 On a humanoid: the state a tracker sees#

A cartpole's state is four numbers. A humanoid's is eighteen rigid bodies, and how they are handed to a network decides how much of the problem the network has to solve twice. A walk at the origin facing north and the same walk twenty metres away facing south are the same motion, so robot_track shows a network only what survives moving into the root's own frame: positions, rotations, velocities and angular velocities, all relative to the root.

Two things deliberately survive that move, because they are not arbitrary. Heights stay in world z, because the floor is real and a pose lying down is not a pose standing up. And an up vector — the world's up, written in the root's frame — says how the character is tilted, which stripping the root's rotation would otherwise throw away. What is left is invariant under a turn about the world's up axis and a horizontal move, and nothing else, which is exactly the set of changes that leave a motion the same motion. The world body is left out: it sits at the world origin, so its position relative to the root is precisely where the character is standing.

State
/// Every body's world pose and velocity: the whole state a tracker cares about.
///
/// Slices are `bodies` long and indexed the way the model indexes bodies, so body 0 is the world
/// and body `root` is the character's root. `positions` are body FRAME origins (not centres of
/// mass) and `velocities` are the velocities of those same points, so the two are consistent -
/// which matters, because a state is differentiated and integrated all over this file.
pub const State = struct {
    positions: []Vec,
    rotations: []Quat,
    velocities: []Vec,
    /// Angular velocities in WORLD axes (robot.zig's `cvel.ang` already is; a body's own frame
    /// would need a rotation, and every formula below wants world).
    angular: []Vec,
    /// Each body's LOWEST POINT above the floor (world z of its collision shapes' lowest point,
    /// `rbt.bodyLowestPoints`) - which body touches the floor, for `TrackingError.unexpected_contact`.
    /// Only `stateOf` knows the geometry, so `init` fills `rbt.no_shape_height`: a state built any other
    /// way (a world model's prediction has frames but no shapes) never reads as touching anything.
    lowest: []f32,

    pub fn init(gpa: Allocator, count: usize) !State {
        const positions: []Vec = try gpa.alloc(Vec, count);
        errdefer gpa.free(positions);
        const rotations: []Quat = try gpa.alloc(Quat, count);
        errdefer gpa.free(rotations);
        const velocities: []Vec = try gpa.alloc(Vec, count);
        errdefer gpa.free(velocities);
        const angular: []Vec = try gpa.alloc(Vec, count);
        errdefer gpa.free(angular);
        const lowest: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, count);
        @memset(lowest, rbt.no_shape_height);
        return .{
            .positions = positions,
            .rotations = rotations,
            .velocities = velocities,
            .angular = angular,
            .lowest = lowest,
        };
    }

    pub fn deinit(self: *State, gpa: Allocator) void {
        gpa.free(self.positions);
        gpa.free(self.rotations);
        gpa.free(self.velocities);
        gpa.free(self.angular);
        gpa.free(self.lowest);
    }

    pub fn bodies(self: State) usize {
        return self.positions.len;
    }

    pub fn copyFrom(self: *State, other: State) void {
        @memcpy(self.positions, other.positions);
        @memcpy(self.rotations, other.rotations);
        @memcpy(self.velocities, other.velocities);
        @memcpy(self.angular, other.angular);
        @memcpy(self.lowest, other.lowest);
    }
};
localSize
/// How many numbers `local` writes for a model with `bodies` bodies.
///
/// Per body: 3 position + 6 rotation + 3 velocity + 3 angular + 1 height, and 3 more for the up
/// vector at the end - counted over the CHARACTER's bodies, which is all of them except the world.
/// The world body is not part of the character, and including it would quietly smuggle the
/// character's absolute position back in: the world's origin, seen from the root, is exactly where
/// the character is standing. The root's own position and rotation stay in (always zero and
/// identity) so that every body sits at the same offset, which is worth more than the sixteen
/// numbers it costs once this is being sliced up inside a kernel.
pub fn localSize(bodies: usize) usize {
    return (bodies - 1) * (3 + 6 + 3 + 3 + 1) + 3;
}
local
/// The state as a network sees it: everything in the root's frame, heights and up kept in world.
///
/// `root` is the character's root body. `out` must be `localSize(bodies)` long.
pub fn local(state: State, root: usize, out: []f32) void {
    assertf(out.len == localSize(state.bodies()), @src(), "local wants {d} numbers, got {d}", .{
        localSize(state.bodies()),
        out.len,
    });
    // Body 0 is the world. Rooting at it would leave every position in world space - the
    // representation would look fine and quietly carry the character's absolute position.
    assertf(root > 0 and root < state.bodies(), @src(), "root body {d} is not a character body", .{root});
    const bodies: usize = state.bodies();
    const to_local: Quat = conjugate(state.rotations[root]);
    const origin: Vec = state.positions[root];
    var at: usize = 0;
    for (1..bodies) |b| {
        writeVec(out, &at, rotate(to_local, state.positions[b] - origin));
    }
    for (1..bodies) |b| {
        writeTwoAxis(out, &at, qmul(to_local, state.rotations[b]));
    }
    for (1..bodies) |b| {
        writeVec(out, &at, rotate(to_local, state.velocities[b]));
    }
    for (1..bodies) |b| {
        writeVec(out, &at, rotate(to_local, state.angular[b]));
    }
    for (1..bodies) |b| {
        out[at] = state.positions[b][2];
        at += 1;
    }
    // The world's up, in the root's frame: everything else here is blind to how the character is
    // tilted, and this is what tells it.
    writeVec(out, &at, rotate(to_local, vec(0, 0, 1)));
}

Rotations are written as two axes — the first two columns of the rotation matrix — rather than as quaternions. A quaternion is an awkward thing for a network to predict: q and −q are the same rotation, so the target jumps, and normalising afterwards does not remove the jump. Two axes vary smoothly with the rotation, and turn back into one by orthonormalising.

twoAxis
/// A rotation as two axes: the first two columns of its matrix, which is what a network should
/// predict instead of a quaternion (continuous, and no sign ambiguity).
pub fn twoAxis(q: Quat) [6]f32 {
    const x: Vec = rotate(q, vec(1, 0, 0));
    const y: Vec = rotate(q, vec(0, 1, 0));
    return .{ x[0], x[1], x[2], y[0], y[1], y[2] };
}
fromTwoAxis
/// Two axes back to a rotation. They needn't be unit or perpendicular - whatever a network hands
/// over gets orthonormalised: the first axis is taken as it is, the second is straightened against
/// it, and the third follows from the cross product.
pub fn fromTwoAxis(axes: [6]f32) Quat {
    // Total, on purpose. The axes come from a network, and early in training a network happily
    // outputs two near-zero vectors, or two parallel ones - either of which would divide by zero
    // here and hand NaN to everything downstream, where it is very hard to trace back. So a
    // degenerate axis falls back to a fixed one, which is wrong but finite, and training moves on.
    const first: Vec = vec(axes[0], axes[1], axes[2]);
    const a: Vec = if (length3(first) > 1.0e-6) normalize3(first) else vec(1, 0, 0);
    const raw: Vec = vec(axes[3], axes[4], axes[5]);
    const across: Vec = raw - a * splat(dot3(raw, a));
    const b: Vec = if (length3(across) > 1.0e-6)
        normalize3(across)
    else
        normalize3(orthogonalTo(a));
    const c: Vec = cross(a, b);
    return quatFromColumns(a, b, c);
}

The other half is turning predicted accelerations back into a state: velocity first, then position with the new velocity — the same order robot.zig steps in, so a predicted state and a simulated one can be compared frame for frame. Each body moves on its own here, with nothing holding the joints together, so a long rollout drifts; over one frame at 60 Hz the drift is tens of microns, and it shrinks with the square of the step.

integrate
/// Move a state forward by `dt` under per-body accelerations, in world axes.
///
/// Velocity first, then position with the NEW velocity - the same semi-implicit order robot.zig
/// steps in, so a state predicted this way and a state the simulator produced can be compared
/// frame for frame. Rotations take the angular velocity on the LEFT (`exp(dt w) * q`) because `w`
/// is in world axes; on the right it would mean the body's own frame, and the two differ by the
/// whole rotation.
///
/// Each body moves independently here - nothing holds the joints together - so a long rollout
/// drifts apart. That is expected: the world model is trained to predict accelerations that keep
/// it together over the window it is rolled out for, and nothing longer.
pub fn integrate(state: *State, linear: []const Vec, angular: []const Vec, dt: f32) void {
    // From 1: body 0 is the world, and a world model that nudged it would move the floor.
    for (1..state.bodies()) |b| {
        state.velocities[b] += linear[b] * splat(dt);
        state.angular[b] += angular[b] * splat(dt);
        state.positions[b] += state.velocities[b] * splat(dt);
        state.rotations[b] = normalize4(qmul(rotationOver(state.angular[b], dt), state.rotations[b]));
    }
}

11.6 Actions: offsets on the reference#

The policy does not command the character. It nudges the clip: its action is an offset added to the reference pose, and the servo drives toward the result. Zero offsets mean "do exactly what the clip says", which is where training starts, and the policy spends its capacity on the part the clip cannot know — keeping the body upright, absorbing a shove, putting a foot where the floor actually is.

An offset is a displacement in velocity space, which is why integratePos applies it: that function already knows a hinge's offset is an angle added and a ball's composes on the right, in the frame a ball's degrees of freedom live in. Doing either by hand is how forearms end up twisted. The free root gets no offsets at all — a policy cannot push on the world.

actionSize
/// How many numbers a policy's action has: one per actuated degree of freedom.
///
/// Every joint DOF except the free root's six. For humanoid_flex2 that is 35 - one per hinge,
/// three per ball.
pub fn actionSize(m: *const rbt.Model) usize {
    return m.nv - rootDofs(m);
}
applyAction
/// The servo's targets for one step: the reference pose, nudged by the policy's action.
///
/// The action is a DISPLACEMENT IN VELOCITY SPACE, which is why `integratePos` applies it - that
/// is the function that already knows a hinge's offset is an angle added, and a ball's is
/// `exp(a/2)` composed on the RIGHT, in the child's frame where a ball's degrees of freedom live.
/// Getting either of those by hand is how forearms end up twisted. The root's six numbers are left
/// alone: a policy cannot push on the world.
///
/// `scale` is how far one unit of action reaches, in radians - the action itself is expected in
/// [-1, 1], which is what a squashed policy produces. `scratch` is `m.nv` long, and `out` is
/// `m.nq`; `out` may alias `reference`.
pub fn applyAction(
    m: *const rbt.Model,
    reference: []const f32,
    action: []const f32,
    scale: f32,
    scratch: []f32,
    out: []f32,
) void {
    assertf(action.len == actionSize(m), @src(), "action has {d} numbers, model wants {d}", .{
        action.len,
        actionSize(m),
    });
    assertf(scratch.len == m.nv and out.len == m.nq, @src(), "scratch {d} (wants {d}), out {d} (wants {d})", .{
        scratch.len,
        m.nv,
        out.len,
        m.nq,
    });
    const root: usize = rootDofs(m);
    @memset(scratch[0..root], 0.0);
    for (action, root..) |a, k| {
        scratch[k] = scale * a;
    }
    if (out.ptr != reference.ptr) {
        @memcpy(out, reference);
    }
    rbt.integratePos(m, out, scratch, 1.0);
}

The servo underneath is a spring and nothing more: it knows where the character is and where the targets say it should be, not where the clip is going next. That is deliberate — the gap it leaves is what the offsets are for. On a fixed base, following a walk, exact computed torque (which does know what comes next) stays within a hundredth of a degree, while the spring lags by about four degrees at 20 Hz, less when stiffer, more when softer.

How the spring's acceleration becomes torque matters more than it looks. Scaling it by the mass matrix's diagonal — the obvious per-joint gain — is unstable: in a chain, a given torque buys more acceleration than the diagonal predicts, so damping the spring asked to apply implicitly gets applied explicitly and amplified, and at 20 Hz with a 60 Hz step that diverges. So the torque is the one that actually produces the requested acceleration, through the model — which the simulator has computed anyway.

Gains
/// What a joint servo is set to: a spring frequency and a damping ratio - the same two knobs the
/// dance's `Tracker` uses, rather than a gain per joint.
pub const Gains = struct {
    frequency: f32 = 20.0,
    damping: f32 = 1.0,
    /// How hard a joint may be driven, as an acceleration in rad/s^2 (or m/s^2 for a slide).
    ///
    /// A spring asked for a large enough error would demand any torque at all, and a policy that
    /// learns to rely on infinite strength learns something no actuator can do. Limiting the
    /// ACCELERATION rather than the torque keeps the limit model-scaled - the same number means the
    /// same thing for a wrist and for a thigh - and it stays exact through the torque conversion,
    /// which a torque clamp would not.
    max_acceleration: f32 = 400.0,
    /// How much of a helping hand the ROOT gets, from 0 (none - the real task) to 1.
    ///
    /// The root of a floating character has no actuator: everything that keeps it up has to come
    /// through the legs and the floor, which is precisely what a policy has not learned yet at the
    /// start. A hard, contact-rich motion like getting up is then barely learnable - the character
    /// falls before anything useful happens. So early in training the root gets a spring toward
    /// the reference like every joint has, realised as an EXTERNAL wrench: inverse dynamics says
    /// what wrench would hold the root on its spring, and a fraction `assist` of it is applied. The
    /// learner fades it to zero on a schedule (residual force control's idea, with the curriculum
    /// that retires it), and a policy is only ever judged at zero.
    assist: f32 = 0.0,
    /// VELOCITY FEEDFORWARD (plan F3): damp each joint toward the reference's velocity over the step
    /// (`referenceVelocity`) instead of toward zero - a servo following MOTION should not brake it
    /// (`pdTorquesToward`). Off: the zero-velocity spring. SuperTrack's paper used the reference's joint
    /// velocities as targets in PhysX and zero in Havok and Bullet, with "final performance reasonably
    /// similar" (sec. 5.1.3) - and F3 measured +1% survival here - so off is the paper-consistent choice.
    velocity_feedforward: bool = false,
};
pdTorques
/// The torques that drive the robot toward `target` - the law the policy acts through.
///
/// It is a spring, and a spring alone: no feedforward, no knowledge of where the reference is
/// going next, only "you are here, you should be there". What the policy adds on top of that is
/// the whole point of the offsets.
///
/// Two steps, and the second one matters more than it looks. First, the acceleration a critically
/// damped spring asks for, evaluated at the END of the step (`robot_maximal.stableSpringAccel`)
/// rather than the start, because an explicit spring stiffer than about 8 Hz explodes at 60 Hz and
/// 20 Hz is where a character servo wants to be. Then the torque that actually PRODUCES that
/// acceleration, through the model - inverse dynamics, or its floating-base cousin when the root
/// is free, since a policy cannot push on the world.
///
/// The obvious shortcut - scale the acceleration by the mass matrix's DIAGONAL and call it a PD
/// gain - does not work here, and fails in an interesting way: for a chain, a given torque buys
/// MORE acceleration than the diagonal predicts, so the damping the spring asked to apply
/// implicitly gets applied explicitly and amplified. At 20 Hz with a 60 Hz step that is
/// unconditionally unstable; measured on a walking clip, the robot passes 100 rad/s within twenty
/// frames. A game engine's per-joint PD avoids this with Tan's stable PD, which solves with the
/// mass matrix anyway - so we may as well use the one the simulator already computes.
///
/// `d` must be forward-current with `rbt.biasForce` already called. `scratch` is `m.nv`, `dense`
/// is `m.nv * m.nv`, `full` is `m.nv` (both are only touched when the root is free).
pub fn pdTorques(
    m: *const rbt.Model,
    d: *rbt.Data,
    target: []const f32,
    gains: Gains,
    dt: f32,
    accel_scratch: []f32,
    scratch: []f32,
    dense: []f32,
    full: []f32,
    out: []f32,
) void {
    pdTorquesToward(m, d, target, null, gains, dt, accel_scratch, scratch, dense, full, out);
}

11.7 Collecting it: rings, segments and a fleet#

Training data for a tracker is windows of motion: eight frames for a world model, thirty-two for a policy rolled out through one. Every frame in a window has to follow from the one before it, and the things that break that are not rare — an episode ends and restarts somewhere else in the clip, or a shove arrives from outside that nothing in the state could have predicted.

So experience is kept per character in a ring, each record tagged with a segment that changes at every reset and every shove, and the sampler only ever returns frames sharing one. What is stored is the simulator's own pose and velocity rather than the features a network sees: half the memory, and it cannot disagree with the model, because forward kinematics reconstructs the rest on the way out.

Several clips. A fleet can track several clips at once - the dance and a fall-and-get-up take, say - each character on one clip per episode, every record tagged with its clip, each clip's reference rows a table of their own. Which clip a new episode is on is the fleet's ClipAssignment. Drawn at random at every restart, each clip's share of the characters is even, but its share of the time follows how long its episodes last - and a harder clip, whose episodes end sooner, quietly gets less of it. Fixed by character - character i always on clip i mod the clips - each clip keeps its share of the characters, and so of the time, however hard it is:

   two clips, four characters        character  0   1   2   3
                                     clip       0   1   0   1        at every restart, the same

Where episodes start. Within its clip, a new episode starts at a random frame - or, with a ResetCurriculum, where the practice is needed. Each clip is cut into bins of a second, and each bin keeps a running failure rate: of the steps whose reference frame fell in it, the share that lost the reference. A restart then draws from a mixture - half uniform over the clip; four tenths toward the bins failing most now, by a softmax of their losses per second of motion; one tenth by each bin's long-run weight, so a stretch once hard keeps some practice after it is learned:

   a 5 s clip in bins of a second        bin       0     1     2     3     4
   losses per second                               0     0     1     0     0
   hard draws: softmax(5 x losses per second)      .006  .006  .974  .006  .006
   starts landing in each bin                      .10   .10   .59   .10   .10
       (0.5 uniform + 0.4 hard + 0.1 long-run, the long-run weights grown from the hard ones)

The scale is absolute on purpose. Late in training every stretch is easy, and bins that differ only by noise - one loss in a hundred seconds against one in two hundred - weigh nearly the same, so the draws return to uniform rather than chasing whichever bin happened to fail last.

Without it, the hard stretches of a clip - a get-up's first push off the floor, a jump's landing - get no more starts than the easy ones, and a policy can track nine tenths of a clip well while failing the same second every time.

The machinery works the same way as zimrnum's general SequenceReplay — a ring per character read in time order across its physical wrap, a window found with just two random numbers (which character, where it starts), a batch laid out step by step for the rollout — which is explained once, with diagrams, in the zimrrl tutorial's SequenceReplay section. What is particular here is the window rule. SequenceReplay lets a window run straight through an episode's end and masks the steps after it; this replay never lets a window cross a segment boundary at all, so every frame of every window is real, unbroken motion. The difference matters because a shove is not an ending: the motion carries on, just not in a way anything in the state could have predicted.

A segment is not an episode, though. A shove begins a new segment but not a new episode, and whatever the controller was applying carries straight through it. So each record also keeps how far into its episode its step was, which is what says what was being applied just before it: rest on an episode's first step, and otherwise the action recorded one step earlier. When that earlier record has already left the ring, the answer is unknown rather than a guess, and a learner that would read it draws another window.

Replay
/// Experience, kept per environment in a ring: what the simulator was, what was done to it, and
/// which stretch of unbroken motion it belongs to.
///
/// What goes in is the simulator's OWN state - a pose and a velocity - rather than the body-space
/// features a network eventually sees. Two reasons: it is half the memory, and it cannot disagree
/// with the model, because forward kinematics reconstructs the rest on the way out. What a learner
/// wants is windows: eight frames for a world model, thirty-two for a policy, and every frame in
/// one has to follow from the one before it.
///
/// Which is what `segment` is for. It changes at every reset and at every shove - anywhere the
/// motion was interrupted by something no model could have predicted from the state - and
/// `sampleWindow` only ever returns frames that share one. Without that a world model spends part
/// of its capacity trying to predict teleports, and a policy trains through them.
pub const Replay = struct {
    gpa: Allocator,
    envs: usize,
    capacity: usize,
    nq: usize,
    nv: usize,
    action_size: usize,
    poses: []f32,
    velocities: []f32,
    actions: []f32,
    /// The reference frame each record was tracking, so the target can be looked up again - and
    /// WHICH CLIP that frame belongs to, because a ring outlives episodes and an environment picks
    /// a new clip every time it restarts. Without it, a window older than the last restart would be
    /// rebuilt against whatever clip the environment happens to be on now.
    frames: []u32,
    clips: []u16,
    segments: []u32,
    /// How far into its EPISODE each record's step was - 0 on an episode's first step - or null for a record that
    /// is not a step of a rollout at all (a teacher's label, a probe's state: `append`). The segment cannot stand in
    /// for it: a segment ends at a SHOVE as well as at a restart, and a shove ends neither the episode nor what the
    /// controller is applying. This can say what was being applied before a record: rest on an episode's first
    /// step, otherwise the action recorded one step earlier, shove or no shove.
    episode_steps: []?u32,
    /// Whether each record's step came AFTER its episode lost the reference - in the aftermath its fleet lets a lost
    /// character live through (`Fleet.Options.aftermath_steps`). A world model learns from these rows (how a body falls
    /// is knowledge); a pathwise policy loss does not start a window on one (`WindowStart.before_loss`): its tracking
    /// gradients through a fall saturate to nothing.
    after_loss: []bool,
    /// How many records this environment has ever written. The ring holds the last `capacity`.
    written: []u64,

    pub fn init(
        gpa: Allocator,
        m: *const rbt.Model,
        envs: usize,
        capacity: usize,
    ) !Replay {
        assertf(envs > 0 and capacity > 1, @src(), "{d} environments of {d} records makes no ring", .{
            envs,
            capacity,
        });
        const slots: usize = envs * capacity;
        const action_size: usize = actionSize(m);
        const poses: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, slots * m.nq);
        errdefer gpa.free(poses);
        const velocities: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, slots * m.nv);
        errdefer gpa.free(velocities);
        const actions: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, slots * action_size);
        errdefer gpa.free(actions);
        const frames: []u32 = try gpa.alloc(u32, slots);
        errdefer gpa.free(frames);
        const clips: []u16 = try gpa.alloc(u16, slots);
        errdefer gpa.free(clips);
        const segments: []u32 = try gpa.alloc(u32, slots);
        errdefer gpa.free(segments);
        const episode_steps: []?u32 = try gpa.alloc(?u32, slots);
        errdefer gpa.free(episode_steps);
        const after_loss: []bool = try gpa.alloc(bool, slots);
        errdefer gpa.free(after_loss);
        @memset(after_loss, false);
        const written: []u64 = try gpa.alloc(u64, envs);
        @memset(written, 0);
        return .{
            .gpa = gpa,
            .envs = envs,
            .capacity = capacity,
            .nq = m.nq,
            .nv = m.nv,
            .action_size = action_size,
            .poses = poses,
            .velocities = velocities,
            .actions = actions,
            .frames = frames,
            .clips = clips,
            .segments = segments,
            .episode_steps = episode_steps,
            .after_loss = after_loss,
            .written = written,
        };
    }

    pub fn deinit(self: *Replay) void {
        self.gpa.free(self.poses);
        self.gpa.free(self.velocities);
        self.gpa.free(self.actions);
        self.gpa.free(self.frames);
        self.gpa.free(self.clips);
        self.gpa.free(self.segments);
        self.gpa.free(self.episode_steps);
        self.gpa.free(self.after_loss);
        self.gpa.free(self.written);
    }

    fn slot(self: Replay, env: usize, index: u64) usize {
        return env * self.capacity + @as(usize, @intCast(index % self.capacity));
    }

    /// Append one frame of experience for `env` that is NOT a step of a rollout - a teacher's label, a probe's
    /// state: the state, the action taken from it, the reference frame it was tracking, and its segment. What was
    /// being applied before it is unknown, and `episodeStepAt` says so (null). A fleet's own steps go through
    /// `appendStep`, which knows.
    pub fn append(
        self: *Replay,
        env: usize,
        pose: []const f32,
        velocity: []const f32,
        action: []const f32,
        frame: u32,
        clip: u16,
        segment: u32,
    ) void {
        self.appendStep(env, pose, velocity, action, frame, clip, segment, null, false);
    }

    /// Append one STEP of a rollout for `env`, `episode_step` steps into its episode (0 on its first step): the
    /// state it was in, the action applied from it, the reference frame it was tracking, its segment, and whether
    /// the step came after its episode lost the reference (`after_loss`).
    pub fn appendStep(
        self: *Replay,
        env: usize,
        pose: []const f32,
        velocity: []const f32,
        action: []const f32,
        frame: u32,
        clip: u16,
        segment: u32,
        episode_step: ?u32,
        after_loss: bool,
    ) void {
        assertf(
            env < self.envs and pose.len == self.nq and velocity.len == self.nv and action.len == self.action_size,
            @src(),
            "env {d} of {d}, pose {d}/{d}, velocity {d}/{d}, action {d}/{d}",
            .{ env, self.envs, pose.len, self.nq, velocity.len, self.nv, action.len, self.action_size },
        );
        const at: usize = self.slot(env, self.written[env]);
        @memcpy(self.poses[at * self.nq ..][0..self.nq], pose);
        @memcpy(self.velocities[at * self.nv ..][0..self.nv], velocity);
        @memcpy(self.actions[at * self.action_size ..][0..self.action_size], action);
        self.frames[at] = frame;
        self.clips[at] = clip;
        self.segments[at] = segment;
        self.episode_steps[at] = episode_step;
        self.after_loss[at] = after_loss;
        self.written[env] += 1;
    }

    pub fn poseAt(self: Replay, env: usize, index: u64) []const f32 {
        return self.poses[self.slot(env, index) * self.nq ..][0..self.nq];
    }

    pub fn velocityAt(self: Replay, env: usize, index: u64) []const f32 {
        return self.velocities[self.slot(env, index) * self.nv ..][0..self.nv];
    }

    pub fn actionAt(self: Replay, env: usize, index: u64) []const f32 {
        return self.actions[self.slot(env, index) * self.action_size ..][0..self.action_size];
    }

    pub fn frameAt(self: Replay, env: usize, index: u64) u32 {
        return self.frames[self.slot(env, index)];
    }

    /// Which clip that frame belongs to.
    pub fn clipAt(self: Replay, env: usize, index: u64) u16 {
        return self.clips[self.slot(env, index)];
    }

    pub fn segmentAt(self: Replay, env: usize, index: u64) u32 {
        return self.segments[self.slot(env, index)];
    }

    /// Whether the record's step came after its episode lost the reference (`after_loss`).
    pub fn afterLossAt(self: Replay, env: usize, index: u64) bool {
        return self.after_loss[self.slot(env, index)];
    }

    /// How far into its episode the record's step was (0 on an episode's first step), or null when the record is
    /// not a step of a rollout (`append`).
    pub fn episodeStepAt(self: Replay, env: usize, index: u64) ?u32 {
        return self.episode_steps[self.slot(env, index)];
    }

    /// A stretch of unbroken motion from one environment: `steps` transitions, which is `steps + 1`
    /// records, all in one segment.
    ///
    /// Counted in TRANSITIONS on purpose. A world model rolled out for eight steps needs nine
    /// states to compare against, and "an eight-frame window" is the kind of phrase that quietly
    /// becomes seven steps somewhere between the plan and the kernel.
    pub const Window = struct {
        env: usize,
        first: u64,
        steps: usize,

        /// The records the window spans: one more than its transitions.
        pub fn frames(self: Window) usize {
            return self.steps + 1;
        }
    };

    /// Draw one, or null if nothing long enough has been recorded yet.
    ///
    /// The candidate is a start that is still IN the ring (not yet overwritten) with `steps + 1`
    /// records after it; it is accepted when the first and last share a segment - which is enough,
    /// since a segment id only ever increases, so equal ends mean an equal middle. A few dozen
    /// tries are plenty: segments are long compared with a window, and a ring full of short
    /// segments deserves to fail rather than to loop.
    pub fn sampleWindow(self: Replay, random: Random, steps: usize) ?Window {
        return self.sampleWindowStarting(random, steps, .anywhere);
    }

    /// `sampleWindow`, its first record chosen as `start` says: anywhere in a segment, or only on a step taken
    /// before its episode lost the reference.
    ///
    /// REJECTION SAMPLING. A candidate is drawn - a character uniformly, then a first record uniformly among those its
    /// ring still holds - and kept only if it is a window at all (every record in one segment) and starts where
    /// `start` allows; otherwise another is drawn. Keeping only the draws that pass a test, from a uniform draw, gives
    /// a uniform draw over the candidates that pass it: every acceptable window of a character stays equally likely.
    /// It also makes the two rules agree exactly when no record follows a loss (a fleet with no aftermath): no draw is
    /// ever rejected for where it starts, so both consume the random stream identically and return the same windows.
    /// After 64 rejected draws the replay is taken to have no window to give (null), which happens only while it is
    /// nearly empty.
    pub fn sampleWindowStarting(
        self: Replay,
        random: Random,
        steps: usize,
        start: WindowStart,
    ) ?Window {
        assertf(steps > 0, @src(), "a window of no transitions is not a window", .{});
        // A window of `steps` transitions spans steps + 1 records: each step's state, and the one it led to.
        const records_per_window: usize = steps + 1;
        const most_draws: usize = 64;
        for (0..most_draws) |_| {
            const env: usize = random.uintLessThan(usize, self.envs);
            const records_written: u64 = self.written[env];
            if (records_written < records_per_window) {
                continue;
            }
            // The ring holds the newest `capacity` records; a window must start late enough to lie inside it and
            // early enough to end at the newest record or before.
            const ring_capacity: u64 = @intCast(self.capacity);
            const oldest_held: u64 = records_written -| ring_capacity;
            const newest_start: u64 = records_written - records_per_window;
            if (newest_start < oldest_held) {
                continue;
            }
            const start_choices: u64 = newest_start - oldest_held + 1;
            const first_record: u64 = oldest_held + random.uintLessThan(u64, start_choices);
            const last_record: u64 = first_record + records_per_window - 1;
            // One segment from the first record to the last: no reset and no push inside the window.
            const is_unbroken: bool = self.segmentAt(env, first_record) == self.segmentAt(env, last_record);
            if (!is_unbroken) {
                continue;
            }
            const starts_after_loss: bool = self.afterLossAt(env, first_record);
            if (start == .before_loss and starts_after_loss) {
                continue;
            }
            if (start == .after_loss and !starts_after_loss) {
                continue;
            }
            return .{ .env = env, .first = first_record, .steps = steps };
        }
        return null;
    }
};

The characters themselves run as a fleet, stepping together: each takes an action, turns it into PD targets on its reference, drives the servo, steps, records, and starts again somewhere new when it loses the reference. Actions arrive in one flat array for the whole fleet — observe, act, step — because that is the shape a GPU wants and there is no reason to learn a different one first.

An episode ends in one of four ways, each recorded with the state it ended in. The reference is lost: the failure rule fired - a failure, with no future. The step cap is reached, or the clip runs out: the episode was cut short, and had a future. Or its aftermath is over: a fleet may let a character that lost the reference live on for a number of steps before the episode ends, simulated and rewarded as usual through its fall. The failure is the step the reference was lost, counted once; the aftermath's steps come after it, so they are not time at risk, and a time to failure leaves them out.

   step            ...   s-1    s       s+1   ...   s+30   s+31
   no aftermath          -      LOST |  a new episode
   aftermath 30          -      lost    in its aftermath  cut |  a new episode
                                ^ the failure, counted once     ^ the end: the state it ended in captured

The aftermath is for a learner that values a state by what follows it and has no notion of termination: with the fall in its data, under a reward that a body lying on the floor barely earns, it learns from the data itself what losing the reference leads to. A fleet keeps none by default - the judge and the learners that end an episode at the loss keep it so.

Returning. An aftermath can also end the other way: by the character coming back. With returns on (return_steps), each step of an aftermath asks the failure rule the other way round - not whether the reference is lost, but whether it is held again - and a character that holds it for return_steps steps in a row has returned: its aftermath ends there and its episode goes on, a later loss counting as a new failure. The reference runs on through the whole aftermath, so a return is to where the motion has got to, not to where it was lost - a character knocked down in the middle of a dance has to get up and catch the dance where it now is. One that has not returned when the aftermath runs out ends its episode, a failure to return:

   step            ...   s-1    s       s+1  ...  s+k-8 ...  s+k   s+k+1 ...
   returns on            -      lost    in its aftermath   holding the reference, 8 in a row
                                                               ^ RETURNED: the episode goes on
   never back            -      lost    in its aftermath  ...  s+60 cut |  a new episode
                                ^ the failure, counted once

The fleet counts its returns and their lengths, and a run's log carries the round's returns and their mean time from the loss.

Learning the way back. The policy learns from windows of the replay, and without returns they all start before a loss: the tracking loss is a squared distance from the goal, so in a fall it is large and so is its gradient, pointing at a reference the fallen body is never asked to reach again. With returns that same window is exactly what the policy must learn from - the way back to a reference still running. So a share of the policy's windows, a quarter by default (return_window_share), is drawn from inside returns, and the rest from before a loss: enough for the way back to be learned, few enough that its large gradients do not drown the precise tracking near the reference. A fleet without returns draws exactly the windows it always did.

The time to return. The critic, the planner and FPO all charge the per-step tracking cost, and a fall's cost is a squared distance in the hundreds or thousands: it says only how far the bodies are from a pose they cannot reach, and summed into the future by a critic it overflows the critic's bins. So for them the cost is bounded far from the reference (return_cost_cap): cap × tanh(cost / cap), the cost itself near the reference and the cap far from it. Then every step of a fall costs the same, and the critic's value of a fallen state is the cap times the steps until the character is near the reference again - its time to return - which the planner and FPO can shorten. The policy's own loss, a gradient through the world model, keeps SuperTrack's cost:

   step cost      near the reference           far from it (a fall)
   SuperTrack     0.06   0.5   2     8          900   2,000
   bounded, 25    0.06   0.5   2     7.7        25    25          (cap x tanh(cost / cap))
   critic's value of a fallen state:  25 x (the discounted steps until it is near again)

Starts in trouble. A share of new episodes can begin with a push (start_share) at the top of the speed range the push schedule has opened - none before the schedule starts, and ever harder starts as it goes on. A character starting in trouble must recover before it can track at all, which puts the beginning of a return in the data even when no push arrives mid-episode.

EfficientTDMPC is such a learner. Its training loop steps a list of environments through a two-function contract - reset starts an episode, step acts once and says what the step earned and whether the episode goes on - and a TrackCharacter is one character of the dance behind it: DReCon's observation and controller, Geno's task, an aftermath after every loss. A cut episode hands the agent the TRUE state it ended in as its successor, not the fresh start that replaced it; the agent's own reset stream chooses where every new episode starts, so the same seeds replay the same run. With no aftermath, a loss would reach the agent as a final state, which its trainer refuses: nothing in its equations could value it as final.

A run's settings for EfficientTDMPC (TdmpcLearner) name its fleet as well as its agent: eight characters, an aftermath of one second (60 physics steps), episodes of at most ten seconds - 300 decisions at DReCon's interval, which gives the discount 0.983 by BMPC's rule - and a replay of a hundred thousand decisions per character. The agent's configuration is the preset's - EfficientTDMPC's own, with its pessimism on, since a fall cuts an episode early - with every setting the run names in place of the preset's. One check ties the two together: the aftermath must last at least as long as the acting planner looks ahead (6 decisions, 12 physics steps), so that wherever a plan from a falling character reaches, the model has seen where a fall leads.

TrackCharacter.step
/// One decision: `action` held for the learner's interval through DReCon's filter; the decision's reward (the mean
/// over its held steps up to the end); the observation that follows into `observation` - when the episode was
/// cut, the TRUE state it ended in, not the fresh start that replaced it - and how the episode went on.
pub fn step(
    character: *TrackCharacter,
    action: []const f32,
    observation: []f32,
) Agent.StepOutcome {
    character.environment.decide(action, &character.outcome, character.ended_observation);
    const outcome: track_env.Outcome = character.outcome[0];
    // At risk: the decision's own steps (up to its episode's end - after it, the hold drives a fresh start that
    // `reset` replaces) that were not in an aftermath. A failure on such a discarded step would need a start
    // that fails within the rest of one hold, which a start on the reference does not under Geno's rule.
    character.steps_at_risk += outcome.credited - outcome.aftermath_steps;
    character.failures += outcome.failures;
    const ending: Agent.EpisodeEnding = switch (outcome.end) {
        .none => .continues,
        .cut => .truncated,
        // Lost with no aftermath: a final state, which the trainer refuses (`Agent.EpisodeEnding.terminated`).
        .stop => .terminated,
    };
    if (outcome.end == .cut) {
        @memcpy(observation, character.ended_observation);
    } else {
        character.environment.observe(0, observation);
    }
    return .{ .reward = outcome.reward, .ending = ending };
}
Fleet
/// A fleet of characters tracking clips, stepping together and filling a `Replay`.
///
/// The loop per character per frame: take an action, turn it into PD targets on the reference
/// (`applyAction`), drive the servo (`pdTorques`), step, record, and look at the result - if the
/// reference has been lost, start a new episode somewhere else in a clip; every so often, shove it.
/// Resets and shoves both begin a new segment.
///
/// Actions come from outside, in one flat array for the whole fleet, because that is the shape the
/// GPU version wants and there is no reason to learn a different one here: `observe`, then act,
/// then `step`.
pub const Fleet = struct {
    pub const Options = struct {
        envs: usize = 16,
        capacity: usize = 1024,
        /// How far one unit of action reaches, in radians. The LEARNER's (see `Task` for why it is not the task's).
        action_scale: f32 = 0.2,
        /// What the characters are asked to do and when they have failed - see `Task`.
        task: Task = .{},
        /// Which clip each new episode is on (`ClipAssignment`).
        clip_assignment: ClipAssignment = .random,
        /// THE PHYSICS' TASKS: how many parts the characters are split into for their physics steps, each part on a
        /// thread of `Fleet.physics_io` when the fleet is given one - 1 is one loop on the calling thread, as on the
        /// web. Only the integration runs apart: recording, measuring, ending, restarting and pushing - every random
        /// draw - stay on the calling thread in the characters' order, so the fleet's numbers are the same, to the
        /// bit, whatever this is.
        physics_threads: u32 = 1,
        /// Where each new episode starts along its clip (`ResetCurriculum`): uniform, unless a curriculum is given.
        curriculum: ResetCurriculum = .{},
        /// The model's body names, indexed like its bodies (`robot_mjcf.Imported.names`) - needed only to resolve
        /// `task.contact_exempt`, which names bodies; a task that exempts nothing needs none.
        body_names: []const []const u8 = &.{},
        /// Every reset pushed off the reference (`perturbStart`) - D5.5's perturbed starts. None by default.
        start_noise: StartNoise = .{},
        /// Pushes from outside (`Pushes`): none by default.
        pushes: Pushes = .{},
        /// Episodes end here even when tracking is fine, so no environment sits in one stretch of
        /// clip forever.
        max_steps: u32 = 600,
        seed: u64 = 1,
        /// Physics steps a character lives on after its reference is LOST before its episode ends (`End.aftermath`).
        /// The step the failure rule fires is the failure, counted once; the character is then simulated and
        /// rewarded as usual - its fall, under the task's reward - and only after that is the episode cut and the
        /// character restarted. A learner that values a state by what follows it then sees in its own data what
        /// losing the reference leads to, with no notion of termination. Zero ends the episode at the loss itself,
        /// as every fleet always has: the judge and the learners that terminate keep it.
        aftermath_steps: u32 = 0,
        /// The share of the fleet's characters that keep that aftermath: the first round(share x envs) of them. The
        /// others end their episodes at the loss, as a fleet with no aftermath does - a POPULATION in one fleet, the
        /// resetting ones keeping the data near the reference, the living-on ones bringing falls and what follows.
        aftermath_share: f32 = 1.0,
        /// THE RETURN: steps in a row a character in its aftermath must track within the failure rule again to have
        /// RETURNED to the reference - its aftermath ends there and its EPISODE GOES ON, a later loss counting as a new
        /// failure; an aftermath that runs out first ends its episode, a failure to return. Each step of an aftermath
        /// asks the rule the other way round: not "is the reference lost?" but "is it held again?" - the reference
        /// running on all the while, so a return is to where the motion has got to, not to where it was lost. 0: no
        /// returns, every aftermath ending its episode as it always has.
        return_steps: u32 = 0,
    };

    gpa: Allocator,
    /// Everything the fleet owns comes from here, and goes back in one call. A dozen buffers
    /// allocated one at a time is a dozen chances to leak the previous eleven when the thirteenth
    /// fails; an arena has one.
    arena: ArenaAllocator,
    /// ONE ARENA PER CHARACTER, for everything its physics step can allocate from - its data, its collision world (and
    /// that world's per-step scratch arena), its bridge - each backed by the fleet's `gpa` directly. Characters step on
    /// several threads at once (`Options.physics_threads`), and an arena is not safe to allocate from on two threads:
    /// with every character's allocations in an arena of its own, the only allocator two steps can reach at once is
    /// `gpa`, which must therefore be thread-safe (Zig's general-purpose allocators are) whenever the fleet has
    /// threads.
    character_arenas: []ArenaAllocator,
    m: *rbt.Model,
    /// The clips themselves are BORROWED - they must outlive the fleet, and they are read every
    /// step - but the list of them is COPIED into the fleet's own memory. A caller naturally builds
    /// that list as a little local array (`&.{&clip}`), and a fleet that kept the caller's slice
    /// would be holding a pointer into a stack frame that is gone the moment the caller returns.
    /// The first phone page did exactly that, and read garbage for its clips on the first step.
    clips: []const *const dance.Clip,
    /// The character's root body, from the model rather than from an assumption about index 1.
    root: usize,
    options: Options,
    data: []rbt.Data,
    /// A collision world and a bridge PER ENVIRONMENT. In this engine the articulated-body
    /// dynamics (`robot`) and collision (`zimrphysics`) are separate things joined by a bridge:
    /// poses go out, contacts come back. A model with a floor geom in its text collides with
    /// nothing until somebody does that - which is how a fleet can run for thousands of frames in
    /// mid-air and look busy the whole time.
    worlds: []zimrphysics.World,
    bridges: []robot_physics.Bridge,
    clip_of: []usize,
    /// The reset curriculum's bins (`ResetCurriculum`), every clip's in a row: where each clip's bins begin
    /// (`bins_start`, one more than the clips - the last the total), each bin's running failure rate, and its long-run
    /// weight. Empty without a curriculum.
    bins_start: []usize,
    bin_failure_rates: []f32,
    bin_history_weights: []f32,
    frame: []u32,
    segment: []u32,
    steps: []u32,
    next_segment: u32,
    /// The hours this fleet's training has run, told each round by the program that trains (the trainer's clock,
    /// saved with its run): the clock the pushes' schedule follows (`Pushes.scheduleShare`). 0 for a fleet nobody
    /// trains with - full pushes, or none before a schedule's start.
    training_hours: f32 = 0,
    /// The pushes given at random or on the schedule, and their speeds' sum - what a run's log reads the
    /// perturbations it met from.
    pushes_given: u64,
    push_speed_sum: f64,
    rng: Random.DefaultPrng,
    replay: Replay,
    /// Per-environment scratch, allocated once.
    reference_data: rbt.Data,
    sim_state: State,
    reference_state: State,
    /// Per body: exempt from `unexpected_contact` (`Task.contact_exempt`, resolved at init).
    contact_exempt: []bool,
    /// The head's body index (`Task.head_body`, resolved at init), or null: no head term.
    head: ?usize,
    /// Scratch for a start's perturbation (`startAt`), on the calling thread.
    scratch: []f32,
    /// One physics scratch per task (`Options.physics_threads`, `DriveScratch`), and each character's flag of a
    /// collision world that failed in its step - raised on whichever thread, reported after they all finish.
    drive_scratches: []DriveScratch,
    drive_failed: []bool,
    /// The threads the physics' tasks run on, given by the program that owns them (`Options.physics_threads`); null:
    /// every character's step on the calling thread.
    physics_io: ?Io = null,
    /// Each environment's reward on the last step, and whether its episode ended there - which a
    /// learner needs per environment, not averaged: an advantage is about one trajectory.
    rewards: []f32,
    dones: []bool,
    /// Of those endings, which were FAILURES - the reference lost - rather than the clip running out
    /// or the episode cap arriving. The difference is the whole of how a tracker is judged: running
    /// out of clip while still with the reference is success, and counting it as an ending shortens
    /// every episode to whatever was left of the clip when it started.
    failures: []bool,
    /// WHY each ending happened (valid where `dones` is set), and the state it ended IN - captured before
    /// the restart replaces it. A learner needs both: an episode that was LOST has no future, but one CUT
    /// SHORT - by the step cap, or a clip running out - does, and its value is the critic's value of the
    /// state it ended in, not of the fresh start that took its place (MimicKit bootstraps its timeouts
    /// exactly so; ours treated every end as a death until Sep 26).
    ends: []End,
    terminal: []State,
    terminal_frame: []u32,
    terminal_clip: []usize,
    /// Physics steps left in each environment's aftermath (`Options.aftermath_steps`), zero when it is in none, and
    /// whether its last step was one of them: after its failure, so not time at risk - a learner counting exposure
    /// for a time to failure leaves such steps out.
    aftermath_steps_left: []u32,
    in_aftermath: []bool,
    /// Each character's steps in a row of its aftermath holding the reference again (`Options.return_steps`), its
    /// steps since its last loss, and whether the last step was the one it RETURNED on - that return's length being
    /// `steps_since_loss`, where `returned` is set: what a learner counts returns and their time from.
    return_streaks: []u32,
    steps_since_loss: []u32,
    returned: []bool,
    /// Every return since the fleet was made, and their lengths' sum in steps.
    returns: u64 = 0,
    return_steps_sum: u64 = 0,
    /// Every failure since the fleet was made, beside `episodes`, which counts every ending.
    failed: u64 = 0,
    /// The last step's reward and how many episodes have ended, for whoever is watching.
    last_reward: f32 = 0.0,
    episodes: u64 = 0,
    steps_total: u64 = 0,

    pub fn init(
        gpa: Allocator,
        m: *rbt.Model,
        clips: []const *const dance.Clip,
        options: Options,
    ) !*Fleet {
        assertf(clips.len > 0 and clips.len <= 0xffff, @src(), "{d} clips", .{clips.len});
        for (clips) |clip| {
            // The servo is driven at the clip's frame time and the simulator steps at the model's:
            // one step per frame is what makes a reference and a simulation the same trajectory,
            // and a clip at another rate would quietly servo at the wrong one.
            assertf(
                @abs(clip.frame_time - m.opt.timestep) < 1.0e-6,
                @src(),
                "clip runs at {d} s a frame, the model steps at {d}",
                .{ clip.frame_time, m.opt.timestep },
            );
            assertf(clip.nq == m.nq, @src(), "clip poses are {d} long, the model wants {d}", .{ clip.nq, m.nq });
            assertf(clip.frame_count > 2, @src(), "a clip of {d} frames is too short to start in", .{clip.frame_count});
        }
        const fleet: *Fleet = try gpa.create(Fleet);
        errdefer gpa.destroy(fleet);
        // whole-init-first: the whole struct first - defaults applied, every field named.
        fleet.* = .{
            .gpa = undefined,
            .arena = undefined,
            .character_arenas = &.{},
            .m = undefined,
            .clips = undefined,
            .root = undefined,
            .options = undefined,
            .data = undefined,
            .worlds = undefined,
            .bridges = undefined,
            .clip_of = undefined,
            .bins_start = &.{},
            .bin_failure_rates = &.{},
            .bin_history_weights = &.{},
            .frame = undefined,
            .segment = undefined,
            .steps = undefined,
            .next_segment = undefined,
            .pushes_given = undefined,
            .push_speed_sum = undefined,
            .rng = undefined,
            .replay = undefined,
            .reference_data = undefined,
            .sim_state = undefined,
            .reference_state = undefined,
            .contact_exempt = undefined,
            .head = undefined,
            .drive_scratches = undefined,
            .drive_failed = undefined,
            .scratch = undefined,
            .rewards = undefined,
            .dones = undefined,
            .failures = undefined,
            .ends = undefined,
            .terminal = undefined,
            .terminal_frame = undefined,
            .terminal_clip = undefined,
            .aftermath_steps_left = undefined,
            .in_aftermath = undefined,
            .return_streaks = undefined,
            .steps_since_loss = undefined,
            .returned = undefined,
        };
        fleet.arena = ArenaAllocator.init(gpa);
        errdefer fleet.arena.deinit();
        const owned: Allocator = fleet.arena.allocator();
        fleet.* = .{
            .gpa = gpa,
            .arena = fleet.arena,
            .character_arenas = try owned.alloc(ArenaAllocator, options.envs),
            .m = m,
            .clips = try owned.dupe(*const dance.Clip, clips),
            .root = rootBody(m),
            .options = options,
            .data = try owned.alloc(rbt.Data, options.envs),
            .worlds = try owned.alloc(zimrphysics.World, options.envs),
            .bridges = try owned.alloc(robot_physics.Bridge, options.envs),
            .clip_of = try owned.alloc(usize, options.envs),
            .bins_start = try curriculumBinStarts(owned, clips, options.curriculum),
            .bin_failure_rates = &.{},
            .bin_history_weights = &.{},
            .frame = try owned.alloc(u32, options.envs),
            .segment = try owned.alloc(u32, options.envs),
            .steps = try owned.alloc(u32, options.envs),
            .rewards = try owned.alloc(f32, options.envs),
            .dones = try owned.alloc(bool, options.envs),
            .failures = try owned.alloc(bool, options.envs),
            .ends = try owned.alloc(End, options.envs),
            .terminal = try owned.alloc(State, options.envs),
            .terminal_frame = try owned.alloc(u32, options.envs),
            .terminal_clip = try owned.alloc(usize, options.envs),
            .aftermath_steps_left = try owned.alloc(u32, options.envs),
            .in_aftermath = try owned.alloc(bool, options.envs),
            .return_streaks = try owned.alloc(u32, options.envs),
            .steps_since_loss = try owned.alloc(u32, options.envs),
            .returned = try owned.alloc(bool, options.envs),
            .next_segment = 0,
            .pushes_given = 0,
            .push_speed_sum = 0,
            .rng = Random.DefaultPrng.init(options.seed),
            .replay = try Replay.init(owned, m, options.envs, options.capacity),
            .reference_data = try rbt.Data.init(owned, m),
            .sim_state = try State.init(owned, m.nbody),
            .reference_state = try State.init(owned, m.nbody),
            .contact_exempt = try contactExemptMask(owned, m.nbody, options.task.contact_exempt, options.body_names),
            .head = try headBody(options.task.head_body, options.body_names),
            .scratch = try owned.alloc(f32, m.nv),
            .drive_scratches = try owned.alloc(DriveScratch, @max(options.physics_threads, 1)),
            .drive_failed = try owned.alloc(bool, options.envs),
        };
        // Every physics task's scratch, and no collision world failed yet.
        for (fleet.drive_scratches) |*drive| {
            drive.* = try DriveScratch.init(owned, m);
        }
        @memset(fleet.drive_failed, false);
        // The curriculum's running failure rates and long-run weights, one per bin, none yet.
        const bin_count: usize = if (fleet.bins_start.len > 0) fleet.bins_start[fleet.bins_start.len - 1] else 0;
        fleet.bin_failure_rates = try owned.alloc(f32, bin_count);
        @memset(fleet.bin_failure_rates, 0);
        fleet.bin_history_weights = try owned.alloc(f32, bin_count);
        @memset(fleet.bin_history_weights, 0);
        // Each character's data, collision world and bridge in its own arena (`character_arenas`): its physics
        // step allocates from nothing another character's can reach at the same time.
        for (fleet.character_arenas) |*character_arena| {
            character_arena.* = ArenaAllocator.init(gpa);
        }
        // They hold `gpa`'s memory, not the fleet arena's: a later failure must free them too.
        errdefer for (fleet.character_arenas) |*character_arena| {
            character_arena.deinit();
        };
        for (fleet.data, fleet.character_arenas) |*d, *character_arena| {
            d.* = try rbt.Data.init(character_arena.allocator(), m);
        }
        for (fleet.terminal) |*state| {
            state.* = try State.init(owned, m.nbody);
        }
        for (fleet.worlds, fleet.bridges, fleet.data, fleet.character_arenas) |*world, *bridge, *d, *character_arena| {
            const character_owned: Allocator = character_arena.allocator();
            world.* = try floorWorld(character_owned, options.task.floor_friction);
            bridge.* = try robot_physics.Bridge.init(character_owned, world, m, d, 256);
            bridge.listen(world);
        }
        @memset(fleet.in_aftermath, false);
        @memset(fleet.return_streaks, 0);
        @memset(fleet.steps_since_loss, 0);
        @memset(fleet.returned, false);
        for (0..options.envs) |env| {
            fleet.restart(env);
        }
        return fleet;
    }

    pub fn deinit(self: *Fleet) void {
        // `rbt.Data` holds its own allocations, so each still gets a `deinit` - it just hands the
        // memory back to the arena, which is about to be thrown away anyway.
        for (self.data) |*d| {
            d.deinit();
        }
        for (self.bridges, self.worlds) |*bridge, *world| {
            bridge.deinit(world);
        }
        // Every character's arena - its world's memory with it.
        for (self.character_arenas) |*character_arena| {
            character_arena.deinit();
        }
        self.reference_data.deinit();
        const gpa: Allocator = self.gpa;
        self.arena.deinit();
        gpa.destroy(self);
    }

    /// Start an environment somewhere new: a random clip, a random frame, a fresh segment.
    /// A new episode for `env` at a RANDOM clip and frame - reference-state initialisation (`startAt`).
    fn restart(self: *Fleet, env: usize) void {
        const random: Random = self.rng.random();
        const clip_index: usize = switch (self.options.clip_assignment) {
            .random => random.uintLessThan(usize, self.clips.len),
            .by_character => env % self.clips.len,
        };
        const frame: usize = self.drawStartFrame(clip_index);
        self.startAt(env, clip_index, frame);
        // A start in trouble (`Pushes.start_share`): drawn only when the fleet asks for them, so a fleet without any
        // consumes its random stream as it always has.
        const pushes: Pushes = self.options.pushes;
        if (pushes.start_share > 0) {
            const schedule_share: f32 = self.pushScheduleShare();
            const starts_in_trouble: bool = random.float(f32) < pushes.start_share * schedule_share;
            if (starts_in_trouble) {
                const top_speed: f32 = pushes.speed_min + (pushes.speed_max - pushes.speed_min) * schedule_share;
                const push_direction_rad: f32 = 2.0 * pi * random.float(f32);
                self.push(env, top_speed, push_direction_rad);
                self.pushes_given += 1;
                self.push_speed_sum += top_speed;
            }
        }
    }

    /// The frame a new episode on clip `clip_index` starts at: uniform over the clip without a curriculum - one draw
    /// from the fleet's stream, as always - and with one, from its mixture (`ResetCurriculum`): uniform, toward the
    /// bins failing most now, or by the bins' long-run weights. Never the clip's first or last frame: a start needs a
    /// frame before it (its velocity) and one after (its first target).
    pub fn drawStartFrame(self: *Fleet, clip_index: usize) usize {
        const random: Random = self.rng.random();
        const clip: *const dance.Clip = self.clips[clip_index];
        const curriculum: ResetCurriculum = self.options.curriculum;
        const uniform_frame: bool = curriculum.bin_seconds <= 0;
        if (uniform_frame) {
            return 1 + random.uintLessThan(usize, clip.frame_count - 2);
        }
        const bins_first: usize = self.bins_start[clip_index];
        const bins_end: usize = self.bins_start[clip_index + 1];
        const rates: []const f32 = self.bin_failure_rates[bins_first..bins_end];
        const history: []f32 = self.bin_history_weights[bins_first..bins_end];
        // The hard draws' weights now - softmax of each bin's losses per second - folded into the long-run weights
        // at every restart.
        const frames_per_second: f32 = 1 / clip.frame_time;
        var hard_total: f32 = 0;
        for (rates) |rate| {
            hard_total += hardWeight(rate, frames_per_second, curriculum.sharpness);
        }
        var history_total: f32 = 0;
        for (history, rates) |*long_run, rate| {
            const hard_share_now: f32 = hardWeight(rate, frames_per_second, curriculum.sharpness) / hard_total;
            long_run.* = curriculum.history_memory * long_run.* + (1 - curriculum.history_memory) * hard_share_now;
            history_total += long_run.*;
        }
        // Which of the three draws.
        const choice: f32 = random.float(f32);
        const hard_end: f32 = curriculum.uniform_share + curriculum.hard_share;
        const is_uniform: bool = choice < curriculum.uniform_share;
        const is_hard: bool = !is_uniform and choice < hard_end;
        if (is_uniform) {
            return 1 + random.uintLessThan(usize, clip.frame_count - 2);
        }
        // A bin by the chosen weights: walk their running sum to a uniform point of their total.
        const target: f32 = random.float(f32) * (if (is_hard) hard_total else history_total);
        var running_total: f32 = 0;
        var bin: usize = rates.len - 1;
        for (rates, history, 0..) |rate, long_run, bin_index| {
            running_total += if (is_hard) hardWeight(rate, frames_per_second, curriculum.sharpness) else long_run;
            if (target < running_total) {
                bin = bin_index;
                break;
            }
        }
        // A frame uniform within the bin, kept off the clip's first and last.
        const bin_frames: usize = binFrames(clip, curriculum);
        const bin_first: usize = bin * bin_frames;
        const bin_end: usize = @min(bin_first + bin_frames, clip.frame_count);
        const within: usize = random.uintLessThan(usize, @max(bin_end -| bin_first, 1));
        const last_start: usize = clip.frame_count - 2;
