        return clamp(bin_first + within, 1, last_start);
    }

    /// A new episode for `env` EXACTLY at `frame` of clip `clip_index`: the character put on the reference there
    /// (and rested on the floor, and pushed off it by `start_noise`, as the task says), its clock at that frame.
    /// `restart` calls it with a random clip and frame - the random draws in the same order as always, so a fleet's
    /// runs are bit-for-bit what they were; a JUDGE calls it with chosen ones (`judge`).
    pub fn startAt(self: *Fleet, env: usize, clip_index: usize, frame: usize) void {
        const clip: *const dance.Clip = self.clips[clip_index];
        assertf(frame >= 1 and frame + 1 < clip.frame_count, @src(), "start frame {d} of a {d}-frame clip", .{
            frame,
            clip.frame_count,
        });
        self.clip_of[env] = clip_index;
        resetToFrame(self.m, &self.data[env], clip, frame);
        if (self.options.task.rest_on_floor) {
            _ = rbt.restOnFloor(self.m, &self.data[env], 0.001);
        }
        perturbStart(self.m, &self.data[env], self.options.start_noise, self.rng.random(), self.scratch);
        self.frame[env] = @intCast(frame);
        self.steps[env] = 0;
        // No aftermath in a fresh episode. `in_aftermath` is left alone: it describes the step just taken, and the step
        // that ends an aftermath is one of its steps, even though the episode it ended is replaced here.
        self.aftermath_steps_left[env] = 0;
        self.return_streaks[env] = 0;
        self.segment[env] = self.next_segment;
        self.next_segment += 1;
    }

    /// What the policy sees for every environment: the simulated character and the reference it is
    /// chasing, each in the root's frame. `out` is `envs * observationSize(m)` long.
    pub fn observe(self: *Fleet, out: []f32) void {
        const size: usize = observationSize(self.m);
        assertf(out.len == self.options.envs * size, @src(), "observations are {d} long, want {d}", .{
            out.len,
            self.options.envs * size,
        });
        const half: usize = size / 2;
        for (0..self.options.envs) |env| {
            const clip: *const dance.Clip = self.clips[self.clip_of[env]];
            rbt.forward(self.m, &self.data[env]);
            stateOf(self.m, &self.data[env], &self.sim_state);
            local(self.sim_state, self.root, out[env * size ..][0..half]);
            self.referenceStateAt(clip, self.frame[env]);
            local(self.reference_state, self.root, out[env * size + half ..][0..half]);
        }
    }

    /// The reference's whole-body state at `frame`, into a caller's `State` with a caller's
    /// scratch `Data` - so a planner can ask about frames ahead without disturbing the fleet's own.
    pub fn referenceStateInto(
        self: *Fleet,
        clip: *const dance.Clip,
        frame: u32,
        d: *rbt.Data,
        out: *State,
    ) void {
        const at: usize = @min(@as(usize, frame), clip.frame_count - 1);
        const root_len: usize = clip.nq - self.m.nq;
        @memcpy(d.pos, clip.pose(at)[root_len..]);
        const previous: usize = if (at == 0) 0 else at - 1;
        rbt.differentiatePos(
            self.m,
            d.vel,
            clip.pose(previous)[root_len..],
            clip.pose(at)[root_len..],
            clip.frame_time,
        );
        d.stage = .stale;
        rbt.forward(self.m, d);
        stateOf(self.m, d, out);
    }

    /// The reference's whole-body state at `frame`, into `reference_state`.
    fn referenceStateAt(self: *Fleet, clip: *const dance.Clip, frame: u32) void {
        const at: usize = @min(@as(usize, frame), clip.frame_count - 1);
        const root_len: usize = clip.nq - self.m.nq;
        @memcpy(self.reference_data.pos, clip.pose(at)[root_len..]);
        const previous: usize = if (at == 0) 0 else at - 1;
        rbt.differentiatePos(
            self.m,
            self.reference_data.vel,
            clip.pose(previous)[root_len..],
            clip.pose(at)[root_len..],
            clip.frame_time,
        );
        self.reference_data.stage = .stale;
        rbt.forward(self.m, &self.reference_data);
        stateOf(self.m, &self.reference_data, &self.reference_state);
    }

    /// The whole-body state of a recorded frame, rebuilt by forward kinematics. `d` is scratch.
    pub fn stateAt(
        self: *Fleet,
        env: usize,
        index: u64,
        d: *rbt.Data,
        out: *State,
    ) void {
        @memcpy(d.pos, self.replay.poseAt(env, index));
        @memcpy(d.vel, self.replay.velocityAt(env, index));
        d.stage = .stale;
        rbt.forward(self.m, d);
        stateOf(self.m, d, out);
    }

    /// The servo targets a recorded frame was driven toward: its reference pose, nudged by the
    /// action that was taken. `scratch` is `m.nv`, `out` is `m.nq`.
    pub fn targetsAt(
        self: *Fleet,
        env: usize,
        index: u64,
        scratch: []f32,
        out: []f32,
    ) void {
        // The clip this RECORD was tracking, not the one its environment is on now - they differ
        // for anything older than the environment's last restart.
        const clip: *const dance.Clip = self.clips[self.replay.clipAt(env, index)];
        // The targets the servo ACTUALLY used for this record's step: the next frame, clamped - exactly
        // as `driveOnce` aims. (This must change whenever that does: the structured world model learns
        // from these, and a target one frame off what the fleet used would be a quiet lie in its data.)
        const frame: usize = @min(@as(usize, self.replay.frameAt(env, index)) + 1, clip.frame_count - 1);
        const root_len: usize = clip.nq - self.m.nq;
        applyAction(
            self.m,
            clip.pose(frame)[root_len..],
            self.replay.actionAt(env, index),
            self.options.action_scale,
            scratch,
            out,
        );
        clampHinges(self.m, out);
    }

    /// Drive one character one frame: turn the action into servo targets on the reference, run the
    /// servo, step, and leave the data forward-current.
    ///
    /// Shared so that a planner imagining a step and the fleet taking one cannot drift apart: an
    /// imagined step that is not the step actually taken is a plan for a different robot.
    pub fn driveOnce(
        self: *const Fleet,
        d: *rbt.Data,
        world: *zimrphysics.World,
        bridge: *robot_physics.Bridge,
        clip: *const dance.Clip,
        frame: u32,
        action: []const f32,
        drive: *DriveScratch,
    ) !void {
        const root_len: usize = clip.nq - self.m.nq;
        // The servo aims where the reference is GOING: during the step from frame i to i+1 it drives
        // toward pose i+1, as SuperTrack's PD targets do (exp(a/2 o) x k_{i+1}). Aiming at pose i left
        // every step a frame (17 ms) behind the motion it was meant to follow - and the tracking error
        // measured after the step is against pose i+1, so aim and score now agree. Clamped at the end.
        const at: usize = @min(@as(usize, frame) + 1, clip.frame_count - 1);
        applyAction(self.m, clip.pose(at)[root_len..], action, self.options.action_scale, drive.scratch, drive.targets);
        clampHinges(self.m, drive.targets);
        // Only when something made the data stale - a restart, a shove, a reset. Every step ENDS
        // with the stages the next one reads, and nothing writes to the data between that and
        // here, so recomputing them would produce the same numbers from the same inputs:
        // measured, that was 28% of a step (127 of 452 us) spent reproducing what was already
        // there. The stage watermark is what makes skipping it safe rather than hopeful.
        if (!d.stage.atLeast(.velocity)) {
            rbt.forward(self.m, d);
        }
        // Collide first, so the step that follows knows about the ground it is standing on.
        try bridge.sync(world, self.m, d);
        try zimrphysics.step(world, clip.frame_time);
        bridge.harvest(d);
        rbt.biasForce(self.m, d);
        const gains: Gains = self.options.task.gains;
        // With feedforward, the velocity of the step the servo aims along: `frame` -> `frame + 1`. At the clip's end
        // the aim is clamped to the last pose - held still - and `referenceVelocity` is zero there, as it must be.
        // (It once asked for `at - 1`: at the end that was the last MOVING step's velocity, telling a joint that
        // should come to rest to keep going - and a one-frame clip underflowed.)
        const moving: ?[]const f32 = if (gains.velocity_feedforward) blk: {
            referenceVelocity(self.m, clip, frame, drive.target_velocity);
            break :blk drive.target_velocity;
        } else null;
        pdTorquesToward(
            self.m,
            d,
            drive.targets,
            moving,
            gains,
            clip.frame_time,
            drive.accel,
            drive.scratch,
            drive.dense,
            drive.full,
            drive.torque,
        );
        @memcpy(d.applied_force, drive.torque);
        // `step` runs a complete `forward` of its own before it integrates, so a full one here
        // would compute the factorisation, the constraints and the dynamics solve only for the
        // next step's `step` to compute them again. What is READ between now and then is less:
        // body poses and velocities (the fleet's state, the bridge's sync) and the mass matrix
        // (the servo's torques). Exactly those four stages, in `forward`'s own order - which
        // leaves the watermark at `velocity`, and the guard above asks for no more than that.
        rbt.step(self.m, d);
        rbt.kinematics(self.m, d);
        rbt.comPos(self.m, d);
        rbt.crb(self.m, d);
        rbt.comVel(self.m, d);
    }

    /// Every character's physics step (`driveOnce`): split into `drive_scratches.len` tasks of consecutive characters
    /// run on `physics_io`'s threads and waited for, or - without threads, or with one task - in one loop here. A
    /// character's collision world failing is flagged (`drive_failed`) for the step to report.
    fn driveEveryCharacter(self: *Fleet, actions: []const f32) void {
        const envs: usize = self.options.envs;
        const task_count: usize = self.drive_scratches.len;
        const io: Io = self.physics_io orelse {
            driveCharacters(self, 0, envs, actions, 0);
            return;
        };
        if (task_count <= 1) {
            driveCharacters(self, 0, envs, actions, 0);
            return;
        }
        var group: Io.Group = .init;
        for (0..task_count) |task| {
            const first: usize = task * envs / task_count;
            const end: usize = (task + 1) * envs / task_count;
            group.async(io, driveCharacters, .{ self, first, end, actions, task });
        }
        group.await(io) catch |err| {
            zm.assertUnreachable(@src(), "the physics' tasks were canceled: {s}", .{@errorName(err)});
        };
    }

    /// Characters [`first`, `end`)'s physics steps, in `task`'s scratch - one of `driveEveryCharacter`'s tasks.
    fn driveCharacters(
        self: *Fleet,
        first: usize,
        end: usize,
        actions: []const f32,
        task: usize,
    ) void {
        const size: usize = actionSize(self.m);
        const drive: *DriveScratch = &self.drive_scratches[task];
        for (first..end) |env| {
            const clip: *const dance.Clip = self.clips[self.clip_of[env]];
            const action: []const f32 = actions[env * size ..][0..size];
            const at: u32 = self.frame[env];
            self.drive_failed[env] = false;
            self.driveOnce(&self.data[env], &self.worlds[env], &self.bridges[env], clip, at, action, drive) catch {
                self.drive_failed[env] = true;
            };
        }
    }

    /// One frame for every environment: act, drive, step, record, and start again where needed.
    /// `actions` is `envs * actionSize(m)` long, each in [-1, 1]. Returns the mean reward.
    /// A ground to stand on: a large static box with its top face at z = 0, as the dance rungs use.
    pub fn floorWorld(gpa: Allocator, friction: f32) !zimrphysics.World {
        var world: zimrphysics.World = try .init(gpa, 64);
        errdefer world.deinit(gpa);
        world.gravity = vec(0, 0, -9.81);
        world.settings.allow_sleeping = false;
        world.settings.penetration_slop = 0.005;
        const ground: zimrphysics.ShapeId = try world.shapes.add(gpa, .{
            .box = .{ .half_extent = vec(20, 20, 0.5), .convex_radius = 0.01 },
        });
        _ = try world.createBody(.{
            .shape = ground,
            .position = vec(0, 0, -0.5),
            .motion_type = .static,
            .friction = friction,
        });
        return world;
    }

    /// Whether character `env` lives on through an aftermath after a loss (`Options.aftermath_share`).
    ///
    /// The living-on characters are the first ones by index, so the split is fixed for the fleet's whole life: a
    /// character is either one that resets at a loss or one that lives on, never one, then the other. That keeps the
    /// population's two kinds of data in fixed proportion - the share asked for - whatever the order in which the
    /// characters happen to fail.
    pub fn keepsAftermath(self: *const Fleet, env: usize) bool {
        const character_count: f32 = float(self.options.envs);
        const living_on_count: usize = @round(self.options.aftermath_share * character_count);
        const is_among_living_on: bool = env < living_on_count;
        return is_among_living_on;
    }

    /// Push character `env` (`Pushes`): its whole body's velocity changed by `speed` m/s in the horizontal direction
    /// `direction_rad` (0 along x, a quarter turn along y), and a new segment begun. What the random pushes, the
    /// scheduled ones and the recovery probe all do.
    ///
    /// WHY ONLY THE ROOT'S VELOCITY CHANGES. The character is a floating-base chain: its generalised velocity is the
    /// root's linear and angular velocity, then every joint's rate relative to its parent. Adding to the root's linear
    /// velocity alone moves every body by the same amount - the joints' relative rates are untouched - which is
    /// exactly an impulse of (total mass x speed) applied at the centre of mass: a push that shoves the whole body
    /// without twisting it. The first two numbers of the generalised velocity are the root's x and y.
    ///
    /// WHY A NEW SEGMENT. The replay's windows must be unbroken stretches of motion that a world model can predict
    /// from the state alone. A push comes from outside the state - nothing in the step before it could have seen it
    /// coming - so the stretch before it and the stretch after it are two segments, and no window spans the push.
    /// How far the pushes' schedule has come (`Pushes.scheduleShare`) at the training hours the fleet was told.
    pub fn pushScheduleShare(self: *const Fleet) f32 {
        return self.options.pushes.scheduleShare(self.training_hours);
    }

    pub fn push(self: *Fleet, env: usize, speed: f32, direction_rad: f32) void {
        const character_data: *rbt.Data = &self.data[env];
        const velocity_change_x: f32 = speed * @cos(direction_rad);
        const velocity_change_y: f32 = speed * @sin(direction_rad);
        character_data.vel[0] += velocity_change_x;
        character_data.vel[1] += velocity_change_y;
        // The velocity changed behind the simulator's back: everything derived from it must be recomputed.
        character_data.stage = .stale;
        self.segment[env] = self.next_segment;
        self.next_segment += 1;
    }

    pub fn step(self: *Fleet, actions: []const f32) f32 {
        const size: usize = actionSize(self.m);
        assertf(actions.len == self.options.envs * size, @src(), "actions are {d} long, want {d}", .{
            actions.len,
            self.options.envs * size,
        });
        const random: Random = self.rng.random();
        var reward_total: f32 = 0.0;
        // Every character's state recorded, in order.
        for (0..self.options.envs) |env| {
            const d: *rbt.Data = &self.data[env];
            const action: []const f32 = actions[env * size ..][0..size];
            const at: u32 = self.frame[env];

            // Record the state the action was taken FROM, so a window reads as
            // (state, action) -> the next record's state.
            // And how far into its episode this step is, which is what says what was being applied before it.
            self.replay.appendStep(
                env,
                d.pos,
                d.vel,
                action,
                at,
                @intCast(self.clip_of[env]),
                self.segment[env],
                self.steps[env],
                self.aftermath_steps_left[env] > 0,
            );
        }
        // Every character's physics, in tasks when the fleet has threads (`Options.physics_threads`): each step
        // touches only its character's own data, world and bridge, and its task's scratch.
        self.driveEveryCharacter(actions);
        for (0..self.options.envs) |env| {
            const clip: *const dance.Clip = self.clips[self.clip_of[env]];
            const d: *rbt.Data = &self.data[env];
            const at: u32 = self.frame[env];
            // Loudly: a collision world that quietly stops working leaves a character quietly
            // falling through the floor, which is exactly the failure this coupling was added for.
            if (self.drive_failed[env]) {
                zm.assertUnreachable(@src(), "the collision world failed mid-step: character {d}", .{env});
            }

            self.frame[env] += 1;
            self.steps[env] += 1;
            self.steps_total += 1;
            stateOf(self.m, d, &self.sim_state);
            exemptFromContact(&self.sim_state, self.contact_exempt);
            self.referenceStateAt(clip, self.frame[env]);
            const sim: State = self.sim_state;
            const err: TrackingError = trackingErrorWithHead(sim, self.reference_state, self.root, self.head);
            const earned: f32 = reward(err, self.options.task.weights);
            self.rewards[env] = earned;
            self.dones[env] = false;
            reward_total += earned;

            // A character whose state is no longer finite is broken, grace or not: every comparison
            // with NaN is false, so the limits alone would let it run on - poisoning the world - forever.
            const broken: bool = !(err.pose_position == err.pose_position and err.pose_rotation == err.pose_rotation and
                err.root_position == err.root_position and err.root_rotation == err.root_rotation);
            const graced: bool = self.steps[env] < self.options.task.termination.grace_steps;
            // In an aftermath the reference is already lost: the rule is not asked again, and the step is not at risk.
            const was_in_aftermath: bool = self.aftermath_steps_left[env] > 0;
            self.in_aftermath[env] = was_in_aftermath;
            const rule_fires: bool = !graced and !was_in_aftermath and terminated(err, self.options.task.termination);
            // The FAILURE: the step the reference is lost - counted once, never again in the aftermath that follows.
            const lost: bool = !was_in_aftermath and (broken or rule_fires);
            // A lost character lives on through its aftermath, unless it is broken - a body that is no longer finite
            // cannot be simulated further - or the fleet keeps none.
            // THE RETURN: in an aftermath the rule is asked the other way round - is the reference held again? - and a
            // character holding it `return_steps` steps in a row has returned (`Options.return_steps`).
            self.returned[env] = false;
            if (was_in_aftermath) {
                self.steps_since_loss[env] += 1;
                const holds_again: bool = !broken and !terminated(err, self.options.task.termination);
                self.return_streaks[env] = if (holds_again) self.return_streaks[env] + 1 else 0;
                const return_steps: u32 = self.options.return_steps;
                self.returned[env] = return_steps > 0 and self.return_streaks[env] >= return_steps;
            }
            const keeps_aftermath: bool = self.keepsAftermath(env);
            const has_aftermath: bool = self.options.aftermath_steps > 0 and keeps_aftermath;
            const aftermath_begins: bool = rule_fires and !broken and has_aftermath;
            if (aftermath_begins) {
                self.aftermath_steps_left[env] = self.options.aftermath_steps;
                self.return_streaks[env] = 0;
                self.steps_since_loss[env] = 0;
            } else if (self.returned[env]) {
                // Back with the reference: the aftermath ends here, and the episode goes on.
                self.aftermath_steps_left[env] = 0;
                self.returns += 1;
                self.return_steps_sum += self.steps_since_loss[env];
            } else if (was_in_aftermath) {
                self.aftermath_steps_left[env] -= 1;
            }
            // An aftermath ends its episode only when it runs out - a failure to return.
            const aftermath_ran_out: bool = self.aftermath_steps_left[env] == 0;
            const aftermath_over: bool = was_in_aftermath and !self.returned[env] and aftermath_ran_out;
            const capped: bool = self.steps[env] >= self.options.max_steps;
            const clip_over: bool = self.frame[env] + 1 >= clip.frame_count;
            const ends_at_loss: bool = lost and !aftermath_begins;
            // A broken body ends its episode whenever it breaks, in an aftermath too.
            const finished: bool = ends_at_loss or broken or aftermath_over or capped or clip_over;
            // The failure is the step the reference was lost, whether the episode ends there or lives on.
            self.failures[env] = lost;
            // The curriculum's running failure rate of the bin this step's reference frame fell in.
            if (self.bins_start.len > 0) {
                const curriculum: ResetCurriculum = self.options.curriculum;
                const clip_index: usize = self.clip_of[env];
                const bin_in_clip: usize = at / binFrames(clip, curriculum);
                const bins_first: usize = self.bins_start[clip_index];
                const bins_end: usize = self.bins_start[clip_index + 1];
                const bin: usize = @min(bins_first + bin_in_clip, bins_end - 1);
                const outcome: f32 = if (lost) 1 else 0;
                const rate: *f32 = &self.bin_failure_rates[bin];
                rate.* += (1 - curriculum.rate_memory) * (outcome - rate.*);
            }
            if (lost) {
                self.failed += 1;
            }
            if (finished) {
                self.episodes += 1;
                self.dones[env] = true;
                // Why it ended, and where - before `restart` replaces the state just measured. An episode that ends
                // during its aftermath - by its end, the cap or the clip - ended because its reference was lost.
                const ended_in_aftermath: bool = was_in_aftermath or aftermath_begins;
                self.ends[env] = if (ends_at_loss)
                    .lost
                else if (ended_in_aftermath)
                    .aftermath
                else if (capped)
                    .cap
                else
                    .clip_end;
                self.terminal[env].copyFrom(self.sim_state);
                self.terminal_frame[env] = self.frame[env];
                self.terminal_clip[env] = self.clip_of[env];
                self.restart(env);
                continue;
            }
            // A push from outside (`Pushes`): on the schedule, or at a random moment.
            //
            // The random moments are a POISSON PROCESS of `rate_per_second`, made one step at a time: each step pushes
            // with probability rate x dt, independently of every other step. Over a second that is about `rate`
            // pushes, with the gaps between them exponentially distributed - no rhythm a policy could learn to expect.
            // (A Bernoulli draw per step is the Poisson process exactly in the limit of small rate x dt; at 60 Hz and a
            // push every few seconds, rate x dt is below 0.01, and two pushes in one step never matter.)
            const push_settings: Pushes = self.options.pushes;
            const is_scheduled_push: bool = push_settings.every > 0 and self.steps[env] % push_settings.every == 0;
            const step_seconds: f32 = self.m.opt.timestep;
            // The random pushes' rate and the speeds' range as far as the schedule has opened them.
            const schedule_share: f32 = self.pushScheduleShare();
            const push_probability_this_step: f32 = push_settings.rate_per_second * schedule_share * step_seconds;
            const pushes_at_random: bool = push_settings.rate_per_second > 0;
            const is_random_push: bool = pushes_at_random and random.float(f32) < push_probability_this_step;
            if (is_scheduled_push or is_random_push) {
                // The speed uniform in its range, the direction uniform round the vertical.
                const full_range: f32 = push_settings.speed_max - push_settings.speed_min;
                const push_speed_range: f32 = full_range * schedule_share;
                const push_speed: f32 = push_settings.speed_min + push_speed_range * random.float(f32);
                const push_direction_rad: f32 = 2.0 * pi * random.float(f32);
                self.push(env, push_speed, push_direction_rad);
                self.pushes_given += 1;
                self.push_speed_sum += push_speed;
            }
        }
        self.last_reward = reward_total / float(self.options.envs);
        return self.last_reward;
    }
};

Living on after a loss. A fleet can let a character live on after it loses the reference, for an aftermath of a few seconds: the step the failure rule fires is the failure, counted once, and the character is then simulated and rewarded as usual - its fall, under the task's reward - before its episode is cut. The fleet can keep this for a share of its characters only: the ones that reset keep the data near the reference, the ones that live on bring falls and what follows them. The replay records, for every row, whether its step came after a loss, and the two networks read that differently. The world model learns from every window, falls included - how a body falls is what it must know to be trusted there. The policy's pathwise loss starts its windows only on steps before a loss: through a fall the tracking loss's gradients saturate to nothing, so a window that starts in an aftermath adds only noise.

   steps      t0 ............ loss ........................ end of aftermath
   rows       before loss     | after loss (flagged) ..........|
   world model windows    [------]   [------]   [------]          from anywhere
   policy windows      [------]  [------]                         start before the loss (may run into it)

11.8 What the world model is asked, and how it is judged#

The question is: given the character as it is, and what the servo has been told to reach for, how does every body accelerate? The state goes in as §11.5's representation. The targets go in as two numbers a hinge (sine and cosine, because an angle wraps) and six a ball — not as the servo's error, tempting as that is, because during a rollout the state is the model's own guess and feeding the error would mix the model's drift into its own input.

worldInputSize
/// What a world model sees: the character in its own frame, and what the servo has been told to
/// reach for.
///
/// Not the servo's ERROR, tempting as that is - the error depends on the state, and during a
/// rollout the state is the model's own guess, so feeding the error would quietly mix the model's
/// drift into its input. The targets are known for the whole window whatever the model predicts.
pub fn worldInputSize(m: *const rbt.Model) usize {
    return localSize(m.nbody) + targetSize(m);
}
encodeTargets
pub fn encodeTargets(m: *const rbt.Model, targets: []const f32, out: []f32) void {
    assertf(out.len == targetSize(m), @src(), "targets encode to {d} numbers, got {d}", .{ targetSize(m), out.len });
    var at: usize = 0;
    for (0..m.njnt) |j| {
        const q: usize = m.jnt_qpos_adr[j];
        switch (m.jnt_type[j]) {
            .free => {},
            .ball => {
                const axes: [6]f32 = twoAxis(.{ targets[q], targets[q + 1], targets[q + 2], targets[q + 3] });
                @memcpy(out[at..][0..6], &axes);
                at += 6;
            },
            .hinge, .slide => {
                out[at] = @sin(targets[q]);
                out[at + 1] = @cos(targets[q]);
                at += 2;
            },
        }
    }
}

The answer comes back as every body's linear and angular acceleration, in the root's frame and divided by a scale, so a network's outputs sit near one instead of near a hundred.

decodeAccelerations
/// And back out, into the world, ready for `integrate`.
pub fn decodeAccelerations(
    state: State,
    root: usize,
    in: []const f32,
    linear: []Vec,
    angular: []Vec,
) void {
    const to_world: Quat = state.rotations[root];
    const bodies: usize = state.bodies();
    linear[0] = vec_zero;
    angular[0] = vec_zero;
    for (1..bodies) |b| {
        const at: usize = (b - 1) * 3;
        linear[b] = rotate(to_world, vec(in[at], in[at + 1], in[at + 2])) * splat(acceleration_scale);
    }
    const half: usize = (bodies - 1) * 3;
    for (1..bodies) |b| {
        const at: usize = half + (b - 1) * 3;
        angular[b] = rotate(to_world, vec(in[at], in[at + 1], in[at + 2])) * splat(acceleration_scale);
    }
}

And then the judgement, which matters more than the training loss: a model that is excellent for one step and hopeless by eight is no use to a policy unrolled for thirty-two. So a model is rolled forward through recorded windows on its own predictions, with the targets coming from the record, and the drift is measured at every step.

measureDrift
/// Roll a source forward through recorded windows and measure how fast it drifts.
///
/// This is the diagnostic that says whether a world model is worth training a policy through: a
/// model that is excellent for one step and hopeless by eight is no use to a policy unrolled for
/// thirty-two. Each rollout starts on a recorded state, then feeds the model its OWN predictions
/// while the targets come from the record - which is exactly how it will be used.
///
/// `steps` is the horizon; `drift.position[k]` is the error after k + 1 steps.
pub fn measureDrift(
    gpa: Allocator,
    fleet: *Fleet,
    source: Source,
    draws: usize,
    steps: usize,
    random: Random,
) !Drift {
    const m: *rbt.Model = fleet.m;
    const position: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, steps);
    errdefer gpa.free(position);
    const rotation: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, steps);
    errdefer gpa.free(rotation);
    const pose: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, steps);
    errdefer gpa.free(pose);
    @memset(position, 0.0);
    @memset(rotation, 0.0);
    @memset(pose, 0.0);

    var predicted: State = try .init(gpa, m.nbody);
    defer predicted.deinit(gpa);
    var actual: State = try .init(gpa, m.nbody);
    defer actual.deinit(gpa);
    const input: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, worldInputSize(m));
    defer gpa.free(input);
    const output: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, worldOutputSize(m));
    defer gpa.free(output);
    const linear: []Vec = try gpa.alloc(Vec, m.nbody);
    defer gpa.free(linear);
    const angular: []Vec = try gpa.alloc(Vec, m.nbody);
    defer gpa.free(angular);
    const targets: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, m.nq);
    defer gpa.free(targets);
    const scratch: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, m.nv);
    defer gpa.free(scratch);
    var scratch_data: rbt.Data = try .init(gpa, m);
    defer scratch_data.deinit();

    var held: State = try .init(gpa, m.nbody);
    defer held.deinit(gpa);
    const held_linear: []Vec = try gpa.alloc(Vec, m.nbody);
    defer gpa.free(held_linear);
    const held_angular: []Vec = try gpa.alloc(Vec, m.nbody);
    defer gpa.free(held_angular);
    const dt: f32 = m.opt.timestep;

    var windows: usize = 0;
    for (0..draws) |_| {
        const window: Replay.Window = fleet.replay.sampleWindow(random, steps) orelse continue;
        windows += 1;
        fleet.stateAt(window.env, window.first, &scratch_data, &predicted);
        if (source == .hold_first) {
            // The window's first real transition, kept for the whole rollout.
            fleet.stateAt(window.env, window.first + 1, &scratch_data, &held);
            accelerationsBetween(predicted, held, dt, held_linear, held_angular);
        }
        for (0..steps) |k| {
            const index: u64 = window.first + k;
            switch (source) {
                .learned => |predictor| {
                    fleet.targetsAt(window.env, index, scratch, targets);
                    encodeWorldInput(m, predicted, fleet.root, targets, input);
                    predictor.predict(input, output);
                    decodeAccelerations(predicted, fleet.root, output, linear, angular);
                },
                .oracle => {
                    // What the simulator did between these two records, in the world - the floor.
                    fleet.stateAt(window.env, index, &scratch_data, &held);
                    fleet.stateAt(window.env, index + 1, &scratch_data, &actual);
                    accelerationsBetween(held, actual, dt, linear, angular);
                },
                .hold_first => {
                    @memcpy(linear, held_linear);
                    @memcpy(angular, held_angular);
                },
            }
            integrate(&predicted, linear, angular, dt);
            fleet.stateAt(window.env, index + 1, &scratch_data, &actual);
            pose[k] += trackingError(predicted, actual, fleet.root).pose_position;
            for (1..m.nbody) |b| {
                position[k] += length3(predicted.positions[b] - actual.positions[b]) / float(m.nbody - 1);
                rotation[k] += angleBetween(predicted.rotations[b], actual.rotations[b]) / float(m.nbody - 1);
            }
        }
    }
    for (position, rotation, pose) |*p, *r, *q| {
        p.* /= float(@max(windows, 1));
        r.* /= float(@max(windows, 1));
        q.* /= float(@max(windows, 1));
    }
    return .{ .position = position, .rotation = rotation, .pose = pose, .windows = windows };
}

Two sources that need no training calibrate that measurement. Fed the accelerations the simulator actually produced, the rollout drifts only by what an explicit integrator costs — a quarter of a millimetre a step, under two millimetres after eight. Given the window's first acceleration and told to hold it, the rollout is 35 cm out by the same point. That is the range a learned model has to land inside, and the two agree exactly on their first step, which is a free check that the harness has no seam in it.

Source
/// Where a rollout's accelerations come from.
///
/// The two reference sources live here rather than behind `Predictor` because neither is a model:
/// both are properties of the RECORD, and a harness that cannot measure them cannot be trusted to
/// measure a network either.
///
///   * `oracle` - the accelerations the simulator actually produced at each step. Its drift is the
///     floor: whatever an explicit integrator costs, nothing can do better.
///   * `hold_first` - the window's first real acceleration, held for the whole rollout. A model
///     that cannot beat this has learned nothing about how a humanoid moves.
pub const Source = union(enum) {
    learned: Predictor,
    oracle,
    hold_first,
};

11.9 The model itself#

With the question fixed and the measurement calibrated, the model is an ordinary network on the kit: the features in, every body's acceleration out. Each training example is one recorded transition — the state the simulator was in, the targets it was driven toward, and the acceleration it actually produced.

WorldModel.Options
pub const Options = struct {
    /// Hidden widths. The kit's buffers hold 2^18 floats and the parameters have to fit beside the
    /// activations, so 256 + 256 is the widest that fits comfortably for this feature set - see
    /// `kit_mlp`'s size check, which says so with numbers if you get it wrong.
    hidden: []const u32 = &.{ 256, 256 },
    /// Transitions per training step.
    rows: u32 = 128,
    rate: f32 = 1.0e-3,
    seed: u64 = 1,
};
WorldModel.trainStep
/// Fill a batch from the replay and take one step on it. Null when the replay cannot yet
/// supply a full batch of transitions.
pub fn trainStep(self: *Self, fleet: *track.Fleet, random: Random) !?f32 {
    const in_dim: usize = track.worldInputSize(self.m);
    const out_dim: usize = track.worldOutputSize(self.m);
    const dt: f32 = self.m.opt.timestep;
    for (0..self.options.rows) |row| {
        const window: track.Replay.Window = fleet.replay.sampleWindow(random, 1) orelse return null;
        fleet.stateAt(window.env, window.first, &self.data, &self.before);
        fleet.stateAt(window.env, window.first + 1, &self.data, &self.after);
        fleet.targetsAt(window.env, window.first, self.scratch, self.servo_targets);
        track.encodeWorldInput(
            self.m,
            self.before,
            fleet.root,
            self.servo_targets,
            self.inputs[row * in_dim ..][0..in_dim],
        );
        track.accelerationsBetween(self.before, self.after, dt, self.linear, self.angular);
        track.encodeAccelerations(
            self.before,
            fleet.root,
            self.linear,
            self.angular,
            self.targets[row * out_dim ..][0..out_dim],
        );
    }
    return try self.net.trainStep(self.inputs, self.targets);
}

That is deliberately simpler than SuperTrack's, which rolls the model through a window and backpropagates the whole rollout's error — and the drift curve is what says whether the simpler thing suffices. Trained on data from a character tracking a clip with noise for a policy, a 256-wide network reaches these errors, against the two calibrated sources:

horizonoracle (the integrator's floor)the learned modelholding the last acceleration
8 steps2.7 mm61 mm357 mm
32 steps9.5 mm1.42 m6.04 m

Which is the whole argument for measuring a model this way rather than by its loss. At eight steps it is worth planning through: six centimetres, a fifth of what the baseline costs, and small against the ten-centimetre scale the tracking reward cares about. At thirty-two it is 1.4 metres out — not a model of anything, with the oracle's 9.5 mm confirming the fault is the model's own error compounding rather than the measurement. So a controller may be unrolled through this model for eight frames and no further, and a policy that wants a longer horizon needs either a value function to carry the rest or a world model trained through its own rollout.

11.10 A world model in its own feature space#

The model above predicts every body's acceleration and integrates it: physically honest, but it means a rollout passes through quaternion updates, rotations into the root's frame and two-axis encodings, and training anything through that rollout means differentiating each of them by hand. The latent world model skips the physics bookkeeping. Its state is the feature vector itself — the character in its own root frame — and one step is

z' = z + Net(z, reference targets, action)

so a rollout is a chain of networks and additions that any automatic differentiation handles unchanged. It is the shape of TD-MPC2's latent dynamics, with the latent space chosen for us: features that already mean something. Three choices carry it:

Everything lives in normalised feature space. Positions, velocities, rotations and angular velocities have spreads that differ by orders of magnitude; standardised once from data, every feature counts alike in the rollout, in the model's loss, and in the tracking loss a policy will later be trained on. The data is the reference clips themselves: every frame of the motion, posed exactly as the reference is posed during training. So one unit of any feature means "as far as the dance itself ranges", fixed before the first step — not whatever a character happened to do while it was still falling over, which would make every normal pose look extreme. The action goes in as itself, beside the reference's encoded targets, rather than being folded into the targets first — so the path from a policy's output to the model's input is linear, and a tracking loss flows back into the policy with nothing hand-derived in between. The first layer is three matrix products summed, one each for the features, the targets and the action: a concatenation of the three, written without one.

It is trained the way a model meant to be unrolled must be: through its own rollouts. Each example is a window of recorded steps; the model starts on the real first state, is fed its own predictions after that, and every step's error counts. Rolled out that way it stays within a few centimetres of the simulator's pose over half a second — long enough for a policy to learn through.

The same model also trains entirely on the GPU, with the kit's ordinary dense kernels — §13.2 shows how.

LatentWorld.step
/// One step of the model on the graph: z + Net(z, ref, act). Public so a policy's graph can
/// roll out through the same weights (`robot_track_st`).
pub fn step(
    g: *Graph,
    v: [8]Var,
    z: Var,
    ref: Var,
    act: Var,
    ones: Var,
) !Var {
    const into: Var = try g.add(
        try g.add(try g.matmul(z, v[0]), try g.matmul(ref, v[1])),
        try g.add(try g.matmul(act, v[2]), try g.matmul(ones, v[3])),
    );
    const h1: Var = try g.tanh(into);
    const h2: Var = try g.tanh(try g.add(try g.matmul(h1, v[4]), try g.matmul(ones, v[5])));
    const delta: Var = try g.add(try g.matmul(h2, v[6]), try g.matmul(ones, v[7]));
    return g.add(z, delta);
}
LatentWorld.trainStep
/// One training step on `batch` windows drawn from the fleet's replay. Null if the replay
/// cannot supply them yet.
pub fn trainStep(self: *LatentWorld, fleet: *track.Fleet) !?f32 {
    // All the windows are drawn BEFORE any is filled in. Filling draws no random numbers, so the
    // sequence of draws is exactly what it was when drawing and filling were interleaved - every
    // test measured before the split (D15, T8d) still sees the same windows.
    const random: Random = self.rng.random();
    for (self.windows) |*window| {
        window.* = fleet.replay.sampleWindow(random, self.options.steps) orelse return null;
    }
    return try self.trainOn(fleet, self.windows);
}

11.11 A policy trained through the model#

PPO learns from a number — how much reward an action earned — and must guess, from very many samples, which way to nudge the policy. A policy trained through a differentiable world model learns from a direction. A window of motion is rolled out with the policy in the loop: the policy acts on the model's predicted features, the model predicts the consequences, and the distance from the reference's features is measured at every step. That distance is backpropagated through every predicted step into the policy's weights, so each sample says not just "worse" but "this joint, this way".

The loop is SuperTrack's: collect with the current policy in the real simulator, with a little exploration noise; train the world model through its own rollouts on windows of what was recorded; train the policy on windows that start on real recorded states — so a window never begins somewhere the simulator has not been — rolled forward through the model. The world model's weights sit in the policy's graph, sharing memory with the model itself, but only the policy's optimiser runs there. Exploration noise lives inside the training rollouts too, so the policy learns corrections that still work when it cannot act exactly as it meant to.

Everything aims at the next frame. During the step from frame i to i+1, the servo drives toward the reference's pose at i+1 — where the motion is going, not where it was — and the tracking error measured after the step is against that same pose, so aim and score agree. The policy is shown that goal too (SuperTrack's Ki+1), and the world model's reference input is the pose the servo actually used. An action is the raw policy output plus its noise; one scale, applied by the fleet where the action becomes a PD offset, turns it into radians — so the world model learns from exactly what the fleet records.

The policy decides thirty times a second, and its hands are filtered. Physics steps sixty times a second; the policy is asked only on every second step and its decision is held for both. What it asks for is not applied directly either: each decision is blended into the action already being applied, a fifth of the new and four fifths of the old (DReCon's filter), so no joint's target ever jumps and a policy that wants a joint to move quickly must ask for more, for longer. Both live inside the training rollouts too, not just in the simulator: a held step reuses the decision, and the blend is differentiated like everything else, so a decision is credited with every later step it still shapes. And the world model is taught with the action that was actually applied — the filtered one the servo received — because that, not what the policy asked for, is what moved the body.

And it sees what it is applying. Behind a filter, the same request means different things from different places: asking for 1.0 while 0.9 is already applied is a nudge, and the same 1.0 from rest is a shove. So what to ask depends on what is already being applied, and a policy that cannot see it is blind to half of its own control state. With sees_applied on, the action being applied just before each decision is a third input to the policy's first layer, beside the character and the reference — DReCon's observation carries the same thing. It is read through a block of weights of its own that starts at zero, so the policy begins exactly as one that cannot see it and learns to read the input as training goes. At an episode's start it is told rest. In the training rollouts it is the filter's state as it stands before each decision, differentiated like everything else, so a decision is also credited with how it changes what later decisions are told.

All of that is one value. The action's reach (0.6 rad a unit), the exploration noise, the 30 Hz clock, the 0.2 filter, seeing what it applies, the normaliser from the clip and a training grace (the paper's shortest episode, 48 steps, during which the task's rule does not end an episode — the judge never has one) are Geno's SuperTrack recipe, robot_geno.supertrack_recipe — handed whole to whatever trains, never rebuilt setting by setting at the place it is used, which is how settings quietly drift apart. It carries the action's reach beside the learner's options because the reach belongs to the fleet: it turns a unit of action into a joint offset before the learner sees anything. An experiment copies the recipe and changes one field. Its tests check each choice against its reason rather than its number: the clock and the filter must agree with DReCon's controller, a filtered policy must see what it applies, and a learner built from the recipe must come out with 30 decisions a second on Geno's own timestep and the clip's normaliser, bit for bit.

A change to the recipe is judged by a learning curve. zig build st-bench builds a bench that trains the CPU learner on the 10-second dance from the recipe and, every so often, judges the policy in the real simulator from the same 20 starts and asks the world model how far it can be trusted where the policy goes. It is deterministic — the same seed gives the same curve, number for number — so two runs that differ in one setting are a comparison rather than two anecdotes. It comes in two builds that give identical numbers: a fast one for long runs, and a checked one, slower, that watches every index and stops on any failed check. A new setting's first stretch is run checked, and the long fast run is then held against it row by row.

One principle governs all of it: a policy trained through a model can only be as right as the model. Where the model cannot yet say what an action does, the policy learns to exploit its mistakes — large actions that look good in prediction and do nothing in the simulator. So the model is trained first, on data whose actions actually vary; the collection noise is wide enough to keep teaching it what actions do; and the policy pays a price for the size of its actions, which keeps it where the model has seen data. And the judge is always the simulator, never the model.

Two models, and where they disagree. The learner can also train a second world model beside the first — the same data, a different starting point (twin_world). Where the data pins them down, the two predict alike; off the data nothing does, and they drift apart. So their disagreement is a map of exactly where the model cannot be trusted — which is also where a policy would exploit it. The policy's rollouts step through the two models' average, and every step pays for the distance between their predictions (w_disagree): steering toward states the models disagree on costs something, and the gradient pulls the policy back toward what both of them know. It knocks nothing the models already predict well: where they agree, it costs nothing at all.

Smooth, not just small. A price on an action's size does not stop it from changing. A policy trained through a model can learn outputs that swing with every small change of state, so on a character every joint's target lurches each frame and the servo spends itself chasing them — a body that looks like it is exploding, and falls more for it. So the policy also pays for how far its action moves from one step of the window to the next, w_smooth · |ak − ak−1|² (the temporal term of CAPS). The gradient reaches both steps of each pair — the later action pulled back toward the earlier and the earlier toward the later — which is the difference between smoothing a trajectory and merely dragging it.

Learner.trainPolicy
/// One policy update on `batch` windows of the replay: start on the real recorded state,
/// then roll the policy through the model. Null until the replay can supply the windows.
pub fn trainPolicy(self: *Learner) !?f32 {
    const random: Random = self.rng.random();
    // Sample and fill row by row, in that order: filling draws the rollout's noise from the same
    // random stream, so drawing every window first would reorder the draws - and silently change
    // every result measured with this learner.
    for (0..self.options.batch) |row| {
        const window: track.Replay.Window = self.drawWindow(random, self.options.window) orelse return null;
        self.fillRow(row, window, random);
    }
    return try self.update();
}

A barrier before the cliff. The task's failure rule is a cliff: one step the character is tracking, the next its episode is lost, and a gradient through the world model cannot see a cliff coming. The policy's loss can carry a barrier that puts a slope in front of it. At every rolled step it adds a smooth hinge on two of the rule's own measures, read from the rolled features: the head's height error against its margin of 0.25 m, and the tilt between the character's up and the reference's - one minus the cosine of their angle - against a margin of 90 degrees. A smooth hinge is width x softplus((value - margin) / width): about nothing well inside the margin, it starts to rise a few widths before the edge, and past it costs the distance in the measure's own units. Its slope is the logistic sigmoid of the same ratio - 0 inside, one half at the margin, 1 past it - so the policy is pushed away from a fall before the rule fires.

   cost                                   /  past the margin: the distance itself
                                        /
                                     _/     at the margin: width x ln 2, slope 1/2
      ______________________....---''
      inside: about nothing, slope ~ 0       ^ margin (0.25 m of head height error; 90 degrees of tilt)

The barrier reads the head's height and the up direction because both are features of the state - each body's world height, and the world's up seen from the root - un-normalised before the hinge. The rule's third measure, the root's distance from the reference's root, is not: the features describe each character in its own root's frame, so how far it has drifted from the reference is not in the state the model rolls. Its weight is a run setting; at 0 the loss is exactly the one without it.

The cost after the window. A window's loss sees the cost of its own steps and nothing after them. A critic estimates what comes after: C(s), the tracking cost a character can expect from state s onward, discounted - the cost of the next state, plus the discount times the critic of that state,

   C(s_k) = c(s_(k+1)) + gamma x C(s_(k+1))        c = (1/features) x |z - g|^2 + barrier weight x hinges
   gamma  = 1 - 1/90 per physics step: a horizon of about a second and a half at 60 Hz

with c exactly the per-step cost the policy's loss charges - the distance from the goal and the barrier - so the window and what follows add up to one objective. Its input is the policy's own: the goal, then the state, both normalised. It is an ensemble of the same two-hot value heads EfficientTDMPC uses (zimrrl 9.5), each with a target copy. Its targets come from the real transitions of the windows the world model trains on: every gathered window holds the real states after each of its steps and the goals beside them, so each step k from the second on gives a transition - its goal and state as the input, the next step's as the target heads', and the cost where it led. A fall is no terminal: in a fleet that lives on after a loss, a fallen state is simply a costly one, and the critic learns its cost-to-go like any other.

The critic learns in every round of the world model's training, on the very windows that round gathered: their real states and goals are still in place after the world model's step, which writes only its own rollout. One update is EfficientTDMPC's value-head update, on these transitions:

   targets   cost + gamma x the target heads' mean, where each transition led
   loss      each online head's two-hot cross-entropy against the targets, averaged over the transitions
   step      the online heads' gradients clipped to a global norm, then Adam
   follow    each target head 1% of the way toward its online twin

Each head learns from its own loss, from its own starting weights - which is what makes the ensemble's members agree where the data is thick and differ where it is thin. The target heads move slowly so that the regression's right side stands nearly still while the heads move toward it: each update moves a target weight 1% of the way to its online twin, which makes the target a running average of the online weights over roughly the last hundred updates, each older one counting 0.99 times as much as the one after it. The value tail's weight ramps up the same way, slowly: with a ramp of 1000 updates, the 250th policy update weighs the tail at a quarter of its full weight, and every update from the 1000th on at all of it.

The value tail. With a critic, the policy's loss can see past its window. It gains, at the window's last rolled state, the critic's estimate of the cost after it - the mean over the windows and over the critic's heads:

   loss = sum over k = 1 .. W of c(z_k)  +  weight x mean over windows and heads of C_h([goal_W | z_W])
          the window's own steps            what the window's end leads to

so that a step which costs a little now and saves the balance later is worth taking: the window alone sees only the cost now. The tail's gradient takes the same road back as the tracking terms. At the last state it goes back through each head's decoded value - a logit pulls the value toward its own bin's position, in proportion to its probability, times the slope of symexp there - and through the head to its input; the state half of that input gradient is added to the last state's gradient, and from there the world model's adjoint carries it back through the window to the policy. The critic itself is not trained by the tail. A critic whose last layer is still zero - as it starts - adds exactly nothing, since no gradient passes a zero layer.

Two horizons. With the critic's tail past its end, the policy's window need not be the world model's. The world model is fit on short windows (window, 8 steps), rolled forward on the actions the simulator took, so it learns to correct its own errors; the policy imagines further (policy_window, 32), and the tail values what lies beyond. One kit serves both: it is as long as the policy's horizon, the windows drawn are that long, and the world model's own passes - its rollout on the recorded actions, its backward, its loss - stop at its window, so its update costs what a short kit's would:

   a gathered window      s0  s1  s2  s3  s4  s5  s6  s7  s8  s9 ... s32
   the world model        |_______ fit on these 8 _______|
   the policy             |_______________ imagines all 32, the tail at s32 _______________|

The horizon matters more than its cost suggests. A policy rolled out for a few steps sees a stumble's cost but not the fall it leads to; the tail repairs that only as far as the critic is right. Measured on a large tracker (Liao et al., 2026), a critic with an 8-step horizon never reached a good return, 16 steps matched a critic-free 32, and 32 learned fastest - long enough for the model's errors to stay small, short enough for the gradient through it to stay useful.

The policy's optimiser. A gradient back-propagated through 32 steps of a learned model is usually well behaved and occasionally huge: a window that crosses a stumble the model predicts badly can multiply it many times over, and one such step can undo many good ones. So the policy's gradient is bounded twice before Adam sees it - its whole length first, then each number on its own - and Adam's second-moment decay is shortened from 0.999 to 0.95, so it follows the gradient's scale over the last few dozen steps rather than the last thousand:

   g               the policy's gradient, every weight's number
   g  x  min(1, L / |g|)          the whole length within L         a broad spike scaled down, its direction kept
   clamp(each, -e, e)             each number within e              a spike in a few weights caught here
   Adam(beta1 0.9, beta2 0.95)    each weight's step

The bounds are in the units of the loss, which differ from one learner to another, so the learner logs the gradient's length before clipping (policy_gradient_norm) and the bounds are set against it - a length bound a few times the usual length catches the spikes and leaves ordinary steps alone. With no bounds set, the clipping's factor is exactly 1 and the step is a plain Adam's, number for number.

The rates' schedule. Every network's learning rate - the world model's, the policy's, the critic's, the flow's - can follow a cosine from its base down to a floor share of it over a given number of its own updates, and stay there (zimrnum 10.10): full steps while the networks are far from good, a smooth descent, then small steps that let the weights settle rather than jitter. A learner that trains from a replay through a model keeps learning to the end, so its rates stop at a floor - a few hundredths of the base - rather than at zero. The rates follow from the update counts the state file keeps, so a resumed run continues on its schedule.

A night's length is known in hours, but how many updates those hours hold is known only once a machine has run them - it depends on the GPU, the cores, the characters. So the schedule can run over the training hours instead (rate_decay_hours), the trainer telling the learner its hours each round from its saved clock, as it tells the fleet for the pushes. Over eight hours down to 3%, the rates are at half their base after four hours, whatever the machine, and stay at the floor if the run goes on past the eighth.

Trust in the critic. An untrained critic's numbers are noise: its slope, its heads' disagreement, the advantages it gives. So everything that leans on it is weighed by one share, the trust in it, which grows linearly from 0 to 1 over the first policy updates - with a ramp of 1000, a quarter at the 250th update, whole from the 1000th:

   weighed by the trust          why it leans on the critic
   the value tail's weight       the critic's estimate past the window
   the tail's pessimism          the heads' disagreement, no warning before they have learned
   the planner's tail            the same estimate, in every plan's score
   teacher 2                     the plans it imitates are scored by that tail
   teacher 3                     its advantages are the critic's

   not weighed: teacher 1, FlowDPG - the world model's gradient, trained from the first round

The tail can be pessimistic: instead of the heads' mean it reads their mean plus beta of their spread, so a state whose cost the heads dispute counts as costlier, and the policy is pushed away from what the critic is unsure of - usually where it has seen too little to know. Its slope gives each head a weight per window, the mean's equal share made larger for a head above the mean and smaller for one below it:

   P = m + beta s           m = mean of the heads' costs,  s = their spread
   dP / dC_h = (1/H) (1 + beta (C_h - m) / s)          every head 1/H when they agree

   worked: two heads say 3 and 5, beta = 0.7      m = 4, s = 1, P = 4.7
           weights  (1/2)(1 - 0.7) = 0.15  for the head at 3,   (1/2)(1 + 0.7) = 0.85  for the head at 5

The weights still add up to 1 - moving both heads' costs up together moves P by the same amount, as for any mean - so pessimism does not make the tail larger in general; it redistributes its pull toward the head that says the state is worse.

11.12 Credit past the window#

A policy trained through the model sees the consequences of its actions only inside its window — eight steps, about a seventh of a second. A get-up takes seconds. How can such a short view teach a long motion?

Because tracking is not a long-horizon problem in disguise. In most reinforcement learning the reward that matters comes late — the goal is reached, or it is not — and a short window cannot see it. Here the reference supplies a goal at every step: where each body should be, right now. Doing well locally is doing well globally, because the long-term plan is the reference itself; the policy's job is only to correct, step by step, toward it. So a window's gradient already points the right way, and a policy trained on eight-step windows keeps its advantage when judged over three times as long — the corrections compound rather than fade.

The usual way to see past a window is a critic: a network estimating the cost still to come after the window's last step, added to the loss there (the SHAC method). It is not free. A critic learns by bootstrapping — its targets are built from its own estimates — so it starts out guessing, and its guess enters the policy's loss with the weight of all the future it stands for: about γH / (1 − γ), some ninety times a single step's cost at γ = 0.99 and eight steps. Until the critic has had very many updates, the policy follows that guess instead of the window's real signal. A critic pays for itself only with a large training budget — many parallel characters, target networks, multi-step targets — which is why this implementation has none, and why, if one is added, it belongs on the GPU, where such budgets exist.

11.13 The flow's correction#

The flow is the extension that lets a character choose between several ways back. It is a flow policy (zimrrl 5.5) whose output is not an action but a correction to the policy's action. How it runs on the GPU is in §13.4.

The flow in SuperTrack's rollout. The flow does not replace SuperTrack's policy; it corrects it. At every step of the rollout the policy computes its raw action as always, the flow chooses k coefficients - one for each of k synergies (zimrrl 5.7) - and their synergies, decoded, are added before the exploration and the write:

The precise tracker stays exactly as SuperTrack builds it; the flow adds what it is for - a choice among ways back - in the few directions such choices need. The flow's noise is its own, apart from the policy's exploration, so a flow at rest with no noise adds exactly nothing: the rollout is then SuperTrack's own, every state to the bit.

How the flow learns from the rollout. The backward gives SuperTrack's policy its gradient exactly as it always does, through its own layers. The flow keeps, at every step, the raw action's gradient projected onto its synergies - the chain rule through raw + BT c gives d/dc = B d/draw - and learns from it by FlowDPG (zimrrl 5.5): each (step, row) of the rollout one training row - its condition, the coefficients the flow chose, the noise it chose them from, a drawn flow time - and the velocity regressed toward the coefficients improved by a step down that gradient. The policy's optimiser and the flow's each take their step.

   the backward, step by step       dL/draw  -->  the policy's layers, as always
                                              -->  B dL/draw, kept for the flow, every step and row
   the training rows, one each      [ goal | state ]_k   the coefficients c_k   their noise   a drawn time t
   FlowDPG                           u* = t (c - x_0) + (1 - t) v^ - alpha (max(|v^|, floor) / |g|) g
   the steps                         the policy's Adam; the flow's, clipped

One approximation is made, and it is said where it is made: the backward does not pass through the flow, so the gradient a correction is given holds every later correction where it was - the policy's own reactions to the states after it are differentiated, as they always are, but not the flow's.

Acting from a mirror. A fleet acts on the host, a character at a time, from a copy of the weights read back from the device. With a flow, a character's raw action is computed as the kit computes it: the policy's raw action, plus the flow's coefficients decoded through the synergies - KitNetwork.forwardHost runs the velocity network on the host as the kernels do (the bias first and the inputs in order, the layer norm from the same zimrmath row statistics, the same Mish), and KitFlow.sampleHost takes the K Euler steps around it - plus SuperTrack's own exploration, as without a flow.

   raw  =  policy(goal, state)  +  B^T c  +  sigma x a fresh normal per action
                                    ^
                                    c = the flow's K Euler steps from this character's own drifting noise

Each character's flow noise is its own and drifts (zimrrl 5.6), so a character keeps to the way back it began; while it plans, the drift is slower still - a correlation time of two seconds instead of half of one - so it commits to that way back. The synergies themselves never change, so the host keeps its own copy of them rather than reading them back.

Learning from what really happened. The first two teachers trust the world model: the gradient it gives, and the plans found by searching it. Recovery is where it is least to be trusted - contacts, falls, states it has rarely seen - so a third teacher learns from the simulator's own results. It is FPO, PPO for a flow (zimrrl 6.4): every step the flow chose for a character in danger, while exploring, is kept as an example, and each is scored by how it turned out against what the critic expected:

   A  =  - c(next state, against the goal it aimed at)  -  gamma C(next state)  +  C(state)

   A > 0    the step did better than expected: the flow is made more likely to give that correction
   A < 0    it did worse: less likely

How likely the flow is to give a correction is read from its flow matching loss on it, averaged over a few draws of a time and a noise; the ratio of new to old likelihood is exp(Lold - Lnew), and PPO's clip keeps one round from moving it far. Each round starts by taking the old losses and the advantages, at the weights and the critic the round starts from, and normalising the advantages over the batch; every update of the round then takes the new losses on the very same draws, so the ratio is exactly 1 until the weights move. The critic is asked what it was trained on: a state beside the goal of its own frame - the goal the step before aimed at - so each example carries that goal too:

   an example     [ own goal | goal | state | coefficients | next state ]

   the flow's likelihood       at [ goal | state ], of the coefficients
   C(state)                    at [ own goal | state ]
   C(next state), the cost     at [ goal | next state ]

Teacher 3 needs the critic, and its signal - single real outcomes - is the noisiest of the three, so its weight starts small. Where the model is right, the first two teachers do most of the work and teacher 3 mostly agrees; where the model is wrong about a way back, teacher 3 is the one that notices.

The flow in the learner. SuperTrack's learner takes a flow as a setting. With one, the flow's velocity network is drawn with its last layer at zero - so the run starts with a flow at rest, correcting nothing but by its noise - and placed after everything else the learner keeps, the critic's weights included, with its synergies beside it among the parameters. The flow's own noise is half of sigma by default: it and SuperTrack's exploration both act while collecting, and their variances add - 1 + 0.25, so the two together explore a quarter more than SuperTrack alone. While collecting, each character's noise takes one step of its drift every frame and, times sigma, is the flow's starting point. Judged, the flow starts from zero noise - its typical action - and nothing is drawn, so judging leaves the random stream, and so the training after it, as it was. A saved state holds the flow's weights and its optimiser's moments with every other network's, and each character's noise: a resumed run picks up its drifts where they were, and acts, step for step, as the run it continues.

11.14 Planning for characters in danger#

SuperTrack's policy learns from windows of tracking: rollouts that start near the reference and are pulled back toward it. That makes it precise, and it makes it weak exactly where it matters most - after a big push, far from anything its windows showed it, where the way back may need a stride, a lean or a hop the reference never makes. A planner answers that one question directly: for a character in danger, it searches over the next few actions by SuperTrack's own objective, through SuperTrack's own world model, and the character acts on the answer. Each answer is also a lesson: the policy can later learn from the plans that brought characters back.

Planning has a cost - a search per planned character every few steps - so it is spent only where it is needed. The whole system is a short loop of pieces, each a few lines of rules:

   piece                           where in the code
   the hazard                      planningHazard, projectedHazard
   who plans, and when             PlanningFlags
   what a plan costs               TrackingScorer                   (zn_mlp: lat_tracking_cost, tracking_plan_scores)
   the search                      TrackingPlanner, KitMppi         (zn_mlp: mppi_begin, mppi_elites, mppi_refit, ...)
   the flow's own plans            TrackingPlanner.FlowPlans
   a decision's rows               TrackingPlanner.gather           (zn_mlp: plan_gather)
   the plans' way back to the host the mailbox                      (zn_mlp: plan_mailbox)
   acting from a plan              plannedAction

Measuring danger. A character's hazard says how far toward a fall it is, by the failure barrier's own measures (11.11) against the barrier's own margins - the larger of the two fractions:

   hazard = max( |head height error| / head margin,  (1 - cos(up, up_ref)) / tilt margin )

   a head 0.1 m low against a margin of 0.25 m:          0.4
   an up direction 60 degrees off (1 - cos = 0.5):       0.5 against a margin of 1      hazard 0.5, halfway to a fall

0 on the reference, 1 at a margin, where the failure rule fires. It is not the barrier's hinged value, which stays near zero until a few widths before the margin - by then a fall is under way. Sharing the barrier's measures and margins, the planner and the policy agree on what danger is.

A hazard that is still low can be climbing fast. So the flags read it projected a few steps ahead along its rise:

   projected = hazard + lookahead x max(0, hazard - hazard one step before)

   rising 0.2 -> 0.3 in a step, ten steps ahead:    0.3 + 10 x 0.1 = 1.3     past a start of 0.5 already
   falling 0.4 -> 0.3:                              0.3                      read as it is

Only a rising hazard is projected. A falling one is not trusted to keep falling - a character that has only begun to recover is still in danger - and stopping is left to the calm wait below. In a fall the rise is steady, a few hundredths a step, so ten steps of it flag the character several steps before its hazard alone would cross the threshold. A rise needs a step to rise from, within the same episode: at a character's first step, and at its first step after a restart, there is none, and its hazard is read as it is - comparing it with the last hazard of an episode that has ended would invent a rise that never happened.

Who plans, and when. A character starts planning when its projected hazard reaches a start threshold and a planner slot is free (the most endangered first when slots are few); it keeps its slot until its hazard has stayed below a lower stop threshold for a run of calm steps; and all planning characters decide together, on one clock - every few steps, and at once when a character starts. The gap between the thresholds and the calm wait are hysteresis: a character keeps planning through a recovery instead of flickering in and out as its hazard wavers.

One clock is what lets the search start warm correctly. Each decision starts from the last plan moved forward by the steps since it was made - the plan age, which each decision reports - and with every character deciding at once, that number is the same for all. While nobody plans, the clock rests.

What a plan is, and what it costs. A plan is H CORRECTIONS around the policy, not H actions. Rolled through the world model, it is the policy reacting to every state the model reaches - closed loop - with the plan's correction for each step added to the policy's raw action:

Corrections rather than actions for two reasons. A search around the policy starts where the policy already is - the plan of zeros - and only has to find what to change. And a plan made of corrections stays meaningful when the state drifts: a plan acted on a step late adds its correction to the policy's reaction to the state actually reached, where a list of actions would replay moves meant for a state the character is no longer in. A plan's cost is SuperTrack's own objective over that future: each rolled step charged as the policy's loss charges one - the distance from the goal, plus the failure barrier - and the critic's pessimistic cost-to-go added after the last step (11.12):

   score = -( c(z_1) + c(z_2) + ... + c(z_H)  +  tail weight x (mean + beta x spread of the critic's heads at z_H) )

Minus, because a search ranks a higher score better. The same cost, model and critic the policy learns from: a plan the search prefers is one the policy would prefer if it could see as far. The candidates roll in a second world model kit, its rows candidates rather than windows, the policy acting in it without exploration - a candidate is its own exploration. Built with the training kit's shapes, it reads the training kit's very weights, the world model's and the policy's - a kit's weights start at the buffer's start - while its own activations are placed after everything else in the buffers, every one of its offsets moved by the same amount.

Finding a good plan. The search is EfficientTDMPC's MPPI, unchanged - only what scores a plan differs. For each planning character it keeps a Gaussian over plans and refines it round by round:

   plans    the flow's own plans: each the policy rolled closed-loop through the world model with the flow's
            correction, from a noise of its own - the first candidates of every character, never resampled
   begin    the last decision's plan moved forward by the plan age (warm), or zero (cold); every spread at its ceiling
   round    the other candidates drawn from the Gaussian, every plan scored, the Gaussian refitted to the best (the
            elites), weighted by their scores
   choose   one elite drawn by its weight: its plan is the decision

The flow's plans are why the flow and the planner fit together. A flow maps different noises to different ways back, so a handful of its samples, each rolled forward with the flow correcting the policy at every step, are already several complete strategies; the search starts from them rather than rediscovering them, and the random candidates explore around and between them. A plan is rolled exactly as SuperTrack's own rollouts are: at each step the policy and the flow read the reference's goal after that step and the state the world model has reached.

MPPI needs to know only what it searches over - how many states, candidates, steps and actions, and where the candidates' actions and scores lie - so EfficientTDMPC's scorer and SuperTrack's each describe themselves in those terms, and one search serves both. Its weights read score differences relative to the elites' own spread (zimrrl 9.8): SuperTrack's costs are hundredths, and read in their own units every elite would weigh almost alike.

A plan judged by every prefix. A plan's score is what it is expected to cost, and the critic supplies the part after the plan: its cost-to-go C obeys C(z0) = c(z1) + γ C(z1), so the plan's first h steps followed by the critic at the state they reach is the same recursion cut at depth h:

   Q_h  =  c(z_1) + gamma c(z_2) + ... + gamma^(h-1) c(z_h)  +  gamma^h C(z_h)

   final              Q_H                       the whole plan, then the critic after its last step
   mean_over_depths   (Q_1 + Q_2 + ... + Q_H) / H   every prefix of the plan (EfficientTDMPC)

Each Qh values a different prefix: the plan followed for h steps, then whatever the policy does from there, which is what the critic measures. Averaging them prefers plans that are good wherever the policy might take over, over plans whose worth only appears at the horizon - where the world model's errors have had the longest to grow, and where a search is most likely to find a plan the model rates wrongly. Both objectives are fixed weights on the step costs and on the critic at each depth: a step's cost appears in every prefix that contains it, the critic at depth h in Qh alone.
