                .w_action = p.options.w_action,
            };
        }

        fn fwd(
            p: *Self,
            x: u32,
            in: u32,
            out: u32,
            activation: M.Act,
            w: u32,
            y: u32,
        ) void {
            var q: M.Params = p.base();
            q.in_dim = in;
            q.out_dim = out;
            q.act = @backingInt(activation);
            q.x_off = x;
            q.w_off = w;
            q.y_off = y;
            p.run("dense_fwd", q, p.rows * out);
        }

        fn mlpFwd(
            p: *Self,
            net: [3]u32,
            x: u32,
            out: u32,
            h1: u32,
            h2: u32,
            y: u32,
        ) void {
            p.fwd(x, 4, p.hidden, .tanh, net[0], h1);
            p.fwd(h1, p.hidden, p.hidden, .tanh, net[1], h2);
            p.fwd(h2, p.hidden, out, .linear, net[2], y);
        }

        fn bwdW(
            p: *Self,
            x: u32,
            in: u32,
            out: u32,
            w: u32,
            dy: u32,
            accumulate: bool,
        ) void {
            var q: M.Params = p.base();
            q.in_dim = in;
            q.out_dim = out;
            q.x_off = x;
            q.w_off = w;
            q.dy_off = dy;
            q.accumulate = @intFromBool(accumulate);
            p.run("dense_bwd_w", q, in * out + out);
        }

        fn bwdX(
            p: *Self,
            in: u32,
            out: u32,
            w: u32,
            dy: u32,
            dx: u32,
        ) void {
            var q: M.Params = p.base();
            q.in_dim = in;
            q.out_dim = out;
            q.w_off = w;
            q.dy_off = dy;
            q.dx_off = dx;
            p.run("dense_bwd_x", q, p.rows * in);
        }

        fn tanhBwd(p: *Self, out: u32, y: u32, dy: u32) void {
            var q: M.Params = p.base();
            q.out_dim = out;
            q.act = @backingInt(M.Act.tanh);
            q.y_off = y;
            q.dy_off = dy;
            p.run("act_bwd", q, p.rows * out);
        }

        fn adam(
            p: *Self,
            start: u32,
            count: u32,
            step: u32,
            rate: f64,
        ) void {
            var q: M.Params = p.base();
            // Adam's bias corrections as zimrnum's Adam forms them, for the betas this dispatch uses.
            const corrections: zn.AdamCorrections(f32) = zn.adamCorrectionMultipliers(f32, q.beta1, q.beta2, step);
            q.w_off = start;
            q.count = count;
            q.rate = @floatCast(rate);
            q.correction1 = corrections.first;
            q.correction2 = corrections.second;
            p.run("adam", q, count);
        }

        /// One integration step's forward: world model on [rates, angle, force], then `cp_step`.
        fn worldForward(
            p: *Self,
            state: u32,
            force: u32,
            in: u32,
            g1: u32,
            g2: u32,
            acc: u32,
            next: u32,
        ) void {
            var q: M.Params = p.base();
            q.x_off = state;
            q.u_off = force;
            q.z_off = in;
            p.run("cp_wm_input", q, p.rows);
            p.mlpFwd(p.wm, in, 2, g1, g2, acc);
            var s: M.Params = p.base();
            s.x_off = state;
            s.y_off = acc;
            s.z_off = next;
            p.run("cp_step", s, p.rows);
        }

        /// A step's backward from the next state's gradient (`cur`): the tracking gradient added
        /// against `target`, the step's adjoint into `nxt`, the world model's input gradient (its
        /// weight gradients only when `world_weights`, summed over steps unless `first`).
        fn stepBackward(
            p: *Self,
            next_state: u32,
            target: u32,
            cur: u32,
            nxt: u32,
            in: u32,
            g1: u32,
            g2: u32,
            first: bool,
            world_weights: bool,
        ) void {
            var t: M.Params = p.base();
            t.x_off = next_state;
            t.t_off = target;
            t.dy_off = cur;
            t.accumulate = @intFromBool(!first);
            p.run("cp_track_bwd", t, p.rows * 4);
            var s: M.Params = p.base();
            s.dy_off = cur;
            s.e_off = nxt;
            s.dx_off = p.d_acc;
            p.run("cp_step_bwd", s, p.rows);
            const h: u32 = p.hidden;
            if (world_weights) {
                p.bwdW(g2, h, 2, p.wm[2], p.d_acc, !first);
            }
            p.bwdX(h, 2, p.wm[2], p.d_acc, p.d_wh2);
            p.tanhBwd(h, g2, p.d_wh2);
            if (world_weights) {
                p.bwdW(g1, h, h, p.wm[1], p.d_wh2, !first);
            }
            p.bwdX(h, h, p.wm[1], p.d_wh2, p.d_wh1);
            p.tanhBwd(h, g1, p.d_wh1);
            if (world_weights) {
                p.bwdW(in, 4, h, p.wm[0], p.d_wh1, !first);
            }
            p.bwdX(4, h, p.wm[0], p.d_wh1, p.d_win);
            var w: M.Params = p.base();
            w.dx_off = p.d_win;
            w.dy_off = nxt;
            w.e_off = p.d_f;
            p.run("cp_wm_input_bwd", w, p.rows);
        }

        /// `SuperTrack.trainWorldWith`, as kernels.
        pub fn trainWorldWith(
            p: *Self,
            states: []const f32,
            forces_unit: []const f32,
        ) void {
            const n: usize = p.options.wm_window;
            const r: usize = p.rows;
            for (0..r) |row| {
                @memcpy(p.staging[p.w_start + row * 4 ..][0..4], states[row * (n + 1) * 4 ..][0..4]);
                for (0..n) |k| {
                    const real: []const f32 = states[(row * (n + 1) + k + 1) * 4 ..][0..4];
                    @memcpy(p.staging[p.w_target[k] + row * 4 ..][0..4], real);
                    p.staging[p.w_force[k] + row] = forces_unit[row * n + k];
                }
            }
            // Only the world step's own region: the policy step's is disjoint (see `uploadAt`).
            p.pipe.uploadAt(.acts, p.w_start, p.staging[p.w_start..p.upload_len]);
            p.pipe.beginRecording();
            for (0..n) |k| {
                const next: u32 = p.w_state[k + 1];
                p.worldForward(p.w_state[k], p.w_force[k], p.w_in[k], p.w_g1[k], p.w_g2[k], p.w_acc[k], next);
            }
            var cur: u32 = p.d_a;
            var nxt: u32 = p.d_b;
            var k: usize = n;
            while (k > 0) {
                k -= 1;
                const last: bool = k == n - 1;
                p.stepBackward(p.w_state[k + 1], p.w_target[k], cur, nxt, p.w_in[k], p.w_g1[k], p.w_g2[k], last, true);
                swap(u32, &cur, &nxt);
            }
            p.wm_step += 1;
            p.adam(p.wm[0], p.wm_count, p.wm_step, p.options.wm_rate);
            p.pipe.submitRecording();
        }

        /// `SuperTrack.trainPolicyWith`, as kernels.
        pub fn trainPolicyWith(p: *Self, starts: []const f32, noise: []const f32) void {
            const n: usize = p.options.policy_window;
            const r: usize = p.rows;
            @memcpy(p.staging[p.p_start..][0 .. r * 4], starts[0 .. r * 4]);
            for (0..n) |k| {
                @memcpy(p.staging[p.p_eps[k]..][0..r], noise[k * r ..][0..r]);
            }
            @memset(p.staging[p.zero..][0 .. r * 4], 0.0);
            // Only the policy step's own region (the zero target, starts, noise).
            p.pipe.uploadAt(.acts, 0, p.staging[0..p.w_start]);
            // ONE submission for the whole window, ~900 dispatches (compute_host's recording, section 8 E1).
            p.pipe.beginRecording();
            for (0..n) |k| {
                p.mlpFwd(p.pol, p.p_state[k], 1, p.p_h1[k], p.p_h2[k], p.p_o[k]);
                var f: M.Params = p.base();
                f.y_off = p.p_o[k];
                f.x_off = p.p_eps[k];
                f.u_off = p.p_f[k];
                p.run("cp_force", f, p.rows);
                p.worldForward(p.p_state[k], p.p_f[k], p.p_in[k], p.p_g1[k], p.p_g2[k], p.p_acc[k], p.p_state[k + 1]);
            }
            var cur: u32 = p.d_a;
            var nxt: u32 = p.d_b;
            const h: u32 = p.hidden;
            var k: usize = n;
            while (k > 0) {
                k -= 1;
                const first: bool = k == n - 1;
                p.stepBackward(p.p_state[k + 1], p.zero, cur, nxt, p.p_in[k], p.p_g1[k], p.p_g2[k], first, false);
                var fb: M.Params = p.base();
                fb.u_off = p.p_f[k];
                fb.y_off = p.p_o[k];
                fb.e_off = p.d_f;
                fb.dy_off = p.d_o;
                p.run("cp_force_bwd", fb, p.rows);
                p.bwdW(p.p_h2[k], h, 1, p.pol[2], p.d_o, !first);
                p.bwdX(h, 1, p.pol[2], p.d_o, p.d_ph2);
                p.tanhBwd(h, p.p_h2[k], p.d_ph2);
                p.bwdW(p.p_h1[k], h, h, p.pol[1], p.d_ph2, !first);
                p.bwdX(h, h, p.pol[1], p.d_ph2, p.d_ph1);
                p.tanhBwd(h, p.p_h1[k], p.d_ph1);
                p.bwdW(p.p_state[k], 4, h, p.pol[0], p.d_ph1, !first);
                p.bwdX(4, h, p.pol[0], p.d_ph1, p.d_pin);
                var add: M.Params = p.base();
                add.dy_off = nxt;
                add.dx_off = p.d_pin;
                add.count = p.rows * 4;
                p.run("add_block", add, p.rows * 4);
                swap(u32, &cur, &nxt);
            }
            p.pol_step += 1;
            p.adam(p.pol[0], p.pol_count, p.pol_step, p.options.policy_rate);
            p.pipe.submitRecording();
        }

        /// `trainWorldWith`, FUSED: four dispatches (forward, backward, reduce, Adam) instead of
        /// ~150 - one thread per row walks the whole window.
        pub fn trainWorldFused(
            p: *Self,
            states: []const f32,
            forces_unit: []const f32,
        ) void {
            const n: usize = p.options.wm_window;
            const r: usize = p.rows;
            for (0..r) |row| {
                @memcpy(p.f_staging[p.f_w_start + row * 4 ..][0..4], states[row * (n + 1) * 4 ..][0..4]);
                for (0..n) |k| {
                    const real: []const f32 = states[(row * (n + 1) + k + 1) * 4 ..][0..4];
                    @memcpy(p.f_staging[p.f_w_target + (k * r + row) * 4 ..][0..4], real);
                    p.f_staging[p.f_w_force + k * r + row] = forces_unit[row * n + k];
                }
            }
            p.pipe.uploadAt(.acts, p.f_w_start, p.f_staging[p.f_w_start..p.f_upload_len]);
            p.pipe.beginRecording();
            var q: M.Params = p.base();
            q.in_dim = p.hidden;
            q.x_off = p.f_w_records;
            q.z_off = p.f_w_start;
            q.y_off = p.f_w_force;
            q.t_off = p.f_w_target;
            q.w_off = p.wm[0];
            q.count = @intCast(n);
            q.dx_off = p.f_wm_grads;
            q.e_off = p.f_scratch;
            p.run("st_world_fwd", q, p.rows);
            p.run("st_world_bwd", q, p.rows);
            var red: M.Params = p.base();
            red.w_off = p.wm[0];
            red.count = p.wm_count;
            red.dx_off = p.f_wm_grads;
            p.run("st_reduce", red, p.wm_count);
            p.wm_step += 1;
            p.adam(p.wm[0], p.wm_count, p.wm_step, p.options.wm_rate);
            p.pipe.submitRecording();
        }

        /// `trainPolicyWith`, FUSED: four dispatches instead of ~900.
        pub fn trainPolicyFused(p: *Self, starts: []const f32, noise: []const f32) void {
            const n: usize = p.options.policy_window;
            const r: usize = p.rows;
            @memcpy(p.f_staging[p.f_p_start..][0 .. r * 4], starts[0 .. r * 4]);
            @memcpy(p.f_staging[p.f_p_eps..][0 .. n * r], noise[0 .. n * r]);
            p.pipe.uploadAt(.acts, p.f_p_start, p.f_staging[p.f_p_start..p.f_w_start]);
            p.pipe.beginRecording();
            var q: M.Params = p.base();
            q.in_dim = p.hidden;
            q.x_off = p.f_p_records;
            q.z_off = p.f_p_start;
            q.y_off = p.f_p_eps;
            q.w_off = p.pol[0];
            q.v_off = p.wm[0];
            q.count = @intCast(n);
            q.dx_off = p.f_pol_grads;
            q.e_off = p.f_scratch;
            p.run("st_policy_fwd", q, p.rows);
            p.run("st_policy_bwd", q, p.rows);
            var red: M.Params = p.base();
            red.w_off = p.pol[0];
            red.count = p.pol_count;
            red.dx_off = p.f_pol_grads;
            p.run("st_reduce", red, p.pol_count);
            p.pol_step += 1;
            p.adam(p.pol[0], p.pol_count, p.pol_step, p.options.policy_rate);
            p.pipe.submitRecording();
        }

        pub fn readParams(p: *Self) ?[]const f32 {
            return p.pipe.readLatest(.params);
        }

        /// The largest difference between the kit's policy and world model and `st`'s.
        pub fn gapsTo(p: *const Self, st: *const SuperTrack, kit: []const f32) [2]f32 {
            return .{ netGap(kit, p.pol, &st.policy), netGap(kit, p.wm, &st.world) };
        }

        fn netGap(kit: []const f32, offsets: [3]u32, net: *const Net) f32 {
            var worst: f32 = 0.0;
            for (net.layers, offsets) |layer, off| {
                for (layer.w.data, 0..) |v, i| {
                    worst = @max(worst, @abs(v - kit[off + i]));
                }
                for (layer.b.data, 0..) |v, i| {
                    worst = @max(worst, @abs(v - kit[off + layer.w.data.len + i]));
                }
            }
            return worst;
        }
    };
}

13.2 The latent world model on the kit#

The latent world model of §11.10 is three dense layers and an addition — z' = z + Net(z, reference, action) — so the kit's ordinary dense kernels nearly suffice. The one thing they cannot do on their own is join the steps of a rollout, and that is where the design lives.

Wide rows. Each step's three inputs sit side by side in one row: the state's features, the reference's encoded targets, the action. The dense kernels read their input rows with a stride, so the first layer reads the whole wide row as a single input — no concatenation is ever performed; it is only a layout. The CPU model's first layer is three weight blocks summed, one per input; stacked in the row's order, they are one layer over the wide row, and the kit adds the inputs in the same order the CPU model does, so the two agree to the last bit.

The join. A small kernel takes a step's state and its predicted change and writes their sum into the next row's state columns — where the next step's first layer will read it — and into a contiguous block beside, where the loss reads it. Its mirror image runs backward: it takes the gradient that reached a row's state columns through the network and adds it to that state's gradient.

Backward through the rollout. Walking back from the last step, each state's gradient gathers from three places: its own term of the loss; the next state's gradient, passed straight back by the addition (the residual path); and whatever flowed back through the network into its row's state columns (the join's mirror). A step's predicted change has exactly the next state's gradient, since the change is added unaltered — so the last layer reads that gradient directly, with nothing copied. The weight gradients of all the steps add up into one, because every step uses the same weights.

Sum, not mean. The kit's loss is the sum of the steps' errors rather than their average — dividing by a constant would need a kernel of its own. It needs none: Adam divides every gradient by its own running size, so a constant factor cancels exactly, provided Adam's small epsilon carries the same factor. The kit's step therefore scales epsilon by the number of steps, and takes precisely the step the averaged loss would.

Checked layouts. A rollout's blocks are laid out in the kit's buffers when it is made, and every region is checked against the buffer it lives in; a layout that does not fit is refused by name. On a GPU, writing past a buffer's end is not an error anywhere — it simply corrupts — so the check has to happen before the first dispatch.

LatentKit.forward
/// The rollout, forward: for every step, three dense layers over the wide block and the
/// join into the next. The caller has staged every block's reference and action columns
/// and block 0's features; the kit fills the rest.
pub fn forward(self: Self) void {
    self.rollout(self.actsWithPolicy());
}
LatentKit.backward
/// The rollout, backward: the gradient of the rollout's loss with respect to every weight,
/// into the kit's gradient buffer (in `packWeights`' layout). `forward` must have run, and
/// the targets be staged at `blockT`.
///
/// THE LOSS IS THE SUM over steps of each step's mean squared error - `steps` times the CPU
/// model's, which averages over steps. The kit has no kernel to divide by a constant, and
/// needs none: Adam divides every gradient by its own running size, so a constant factor
/// cancels (bar the epsilon). Stated here so nobody mistakes the factor for a bug.
///
/// Walking back from the last step: a step's change has exactly the next state's gradient
/// (z' = z + change), so layer 3 reads dZ_{k+1} directly. Through the three layers, weight
/// gradients ACCUMULATED across steps; then a state's own gradient is its loss term, plus
/// the next state's (the residual path, `add_block`), plus what came back through the
/// network into its block's z columns (`lat_take`).
pub fn backward(self: Self) void {
    const tanh: u32 = @backingInt(M.Act.tanh);
    // The world model's own window (`world_steps`): its loss, and so its gradient, ends there.
    var step: u32 = self.world_steps;
    self.mse(step);
    self.weighLoss(step);
    var first: bool = true;
    while (step > 0) {
        step -= 1;
        const k: u32 = step;
        const h1: u32 = self.h1_at + k * self.rows * self.hidden;
        const h2: u32 = self.h2_at + k * self.rows * self.hidden;
        const accumulate: u32 = if (first) 0 else 1;
        first = false;
        // Layer 3: into the change, whose gradient is the next state's - in the network's own units.
        const change_gradient: u32 = self.changeGradient(k + 1);
        self.weightGrads(h2, 0, self.hidden, self.features, change_gradient, self.w3, accumulate);
        self.inputGrads(self.hidden, self.features, change_gradient, self.w3, self.dh2_at);
        self.activationGrads(h2, self.dh2_at, tanh, self.hidden);
        // Layer 2.
        self.weightGrads(h1, 0, self.hidden, self.hidden, self.dh2_at, self.w2, accumulate);
        self.inputGrads(self.hidden, self.hidden, self.dh2_at, self.w2, self.dh1_at);
        self.activationGrads(h1, self.dh1_at, tanh, self.hidden);
        // Layer 1, over the wide block.
        self.weightGrads(
            self.blockX(k) + self.lead,
            self.width,
            self.inputs,
            self.hidden,
            self.dh1_at,
            self.w1,
            accumulate,
        );
        if (k == 0) {
            break;
        }
        self.inputGrads(self.inputs, self.hidden, self.dh1_at, self.w1, self.dx_at);
        // State k's gradient: its own loss term, the residual path, and the network path.
        self.mse(k);
        self.weighLoss(k);
        self.pipe.params = .{
            .count = self.rows * self.features,
            .dy_off = self.blockDZ(k),
            .dx_off = self.blockDZ(k + 1),
        };
        self.pipe.run("add_block", self.rows * self.features);
        self.pipe.params = .{
            .rows = self.rows,
            .count = self.features,
            // The input-gradient block's rows are `inputs` apart, not `width`.
            .stride = self.inputs,
            .dy_off = self.blockDZ(k),
            .dx_off = self.dx_at,
        };
        self.pipe.run("lat_take", self.rows * self.features);
    }
}
lat_advance — the join
/// The next state, in two places at once: z_{k+1} = z_k + change, written into the next block's z
/// columns (strided, so the next step's first layer reads it) AND into a contiguous block (the
/// loss kernels read contiguous rows). z_k is read strided from X_k at `x_off`; the change is
/// contiguous at `t_off`; the next block at `y_off`, the contiguous copy at `z_off`. One thread per
/// (row, feature); the next block's other columns - its reference and action - are not touched.
pub fn lat_advance(id: u32) void {
    if (id >= params.rows * params.count) {
        return;
    }
    const r: u32 = id / params.count;
    const c: u32 = id % params.count;
    // The network's output is the change itself - or, with the increments' statistics on, the change in units of
    // the feature's typical change: mean + spread x output (`LatentKit.increments_at`).
    var change: f32 = b_acts[params.t_off + r * params.count + c];
    if (params.lat_increments_on != 0) {
        const change_mean: f32 = b_acts[params.lat_increments_at + c];
        const change_spread: f32 = b_acts[params.lat_increments_at + params.count + c];
        change = change_mean + change_spread * change;
    }
    const next: f32 = b_acts[params.x_off + r * params.stride + c] + change;
    b_acts[params.y_off + r * params.stride + c] = next;
    b_acts[params.z_off + r * params.count + c] = next;
}
lat_take — its mirror
/// The backward join: the gradient that reached a block's z columns (strided, at `dx_off`) added
/// into the state's contiguous gradient (at `dy_off`) - the path by which the loss at later steps
/// reaches earlier states THROUGH the network, beside the residual path `add_block` carries. One
/// thread per (row, feature).
pub fn lat_take(id: u32) void {
    if (id >= params.rows * params.count) {
        return;
    }
    const r: u32 = id / params.count;
    const c: u32 = id % params.count;
    b_dacts[params.dy_off + r * params.count + c] += b_dacts[params.dx_off + r * params.stride + c];
}

13.3 The policy on the kit#

The policy trains through the world model entirely on the GPU too, and the whole design rests on one row layout. Each step's wide row gains the goal in front — [goal | state | reference | action] — so the policy's input, goal and state, is the row's first slice, and the world model's, state, reference and action, is the rest. Both are contiguous slices of the same row; nothing is ever copied between the two networks.

The policy acts first. At every step its three layers read their slice, and a small kernel writes the scaled action into the row's action columns — where the world model's layers will read it a moment later. Exploration noise is added there, and it is made on the GPU from nothing but integer hashing: a hash of the step, the row and the column, turned into four uniform numbers and summed. Integer arithmetic gives the same bits on every device, so the noise is exactly reproducible, and the CPU reference computes it with the very same function.

Backward through a model that stays fixed. The policy's loss — each step's distance from its goal, plus a small price on the size of its actions — is backpropagated through the world model, whose layers pass gradients along but keep their weights. The action columns' gradient becomes the policy's output gradient (the noise was only added, so it contributes nothing), and each state's gradient gathers from four places: its own tracking term, the next state through the residual, the world model's input gradient, and the policy's, since the policy reads the state too.

Adam on the policy alone. The policy's weights live beside the world model's in one parameter buffer, and the optimiser step is confined to the policy's region — weights, gradients and both moments offset together — so the world model's weights and optimiser state never move.

LatentKit.policyStep
/// The policy's turn at step k: its three layers over the row's [goal | state] slice, and
/// its action written into the row's action columns - before the world model reads the row.
fn policyStep(self: Self, k: u32) void {
    // A correction corrects a policy: without one there is nothing to correct. And it comes from one place.
    const has_flow: bool = self.flow_actor != null;
    const has_given: bool = self.given_corrections != null;
    const correction_without_policy: bool = (has_flow or has_given) and self.policy_hidden == 0;
    assertf(!correction_without_policy, @src(), "a correction corrects a policy: this kit has none", .{});
    assertf(!(has_flow and has_given), @src(), "corrections from a flow and given ones, both: one only", .{});
    const tanh: u32 = @backingInt(M.Act.tanh);
    const linear: u32 = @backingInt(M.Act.linear);
    const hp: u32 = self.policy_hidden;
    const h1: u32 = self.ph1_at + k * self.rows * hp;
    const h2: u32 = self.ph2_at + k * self.rows * hp;
    const raw: u32 = self.raw_at + k * self.rows * self.actions;
    const w1: u32 = self.p_at;
    const w2: u32 = w1 + (self.lead + self.features) * hp + hp;
    const w3: u32 = w2 + hp * hp + hp;
    // The policy's slice: the row's first `lead + features` columns - the goal and the state -
    // read with the row's full stride, so the reference and action columns beyond them are
    // simply not part of this layer's input. Its weights are stacked in that same order
    // (`packPolicy`), which is what makes one matrix multiply do the work of two.
    self.dense(self.blockX(k), self.width, self.lead + self.features, hp, w1, h1, tanh);
    self.dense(h1, 0, hp, hp, w2, h2, tanh);
    self.dense(h2, 0, hp, self.actions, w3, raw, linear);
    // A correction - a flow's, or one given - added to the policy's raw action before the exploration and the
    // write.
    if (self.flow_actor) |flow_actor| {
        self.flowCorrection(flow_actor, k, raw);
    } else if (self.given_corrections) |given| {
        self.givenCorrection(given, k, raw);
    }
    // And the action into the row: `lat_act` scales the raw output (and adds this step's noise)
    // straight into the action columns the world model's layers will read next - the two
    // networks never exchange a buffer, only columns of one row.
    self.pipe.params = .{
        .rows = self.rows,
        .count = self.actions,
        .stride = self.width,
        .x_off = raw,
        .y_off = self.blockX(k) + self.lead + self.features + self.references,
        .lat_scale = self.action_scale,
        .lat_sigma = self.sigma,
        .lat_seed = M.latStepSeed(self.seed, k),
    };
    self.pipe.run("lat_act", self.rows * self.actions);
}
latNoise
pub fn latNoise(seed: u32, row: u32, column: u32) f32 {
    const key: u32 = latHash(seed ^ latHash(row *% 0x9e3779b9 +% column));
    var sum: f32 = 0.0;
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < 4) : (i += 1) {
        const bits: u32 = latHash(key +% i *% 0x85ebca6b) >> 8;
        sum += float(bits) * (1.0 / 16777216.0);
    }
    return (sum - 2.0) * 1.7320508;
}
LatentKit.policyBackward
/// The rollout, backward, for the POLICY: the gradient of its loss - every step's mean squared
/// distance from the reference's GOAL, plus the price on the raw action's size - with respect
/// to the policy's weights, into the gradient buffer at `p_at`, through the world model held
/// FIXED (its layers pass input gradients only; its weights get none). Summed over steps, like
/// `backward`: `steps` times the CPU learner's mean. `forward` must have run with the policy.
///
/// A state's gradient now gathers from FOUR places: its own tracking term; the next state's
/// (the residual); the world model's input gradient in its state columns; and the POLICY's -
/// the policy reads the state too - which sits at offset `lead` of the policy's input block,
/// a block `lead + features` wide (a third width, beside `width` and `inputs`).
pub fn policyBackward(self: Self) void {
    const tanh: u32 = @backingInt(M.Act.tanh);
    const hp: u32 = self.policy_hidden;
    const policy_inputs: u32 = self.lead + self.features;
    const w2p: u32 = self.p_at + policy_inputs * hp + hp;
    const w3p: u32 = w2p + hp * hp + hp;
    var step: u32 = self.steps;
    self.trackingGrad(step);
    self.barrierGrad(step);
    // The window's last state also carries the cost after the window: the critic's value tail.
    if (self.value_tail) |value_tail| {
        // Its heads' values decoded for the log when the learner keeps one (`policy_tail_value`).
        const decode_values: bool = self.stats_at != null;
        const goals_at: u32 = self.blockG(step);
        const states_at: u32 = self.blockZ(step);
        value_tail.addGradient(self.pipe, goals_at, states_at, self.blockDZ(step), decode_values);
    }
    var first: bool = true;
    while (step > 0) {
        step -= 1;
        const k: u32 = step;
        const h1: u32 = self.h1_at + k * self.rows * self.hidden;
        const h2: u32 = self.h2_at + k * self.rows * self.hidden;
        // The world model, frozen: input gradients only, down to its wide-row slice.
        self.inputGrads(self.hidden, self.features, self.changeGradient(k + 1), self.w3, self.dh2_at);
        self.activationGrads(h2, self.dh2_at, tanh, self.hidden);
        self.inputGrads(self.hidden, self.hidden, self.dh2_at, self.w2, self.dh1_at);
        self.activationGrads(h1, self.dh1_at, tanh, self.hidden);
        self.inputGrads(self.inputs, self.hidden, self.dh1_at, self.w1, self.dx_at);
        // The action columns' gradient, back to the policy's raw output - plus the price.
        const raw: u32 = self.raw_at + k * self.rows * self.actions;
        self.pipe.params = .{
            .rows = self.rows,
            .count = self.actions,
            .stride = self.inputs,
            .dx_off = self.dx_at + self.features + self.references,
            .x_off = raw,
            .dy_off = self.draw_at,
            .lat_scale = self.action_scale,
            .lat_penalty = 2.0 * self.w_action / float(self.rows * self.actions),
            .lat_smooth = 2.0 * self.w_smooth / float(self.rows * self.actions),
            // A missing neighbour is this step itself: raw - raw, exactly zero.
            .lat_prev = if (k > 0) raw - self.rows * self.actions else raw,
            .lat_next = if (k + 1 < self.steps) raw + self.rows * self.actions else raw,
        };
        self.pipe.run("lat_act_bwd", self.rows * self.actions);
        // A flow actor keeps the raw action's gradient projected onto its synergies, as its training row's
        // cost gradient; the policy then takes the gradient as it always does.
        if (self.flow_actor) |flow_actor| {
            self.keepFlowCostGradient(flow_actor, k);
        }
        // The policy: weight gradients accumulated across the steps, input gradients down.
        const accumulate: u32 = if (first) 0 else 1;
        first = false;
        const ph1: u32 = self.ph1_at + k * self.rows * hp;
        const ph2: u32 = self.ph2_at + k * self.rows * hp;
        self.weightGrads(ph2, 0, hp, self.actions, self.draw_at, w3p, accumulate);
        self.inputGrads(hp, self.actions, self.draw_at, w3p, self.dph2_at);
        self.activationGrads(ph2, self.dph2_at, tanh, hp);
        self.weightGrads(ph1, 0, hp, hp, self.dph2_at, w2p, accumulate);
        self.inputGrads(hp, hp, self.dph2_at, w2p, self.dph1_at);
        self.activationGrads(ph1, self.dph1_at, tanh, hp);
        self.weightGrads(self.blockX(k), self.width, policy_inputs, hp, self.dph1_at, self.p_at, accumulate);
        if (k == 0) {
            break;
        }
        self.inputGrads(policy_inputs, hp, self.dph1_at, self.p_at, self.dp_at);
        // State k's gradient, from all four places - and the barrier, when there is one.
        self.trackingGrad(k);
        self.barrierGrad(k);
        self.pipe.params = .{
            .count = self.rows * self.features,
            .dy_off = self.blockDZ(k),
            .dx_off = self.blockDZ(k + 1),
        };
        self.pipe.run("add_block", self.rows * self.features);
        self.take(self.dx_at, self.inputs, k);
        self.take(self.dp_at + self.lead, policy_inputs, k);
    }
    // The flow learns from every (step, row) of the rollout at once, its cost gradients now all kept.
    if (self.flow_actor) |flow_actor| {
        self.flowTrainingGradient(flow_actor);
    }
}

13.4 The flow on the kit#

A flow policy (zimrrl 5.5) makes an action from noise by following a learned velocity v(c, x, t) for K Euler steps. On the kit (KitFlow) the velocity is an ordinary KitNetwork, built from the flow's own network, so the CPU reference's numbers carry over unchanged. It reads wide rows [condition | x | time features], and four small kernels surround it.

   sampling, one block of wide rows and one application per step:

   block 0     [ c | x_0 = noise | time 0   ]  --v-->  Euler step  -->  block 1's x columns
   block 1     [ c | x_1         | time 1/K ]  --v-->  Euler step  -->  block 2's x columns
   ...
   block K-1   [ c | x_(K-1)     | ...      ]  --v-->  Euler step  -->  the action, wherever it is read next

   training, one application forward and backward:

   [ c | x_t = (1 - t) x_0 + t a | time t ]  --v-->  gradient at v  -->  back into the weights
          flow matching:  2 (v - (a - x_0)) / n          FlowDPG:  2 [(v - u*) + lambda (v - u)] / n

The time features are written per block when sampling - one time for every row - and per row when training, each row at its own drawn time. The last Euler step writes the action wherever its reader wants it: its own packed rows, or straight into the action columns of the rows that read it next, such as a world model's. Nothing is differentiated through the sampler's chain; the flow learns through its training rows alone.

The flow can learn from more than one teacher at once - SuperTrack's gradient through FlowDPG, a planner's answers by flow matching - so each of its training gradients takes a weight and says whether it is written over the network's weights' gradients or added to what another teacher left there. One teacher writes, the others add, and one optimiser step follows on the sum.

What the flow is for, how it corrects SuperTrack's policy and how the learner trains it, is in §11.13; this section is how it runs on the kit.

13.5 Keeping the data on the GPU#

A training step needs windows of recorded motion, and each window needs features: forward kinematics and the feature map for every recorded state in it, and the same for the reference. Done on the CPU for every sampled window, every training step, that would be the most expensive part of training — on the one processor that has no time to spare. So each thing is computed once, when it is new, and kept on the GPU.

Reference tables, once per clip. For every frame of every clip: the reference's features (the policy's goal) and its encoded targets (the world model's reference input). A clip never changes, so its table is computed and uploaded when training starts, and never again.

A feature ring, once per step. For every character, every step: its features, the action it took, and which table row its frame is. The ring has the same capacity as the CPU's replay, so it holds exactly the records the CPU can still draw windows from — and the CPU keeps doing the drawing, because it knows where episodes begin and end. Only the chosen starting points need to travel. The records are laid out step-major: all characters' records for one step side by side. Every character records at every step, so a whole step is a single upload rather than one per character.

Raw features. The ring and tables hold features as they are, not normalised. Normalisation is applied as windows are read, so the statistics it uses can be refreshed at any time without rewriting a single stored record.

Why it all lives in one buffer. WebGPU guarantees only eight storage buffers to a shader stage, and the kit already binds seven. A binding past the limit does not fail — its writes are silently dropped — so adding buffers for the ring and the tables is exactly what must not happen. Instead the kit sizes each buffer on its own, and the activation buffer is the large one: the rollout's blocks at its start, the tables and the ring beyond them. Its size is paid twice, in GPU memory and in the page's wasm memory, where the CPU twin keeps its copy.

One more rule follows from WebGPU's queue: uploads made during a frame all land before the frame's work runs, so two uploads to the same place in one frame leave only the second. Everything uploaded per step therefore goes to its own place — the ring's slots are distinct by construction.

Assembling windows on the GPU. A training step names its windows by where they start — a character and a slot — and a gather kernel does the rest, one thread per number: the first state and every target, normalised; each step's reference, copied from its frame's table row; each action, from its record. Only two numbers per window ever cross from the CPU.

lat_gather
/// A batch of training windows, assembled on the GPU from what is resident there: the feature ring
/// (a record per character per step: raw features, action, table row), the reference tables (a row
/// per clip frame: raw goal features, encoded targets) and the normaliser (means, then spreads).
/// Per window, the host uploads only where it starts: the character, and its first record's slot -
/// two floats, holding integers (exact below 2^24).
///
/// One thread per number written, over `rows x (steps + 1) x width`, a thread (row, k, column):
///   * state columns - step 0 writes the window's first state into the first wide row; step k >= 1
///     writes the state the simulator reached after k steps, into target block k. Both normalised
///     as `(x - mean) / spread`: the CPU normaliser's operations, in its order, so the two agree
///     bit for bit.
///   * reference columns (k < steps) - copied from the table row of step k's frame. A table row is
///     [goal | encoded targets] and a wide row [state | reference | action], so the reference sits
///     at the SAME offset in both and one index serves.
///   * action columns (k < steps) - copied from step k's record.
/// The wide rows' state columns for k >= 1 are left alone: the rollout fills them.
pub fn lat_gather(id: u32) void {
    const f: u32 = params.lat_features;
    const r: u32 = params.lat_references;
    const a: u32 = params.lat_actions;
    const lead: u32 = params.lat_lead;
    // The wide row's stride: the goal columns (if any), then the world model's slice.
    const width: u32 = lead + f + r + a;
    const steps: u32 = params.lat_steps;
    if (id >= params.rows * (steps + 1) * width) {
        return;
    }
    // Unpack the thread: `column` of a wide row, `step` 0..steps (one more than the rollout's steps
    // - step `steps` exists only to write the last target and goal), `row` the window.
    const column: u32 = id % width;
    const step: u32 = (id / width) % (steps + 1);
    const row: u32 = id / (width * (steps + 1));
    // The two integers each window travels as, and the table row a record holds, are stored as
    // floats (the buffer holds nothing else) - exact below 2^24 - and `@trunc` makes them integers.
    const env: u32 = @trunc(b_acts[params.starts_off + row * 2]);
    const first_slot: u32 = @trunc(b_acts[params.starts_off + row * 2 + 1]);
    // The ring is step-major: slot s holds every character's record for one replay index, side by
    // side, so a character's consecutive records are `envs` records apart - and the ring wraps.
    const slot: u32 = (first_slot + step) % params.lat_capacity;
    const record: u32 = params.ring_off + (slot * params.lat_envs + env) * latRecordWidth(f, a);
    const table_row: u32 = @trunc(b_acts[record + latRecordTableRow(f, a)]);
    if (column < lead) {
        // GOAL columns (lead is the feature count): the reference where step `step - 1` was GOING -
        // this record's frame - normalised like every state. It is the policy's input at step - 1
        // (SuperTrack's Local(K_{i+1})), and the tracking target for the state that step produced.
        if (step == 0) {
            return;
        }
        const raw_goal: f32 = b_acts[params.table_off + table_row * latTableWidth(f, r) + column];
        const goal: f32 = normalisedFeature(raw_goal, column, f);
        b_acts[params.blocks_off + ((step - 1) * params.rows + row) * width + column] = goal;
        b_acts[params.goals_off + ((step - 1) * params.rows + row) * f + column] = goal;
        return;
    }
    // The world model's slice: `c` counts from its first column.
    const c: u32 = column - lead;
    if (c < f) {
        // STATE columns: step 0's state is the rollout's starting point (the first wide row); every
        // later step's state is a TARGET - what the simulator reached, which the rollout's prediction
        // is scored against. The later rows' state columns are the rollout's to fill, with its own
        // predictions: the whole point of training through rollouts.
        const value: f32 = normalisedFeature(b_acts[record + c], c, f);
        if (step == 0) {
            b_acts[params.blocks_off + row * width + lead + c] = value;
        } else {
            b_acts[params.targets_off + ((step - 1) * params.rows + row) * f + c] = value;
        }
    } else if (c < f + r) {
        // REFERENCE columns: the encoded targets the servo aimed at during step `step - 1` - this
        // record's frame, the one that step was driving toward. A table row is [goal | encoded
        // targets] and the slice [state | reference | action], so they sit at the same offset `c`.
        if (step > 0) {
            const block: u32 = params.blocks_off + ((step - 1) * params.rows + row) * width + lead;
            b_acts[block + c] = b_acts[params.table_off + table_row * latTableWidth(f, r) + c];
        }
    } else if (step < steps) {
        // ACTION columns: the action this record's step took.
        const block: u32 = params.blocks_off + (step * params.rows + row) * width + lead;
        b_acts[block + c] = b_acts[record + latRecordAction(f) + (c - f - r)];
    }
}
Resident.appendLatest
/// The step the fleet just took, into the ring - one upload for every character. Call it
/// after every `Fleet.step`: the replay's newest record is the state that step started from. The step's
/// records built where the characters are (`buildStepRecords`), then placed (`uploadStep`): an actor builds
/// them on its own thread or worker, and the learner places what it is given.
pub fn appendLatest(self: *Self, fleet: *track.Fleet) void {
    const index: u64 = fleet.replay.written[0] - 1;
    const records: []f32 = self.staging[0 .. self.envs * self.record];
    const features: u32 = self.features;
    const actions: u32 = self.actions;
    buildStepRecords(fleet, index, features, actions, self.clip_rows, &self.data, &self.state, records);
    self.uploadStep(index, records);
}
Resident.recordAt
/// Where a character's record for replay index `index` starts: step-major, so the index
/// picks a block of `envs` records and the character one record within it.
pub fn recordAt(self: Self, env: usize, index: u64) u32 {
    const slot: u32 = @intCast(index % self.capacity);
    return self.ring_at + (slot * self.envs + @as(u32, @intCast(env))) * self.record;
}

13.6 The loop, resident#

All the pieces meet in one round, which is SuperTrack's iteration split by what each processor is good at.

The simulation runs on the CPU, and acts from a mirror. For every character, every step: its features and its goal, the policy's action, the step itself. The policy's weights live on the GPU, so acting uses a mirror — a host copy, refreshed whenever a readback arrives. That is not a shortcut: a readback is asynchronous and lands a frame or so later, while the simulator needs its action now. Being a frame behind costs nothing, because weights move slowly. Each step is then appended to the ring as one upload for all the characters together.

The learning runs on the GPU, and never leaves it. The world model trains through its own rollouts, the policy trains through the world model, and each update gathers its own windows from the ring and the reference tables. The CPU chooses which windows — it knows where episodes begin and end — and sends only where each one starts, into that update's own slot.

Two things the loop owns. It seeds both networks so each begins as the identity of its job: the world model predicting that nothing changes, the policy proposing no correction, which is the servo alone. And it takes the normaliser as a given, so the statistics can come from the reference clips — motion the character is supposed to follow — rather than from whatever the simulator happened to do early on.

The loop's correctness does not rest on watching it train. Every piece under it is checked against the CPU implementation on identical inputs: the gather bitwise, a world-model update to about one part in a hundred thousand, a policy update to one in ten million. What remains for the loop itself is that the pieces fit and that it moves: the ring stays in step with the replay, the slots keep their windows apart, and the mirror follows the GPU.

Resident.simulateAndTrain
/// One round of the loop: simulate, then train each network, each update in its own slot.
///
/// ONE RECORDING PER ROUND, and not one for several. Every `run` inside a recording carries
/// its own parameters - without it each dispatch would read whichever parameters were written
/// last, which on a device means every kernel in the frame running with the final one's. But a
/// recording may not span rounds either: an upload made while one is open lands before the
/// WHOLE recording executes, so a later round's appends would overwrite ring slots this
/// round's gathers are still about to read. Simulate, record this round's dispatches, submit.
pub fn simulateAndTrain(self: *Self) void {
    self.act(self.options.collect, 1.0);
    self.train();
}
Resident.act
/// `steps` simulation steps with the policy acting - its raw output plus exploration noise,
/// which the fleet scales into a pose offset - every one recorded into the ring.
///
/// `noise_scale` of zero is the policy ALONE: no draw is made at all (so judging cannot shift
/// the random stream and change what training does afterwards), and those steps are counted
/// into the judged pair rather than the collected one. They are still recorded: noise-free
/// on-policy steps are perfectly good data, and the ring must stay in step with the replay.
///
/// ONE STEP. Every character in turn - all from the same mirror, then they step together:
///
///     features            its goal and state                                      `features`
///     teacher 3           where its last flow step led, completing its pending     `completeFpoExample`
///                         example
///     hazard              projected a few steps ahead, for the planning flags      `projectHazard`
///     action              its plan's correction on the policy, when it has one     `computeAction`
///                         (teacher 2's example) - or the policy with the flow's
///                         correction and exploration (teacher 3's, pending)
///     own goal            the goal it aims at: the next state's own                 `rememberFpoOwnGoal`
///     written             never a non-finite action into the physics               `writeAction`
///
/// then the fleet steps; a character whose episode ended forgets what was its episode's
/// (`forgetEndedEpisodes`); the flags decide who plans next; and the step is counted and recorded.
pub fn act(self: *Self, steps: u32, noise_scale: f32) void {
    const random: Random = self.rng.random();
    // How much of itself each character's flow noise keeps from one step to the next - the same for every
    // character and step of the call; a character that plans keeps it longer, so it commits to the way back
    // it began. A judged call (no noise) is the policy alone: no character acts from a plan in it.
    const step_seconds: f32 = self.fleet.m.opt.timestep;
    const correlation_seconds: f32 = self.options.flow.noise_correlation_seconds;
    const flagged_seconds: f32 = self.options.flow.flagged_noise_correlation_seconds;
    const acting: Acting = .{
        .noise_scale = noise_scale,
        .may_act_from_plans = noise_scale != 0.0,
        .noise_correlation = zrl.ouCorrelation(f32, step_seconds, correlation_seconds),
        .flagged_noise_correlation = zrl.ouCorrelation(f32, step_seconds, flagged_seconds),
    };
    // Decisions only at the round's LAST step. A decision's work on the device is submitted with the frame
    // wherever in the round it is called, so its plans arrive with the next frame's readback either way;
    // made at the end it plans from the freshest states, rather than from ones up to a round old by the time
    // its plans are acted on. One falling due earlier waits, pending, its warm start shifted by every step it
    // waited (`PlanningFlags.step`) - and a round decides at most once, so a second decision can never
    // overwrite a first one's inputs before they are read.
    // THE PLANS IN HAND before the round acts. A round's decision is made at its end and its plans cover the
    // round after it; but they reach the host only with a readback, and a readback lands when the device has
    // finished the round's work - training included - which is after the next round has begun. Read without
    // waiting, the plans would arrive a round late, every one of them already past its horizon, and the search
    // would be thrown away: so a learner that plans waits for the newest readback before it explores. The
    // device's round is short beside the round's acting, so the wait is small.
    const acts_from_plans: bool = self.planner != null and noise_scale != 0.0;
    if (acts_from_plans) {
        self.waitForReadback();
    }
    for (0..steps) |step_index| {
        const is_last_step: bool = step_index + 1 == steps;
        // The newest plans the readback has brought, before anyone acts.
        if (self.planner != null) {
            self.refreshMailbox();
        }
        // Every character chooses its action from the SAME mirror within a step - the weights
        // as of the last readback - and then they all step together, which is what lets the
        // whole step become one upload into the ring.
        //
        // In three phases: every character's plan and random numbers, in the characters' order
        // (`prepareActing`); every character's features and action, each from its own numbers and nothing
        // shared (`computeAction`); then the bookkeeping, in order (`finishActing`). The numbers are those of
        // one character after another, and the middle phase - the policy and the flow, the expensive part -
        // could run on any thread.
        const character_count: usize = self.fleet.options.envs;
        for (0..character_count) |env| {
            self.prepareActing(env, acting, random);
        }
        self.computeEveryAction(acting);
        for (0..character_count) |env| {
            self.finishActing(env, acting);
        }
        _ = self.fleet.step(self.actions);
        self.acting_steps += 1;
        self.forgetEndedEpisodes();
        // Who plans next, from the hazards of the step just taken: decisions are made between steps, so a
        // character that starts planning acts from its plan from the next step on. Only while exploring -
        // a judged step is the policy alone.
        if (self.planning_flags) |*flags| {
            if (noise_scale != 0.0) {
                const settings: PlanningFlags.Settings = self.options.planning.flags;
                if (flags.step(self.hazards, settings, is_last_step, self.deciding)) |plan_age| {
                    for (self.deciding) |decides| {
                        self.planning_decisions += @intFromBool(decides);
                    }
                    self.planDecision(plan_age);
                }
            }
        }
        // One step watched per character, and a failure for each that just lost its reference.
        // The fleet raises that flag on the step an episode ENDS, and only when it ended badly
        // - a clip running out is a character that survived to the end of the motion.
        //
        // Noise-free steps are counted apart: those are the policy being judged, not explored
        // with, and mixing the two would leave a number that answers neither question.
        //
        // Each step counted on its clip too: the clip it was on - the one its episode ended on, when it just
        // ended (`terminal_clip`, kept before the restart chose the next), and otherwise the one it is still
        // on.
        const fleet: *track.Fleet = self.fleet;
        //
        // A step taken in an aftermath - after its character lost the reference, on its way back or falling
        // - is not time at risk (`track.Fleet.in_aftermath`), so it is not watched: counted, it would lengthen
        // the time to failure of a run with aftermaths and returns against one without.
        for (fleet.failures, fleet.dones, fleet.in_aftermath, 0..) |lost, ended, after_loss, env| {
            const clip: usize = if (ended) fleet.terminal_clip[env] else fleet.clip_of[env];
            const at_risk: u64 = if (after_loss) 0 else 1;
            if (noise_scale == 0.0) {
                self.judged_exposure += at_risk;
                if (lost) {
                    self.judged_failures += 1;
                }
            } else {
                self.exposure += at_risk;
                self.exposure_by_clip[clip] += at_risk;
                if (lost) {
                    self.failures += 1;
                    self.failures_by_clip[clip] += 1;
                }
            }
        }
        self.data.appendLatest(self.fleet);
    }
}
Resident.syncMirror
/// The policy's weights as the CPU sees them from here on. On a GPU the readback is a frame or
/// so old, which is why acting can use it at all: waiting for a fresh one would stall the
/// simulation every step.
pub fn syncMirror(self: *Self) void {
    // No readback yet (nothing has come back from the device), or one too narrow to reach the
    // policy's weights: keep the mirror as it is rather than copy half a policy. `init` widens
    // the readback so this cannot be the steady state - it is the first frame or two, when the
    // mirror still holds the weights the driver seeded.
    const params: []const f32 = self.kit.pipe.readLatest(.params) orelse return;
    if (params.len < self.kit.p_at + self.kit.policy_count) {
        return;
    }
    const weights: []const f32 = params[self.kit.p_at..][0..self.kit.policy_count];
    for (weights) |w| {
        if (!(w == w and @abs(w) < 1.0e30)) {
            self.mirror_rejected += 1;
            return;
        }
    }
    @memcpy(self.host.mirror, weights);
    // The flow's weights, when it acts: its range of the buffer into its mirror, all finite or none.
    if (self.kit.flow_actor) |flow_actor| {
        const flow_start: u32 = flow_actor.flow.network.paramsStart();
        const flow_end: u32 = flow_actor.flow.network.paramsEnd();
        if (params.len < flow_end) {
            return;
        }
        const flow_weights: []const f32 = params[flow_start..flow_end];
        for (flow_weights) |weight| {
            if (!(weight == weight and @abs(weight) < 1.0e30)) {
                self.mirror_rejected += 1;
                return;
            }
        }
        @memcpy(self.host.flow_mirror[flow_start..flow_end], flow_weights);
    }
}

13.7 Stopping and resuming#

A night of training can be stopped - a crash, a reboot, a laptop closed - and must carry on from where it was, as the same run. The learner therefore writes its whole state to a file and reads it back. Its state is more than its weights: a learner that resumed with the right weights and the wrong rest would train differently from the run it claims to continue, and its curves could not be read as one.

What the file holds. A header, then numbers, every one an f32:

  header   magic "ZSTSTAT1"                         the layout's version
           shape     features, references, actions,  a file from another learner is refused
                     world and policy parameter counts
           options   every Options field              a run continued under another setting is another run
           counters  world and policy updates,        Adam's step counts, and the curves' x axis
                     exposure, failures (collected and judged),
                     rejected mirrors, non-finite actions
           random    the generator's four words       every window drawn and every exploration draw from here on
  numbers  parameters      world model, then policy   as the kit packs them
           Adam's first moments                      laid out like the parameters
           Adam's second moments                     likewise
           normaliser      means, then spreads        the features the policy reads

The replay is not kept. A resumed learner refills it by acting before its first update - a few rounds of simulation, against hours of training - and the file stays the size of the networks rather than of their experience.

Why Adam's step count is part of the state. Adam keeps two running averages of each gradient, both started at zero, and corrects their start by dividing the first by 1 - beta1^t and the second by 1 - beta2^t. With the kit's betas, 0.9 and 0.999, a worked example after 1000 updates:

                       t = 1000 (the run as it was)     t = 1 (count restarted, moments kept)
  first divisor        1 - 0.9^1000   = 1.000            1 - 0.9   = 0.1     first moment 10x too large
  second divisor       1 - 0.999^1000 = 0.632            1 - 0.999 = 0.001   second moment 632x too large
  step  ~ first / sqrt(second)                           10 / sqrt(632) = 0.40 of the right size

The update counters are those step counts, so they travel in the header, and a resumed learner's first update is the step the stopped one would have taken next.

Refused, by name. Before a single number is trusted, the header is compared field by field with the learner reading it: the magic, then the shape, then every option, then the file's length. The first disagreement is returned as a path - shape.actions, options.policy_rate - and the file is not loaded. Then every number is checked before any is copied: a NaN weight or moment would poison every update that reads it, and a spread of zero would divide a feature by zero, so the numbers must be finite, Adam's second moments (averages of squares) not below zero, and the normaliser's spreads above zero. Every option must agree, the step sizes and the noise included: a resumed run is the same run carried on, and a change of recipe starts a run of its own.

On a GPU, saved when the readback is current. The parameters and the moments come back from the device a frame or so late, while the counters are the CPU's own. A file saved between the two would pair one update's weights with the next update's step count, so a program without frames waits until the readback reflects every update it has dispatched before it saves. After loading, the mirror takes the saved policy straight from the file, so acting does not wait for a readback to catch up with the upload.

What makes the file trustworthy is one check: a learner trained a few rounds is saved, a fresh learner loads the file and saves again, and the two files are the same bytes - every parameter, moment, normaliser value, counter and the random stream's state. The loaded learner then chooses the saved learner's action on the same features, bit for bit. A file with one exponent bit of the policy's last parameter changed loads, and acts otherwise - the control showing that the agreement comes from the file.

StateHeader
/// Everything a state file holds before its numbers.
///
/// THE SHAPE comes first - how many features, references and actions the networks were built for, and how many
/// parameters each network has - so that a file from a differently built learner is refused by name instead of
/// loaded as the first N numbers of something else. THE OPTIONS the learner was trained with follow, then THE
/// COUNTERS, which are what makes a resumed learner the same learner rather than a new one holding old weights:
/// the update counters are also Adam's step counts, and the random stream's state decides every window drawn and
/// every exploration draw from here on.
///
/// Why Adam's step count matters: Adam divides its first moment by `1 - beta1^t` and its second by `1 - beta2^t`,
/// to undo their start at zero. With the kit's betas (0.9 and 0.999), after 1000 updates those divisors are about 1
/// and 0.632. A learner resumed with its moments but its count restarted at `t = 1` would divide by 0.1 and 0.001
/// instead: the first moment read 10 times too large, the second 1000 / 1.58 = 632 times, and the step - their
/// ratio, the second under a square root - `10 / sqrt(632)`, about 0.4 times what it should be, recovering only
/// over the next few thousand updates.
///
/// Numbers follow the header, every one an f32, in this order: the parameters of both networks (the world model's
/// then the policy's, as the kit packs them), Adam's first moments, Adam's second moments (each laid out like the
/// parameters), then the feature normaliser's means and spreads.
pub const StateHeader = extern struct {
    magic: [8]u8,
    feature_count: u32,
    reference_count: u32,
    action_count: u32,
    world_parameter_count: u32,
    policy_parameter_count: u32,
    /// The critic's parameters (its online and target heads), saved straight after the policy's - 0 without one.
    critic_parameter_count: u32,
    /// The flow actor's parameters, saved straight after the critic's - 0 without one - and how many numbers its
    /// characters' noise holds (characters x actions - 0 without a flow): a file from a fleet of another size is
    /// refused by name, not only by its length.
    flow_parameter_count: u32,
    flow_noise_count: u32,
    /// The skip model's parameters, saved straight after the flow's - 0 without one - and a word that keeps the header
    /// free of padding (`hasNoPadding`).
    skip_parameter_count: u32,
    reserved_after_skip: u32 = 0,
    options: SavedOptions,
    world_updates: u32,
    policy_updates: u32,
    /// The critic's updates - its Adam step count - and a word that keeps the counters after it 8-byte aligned.
    critic_updates: u32,
    reserved: u32 = 0,
    exposure: u64,
    failures: u64,
    judged_exposure: u64,
    judged_failures: u64,
    mirror_rejected: u64,
    nonfinite_actions: u64,
    /// The steps the fleet has taken under the learner (`Resident.acting_steps`): every hashed noise stream - the
    /// flow's, FPO's draws, the planner's - is seeded from it, so a resumed run carries on from it rather than starting
    /// them all over.
    acting_steps: u64,
    /// The xoshiro256 generator's four words - the whole of its state.
    random_stream_state: [4]u64,
};
Resident.exportState
/// The learner's whole state as a file's worth of bytes: its shape, options and counters (`StateHeader`),
/// then both networks' parameters, Adam's two moments and the feature normaliser. Enough to carry training on
/// exactly; the replay is not kept - a resumed learner refills it by acting before its first update.
///
/// The parameters and moments come from the latest readback, so call `waitForReadback` first in a program
/// that has no frames. Memory: the bytes are allocated with `gpa` and become the caller's to free.
pub fn exportState(self: *Self, gpa: Allocator) ![]u8 {
    const parameter_count: usize = self.parameterCount();
    const parameters: []const f32 = self.kit.pipe.readLatest(.params) orelse return error.NoReadback;
    const first_moments: []const f32 = self.kit.pipe.readLatest(.adam_m) orelse return error.NoReadback;
    const second_moments: []const f32 = self.kit.pipe.readLatest(.adam_v) orelse return error.NoReadback;
    const parameters_reached: bool = parameters.len >= parameter_count;
    const moments_reached: bool = first_moments.len >= parameter_count and
        second_moments.len >= parameter_count;
    if (!parameters_reached or !moments_reached) {
        return error.NoReadback;
    }
    const header: StateHeader = self.stateHeader();
    const state_bytes: []u8 = try gpa.alloc(u8, self.stateByteCount());
    @memcpy(state_bytes[0..@sizeOf(StateHeader)], asBytes(&header));
    // The numbers in the order `StateHeader` documents, each section's bytes straight after the last.
    const sections: [6][]const f32 = .{
        parameters[0..parameter_count],
        first_moments[0..parameter_count],
        second_moments[0..parameter_count],
        self.norm.mean,
        self.norm.spread,
        self.flow_noise,
    };
    var write_offset: usize = @sizeOf(StateHeader);
    for (sections) |section| {
        const section_bytes: []const u8 = sliceAsBytes(section);
        @memcpy(state_bytes[write_offset..][0..section_bytes.len], section_bytes);
        write_offset += section_bytes.len;
    }
    assertf(write_offset == state_bytes.len, @src(), "exportState: wrote {d} of {d} bytes", .{
        write_offset,
        state_bytes.len,
    });
    return state_bytes;
}
Resident.stateProblem
/// Why `state_bytes` cannot be this learner's state, named - `"shape.actions"`, `"options.hidden"`, ... - or
/// null when it can. The header is read and compared field by field before any number is trusted: a file of
/// another layout, another shape or other options is refused, never read as the wrong thing. Then every number
/// is checked: finite, Adam's second moments not below zero, the normaliser's spreads above zero.
pub fn stateProblem(self: *const Self, state_bytes: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    const header_size: usize = @sizeOf(StateHeader);
    if (state_bytes.len < header_size) {
        return "not a SuperTrack state file: shorter than its header";
    }
    const saved: StateHeader = std.mem.bytesToValue(StateHeader, state_bytes[0..header_size]);
    if (!eql(u8, &saved.magic, &state_file_magic)) {
        return "not a SuperTrack state file of this layout: magic";
    }
    const own: StateHeader = self.stateHeader();
    if (saved.feature_count != own.feature_count) {
        return "shape.features";
    }
    if (saved.reference_count != own.reference_count) {
        return "shape.references";
    }
    if (saved.action_count != own.action_count) {
        return "shape.actions";
    }
    const same_network_sizes: bool = saved.world_parameter_count == own.world_parameter_count and
        saved.policy_parameter_count == own.policy_parameter_count and
        saved.critic_parameter_count == own.critic_parameter_count and
        saved.flow_parameter_count == own.flow_parameter_count and
        saved.skip_parameter_count == own.skip_parameter_count;
    if (!same_network_sizes) {
        return "shape.parameters";
    }
    if (saved.flow_noise_count != own.flow_noise_count) {
        return "shape.flow_noise: another number of characters";
    }
    if (optionsProblem(saved.options, self.options)) |differing_option| {
        return differing_option;
    }
    if (state_bytes.len != self.stateByteCount()) {
        return "the file's length";
    }
    // The numbers themselves, section by section: a NaN weight or moment would poison every update that reads
    // it, and a spread of zero divides a feature by zero. Adam's second moments are averages of squares, so
    // they may be zero but never negative; the spreads must be above zero.
    const float_size: usize = @sizeOf(f32);
    const parameter_bytes: usize = self.parameterCount() * float_size;
    const feature_bytes: usize = self.norm.mean.len * float_size;
    const parameters_at: usize = header_size;
    const first_moments_at: usize = parameters_at + parameter_bytes;
    const second_moments_at: usize = first_moments_at + parameter_bytes;
    const means_at: usize = second_moments_at + parameter_bytes;
    const spreads_at: usize = means_at + feature_bytes;
    const parameter_section: []const u8 = state_bytes[parameters_at..][0..parameter_bytes];
    const first_moment_section: []const u8 = state_bytes[first_moments_at..][0..parameter_bytes];
    const second_moment_section: []const u8 = state_bytes[second_moments_at..][0..parameter_bytes];
    const mean_section: []const u8 = state_bytes[means_at..][0..feature_bytes];
    const spread_section: []const u8 = state_bytes[spreads_at..][0..feature_bytes];
    if (!numbersAreUsable(parameter_section, false)) {
        return "numbers.parameters: not finite";
    }
    if (!numbersAreUsable(first_moment_section, false)) {
        return "numbers.first_moments: not finite";
    }
    const second_moments_usable: bool = numbersAreUsable(second_moment_section, false) and
        noNumberIsNegative(second_moment_section);
    if (!second_moments_usable) {
        return "numbers.second_moments: not finite, or below zero";
    }
    if (!numbersAreUsable(mean_section, false)) {
        return "numbers.normalizer_means: not finite";
    }
    if (!numbersAreUsable(spread_section, true)) {
        return "numbers.normalizer_spreads: not finite, or not above zero";
    }
    const flow_noise_at: usize = spreads_at + feature_bytes;
    const flow_noise_section: []const u8 = state_bytes[flow_noise_at..][0 .. self.flow_noise.len * float_size];
    if (!numbersAreUsable(flow_noise_section, false)) {
        return "numbers.flow_noise: not finite";
    }
    return null;
}
optionsProblem
/// The path of the first option a saved learner was trained with that differs from `wanted_options` - for example
/// `"options.policy_rate"` - or null when every option agrees.
///
/// Every option must agree, the step sizes and the noise included, and not only the ones that shape the networks. A
/// resumed run is meant to be the SAME run carried on, so its curves can be read as one; a run continued under
/// another setting is a different experiment, and is started as a run of its own.
fn optionsProblem(saved_options: SavedOptions, wanted_options: Options) ?[]const u8 {
    inline for (@typeInfo(Options).@"struct".field_names) |field_name| {
        const saved_value: @FieldType(Options, field_name) = @field(saved_options, field_name);
        const wanted_value: @FieldType(Options, field_name) = @field(wanted_options, field_name);
        // Field by field for a struct option (the failure barrier), as `==` is for a number.
        if (!metaEql(saved_value, wanted_value)) {
            return "options." ++ field_name;
        }
    }
    return null;
}
Resident.importState
/// Carry on from a state saved by `exportState` - on this device or another - or fail with
/// `error.StateFileRefused`, `stateProblem` saying why. The weights, Adam's moments and the normaliser go to
/// the GPU; the counters and the random stream to this learner; and the mirror takes the saved policy at once,
/// so acting does not wait for a readback to catch up with the upload.
///
/// Memory: `gpa` holds a temporary aligned copy of the numbers (a file's bytes owe nothing to an f32's
/// alignment), freed before this returns; nothing allocated outlives the call.
pub fn importState(self: *Self, gpa: Allocator, state_bytes: []const u8) !void {
    if (self.stateProblem(state_bytes) != null) {
        return error.StateFileRefused;
    }
    const header_size: usize = @sizeOf(StateHeader);
    const saved: StateHeader = std.mem.bytesToValue(StateHeader, state_bytes[0..header_size]);
    const number_bytes: []const u8 = state_bytes[header_size..];
    const saved_numbers: []f32 = try gpa.alloc(f32, number_bytes.len / @sizeOf(f32));
    defer gpa.free(saved_numbers);
    @memcpy(sliceAsBytes(saved_numbers), number_bytes);
    // The sections, in the order `StateHeader` documents.
    const parameter_count: usize = self.parameterCount();
    const feature_count: usize = self.norm.mean.len;
    const normalizer_at: usize = 3 * parameter_count;
    const parameters: []const f32 = saved_numbers[0..parameter_count];
    const first_moments: []const f32 = saved_numbers[parameter_count..][0..parameter_count];
    const second_moments: []const f32 = saved_numbers[2 * parameter_count ..][0..parameter_count];
    const means: []const f32 = saved_numbers[normalizer_at..][0..feature_count];
    const spreads: []const f32 = saved_numbers[normalizer_at + feature_count ..][0..feature_count];
    const flow_noise_at: usize = normalizer_at + 2 * feature_count;
    const saved_flow_noise: []const f32 = saved_numbers[flow_noise_at..][0..self.flow_noise.len];
    self.kit.pipe.upload(.params, parameters);
    self.kit.pipe.upload(.adam_m, first_moments);
    self.kit.pipe.upload(.adam_v, second_moments);
    // A readback copy encoded before these uploads would bring back the replaced weights, and the next
    // `syncMirror` would put them in the mirror: forget it, so that the mirror takes only a copy made after.
    self.kit.pipe.discardReadback();
    @memcpy(self.norm.mean, means);
    @memcpy(self.norm.spread, spreads);
    self.data.uploadNormalizer(self.norm);
    // The mirror takes the saved policy at once: acting does not wait for a readback to catch up.
    const saved_policy: []const f32 = parameters[self.kit.p_at..][0..self.kit.policy_count];
    @memcpy(self.host.mirror, saved_policy);
    // And the flow's - its mirror, its synergies and each character's noise - so acting resumes where it
    // stopped.
    if (self.host.flow_mirror.len > 0) {
        @memcpy(self.host.flow_mirror, parameters[0..self.host.flow_mirror.len]);
    }
    if (self.kit.flow_actor) |flow_actor| {
        const synergies_at: u32 = flow_actor.correction.synergies_at;
        @memcpy(self.host.synergies, parameters[synergies_at..][0..self.host.synergies.len]);
    }
    @memcpy(self.flow_noise, saved_flow_noise);
    self.world_updates = saved.world_updates;
    self.policy_updates = saved.policy_updates;
    self.critic_updates = saved.critic_updates;
    self.exposure = saved.exposure;
    self.failures = saved.failures;
    self.judged_exposure = saved.judged_exposure;
    self.judged_failures = saved.judged_failures;
    self.mirror_rejected = saved.mirror_rejected;
    self.nonfinite_actions = saved.nonfinite_actions;
    self.acting_steps = saved.acting_steps;
    self.rng.s = saved.random_stream_state;
    // The trust in the critic the restored updates have earned, before anything is planned or trained.
    self.applyCriticTrust();
}

Everything a learner keeps lies in one range at the start of the parameter buffer, in the order it is placed - the world model, the policy, then the critic's heads and a flow's network after them. The state file saves that range, and the readback reaches it, both from where the range ends; the header names each part only to check a file's shape.

13.8 EfficientTDMPC's update on the kit#

EfficientTDMPC's update - its world model's and its policy's - runs on the kit as it runs in the CPU agent (robot_bmpc), with the same arithmetic, so the two compute the same update from the same batch. What the update does is zimrrl's subject - the latent rollout and its consistency (zimrrl 9.4), the world model's loss (9.5), the running scale (9.12), the policy and its distillation (9.13, 9.14) and the whole update (9.19). This section is about how the kit lays it out: where every number lives, which kernels run, and in what order. It is built of the networks of §12.5, in robot_bmpc_kit.zig.

One update, in order - each piece below is one of this section's passages:

   the batch           sampled from the replay, laid out, uploaded region by region   KitLearner.update
   the window          encoded once, every dynamics head rolled through it             KitRollout.forward
   the value targets   what each stored step is worth, through the target heads        KitValueTargets.compute
   the losses          consistency, reward, value - finished windows counting nothing,
                       the value heads dropping out
   the backward        the heads first, then back through time into the encoder        KitWorldModel.backward
   the update          one clip of the global norm, two Adams, the targets' follow     KitWorldModel.update
   the policy          on every head's rolled latents: the running scale, the
                       distillation, its own clip and Adam                             KitPolicyLearner.update

The rollout. A replay window is laid out step by step. The encoder runs once over all of its observations; each dynamics head then rolls the first step's latent forward with the actions really taken. A head's input at every step is a WIDE ROW - the latent, then the action - which its first layer reads through its stride, so the concatenation [z | a] is only a layout. place_columns copies a latent into the latent columns of a wide row: the encoder's first latents into every head's first row, and each step's prediction into the next step's row.

   encoder pass     z_0 | z*_1 | z*_2 | z*_3          the window's observations, encoded once
   head, step 0     X_0 = [ z_0  | a_0 ]  ->  z_1       place_columns copies z_0 into X_0
   head, step 1     X_1 = [ z_1  | a_1 ]  ->  z_2       ... and each prediction into the next X
   head, step 2     X_2 = [ z_2  | a_2 ]  ->  z_3
   consistency      each z_(t+1) against z*_(t+1), weighted rho^t / H, averaged over the heads

The backward runs each head's steps in reverse - back-propagation through time. Each step is an application of its own (12.4), so every step's activations are still in place when its backward comes, and the head's weight gradients are summed over the steps: the last step's backward, the first one run, writes them, every earlier one adds. The gradient at a prediction z_(t+1) is gathered from every road that leads away from it (9.5 draws them) before the head at step t back-propagates: its own consistency error (mse_bwd, with the step's weight), the next step's input gradient (lat_take adds the latent columns of it), and every other network that read z_(t+1). The latent columns of each head's first input gradient are the gradient at z_0, which the encoder back-propagates - over the first block of rows only, the targets taking no gradient.

KitRollout.headBackwardThroughTime
/// One head's steps in reverse (this type's head, "the backward"): at each step, the gradient at the step's
/// prediction from its two roads, then back through the head to the step's wide row.
fn headBackwardThroughTime(
    rollout: Self,
    pipe: *Pipe,
    dynamics_head: DynamicsHead,
    loss_scale: f32,
) void {
    const window_count: u32 = rollout.options.window_count;
    const latent_width: u32 = rollout.latent_width;
    const wide_row_width: u32 = rollout.wideRowWidth();
    const horizon: u32 = rollout.options.horizon;
    const latent_value_count: u32 = window_count * latent_width;
    var step: usize = horizon;
    while (step > 0) {
        step -= 1;
        const step_application: Network.Application = dynamics_head.step_applications[step];
        const prediction_gradient_offset: u32 = dynamics_head.prediction_gradient_offsets[step];
        // 1. This step's own consistency error, as its share of the whole loss.
        pipe.params = .{
            .rows = window_count,
            .out_dim = latent_width,
            .y_off = step_application.outputsOffset(),
            .t_off = rollout.encodedLatentsOffset(@intCast(step + 1)),
            .dy_off = prediction_gradient_offset,
            .loss_weight = rollout.stepLossWeight(step, loss_scale),
