            // Only the windows still counting at this step, their mean over themselves.
            .row_mask = @backingInt(M.RowMask.counting_column),
            .mask_off = rollout.countingAt(step),
            .mean_factor_off = rollout.meanFactorAt(step),
        };
        pipe.run("mse_bwd", latent_value_count);
        // 2. The road through the next step: what the next step's input took back through the network, its
        //    z columns added. The last step's prediction feeds nothing.
        const is_last_step: bool = step + 1 == horizon;
        if (!is_last_step) {
            const next_step_application: Network.Application = dynamics_head.step_applications[step + 1];
            const next_step_inputs_gradient: u32 = next_step_application.inputsGradientOffset();
            pipe.params = .{
                .rows = window_count,
                .count = latent_width,
                .stride = wide_row_width,
                .dx_off = next_step_inputs_gradient,
                .dy_off = prediction_gradient_offset,
            };
            pipe.run("lat_take", latent_value_count);
        }
        // 3. The other networks that read this prediction - the reward and value heads at step t + 1 - add
        //    theirs.
        const readers: []const LatentReader = dynamics_head.latent_readers[step + 1].items;
        rollout.addReadersGradients(pipe, readers, prediction_gradient_offset);
        // 4. Back through the head at this step, to its wide row. Its weights' gradients: the last step's
        //    backward (the first one run) overwrites, every earlier step's adds.
        const parameter_gradients: ParameterGradients = if (is_last_step) .overwrite else .add;
        const wide_row_offset: u32 = dynamics_head.wide_row_offsets[step];
        step_application.backward(
            pipe,
            window_count,
            wide_row_offset,
            wide_row_width,
            prediction_gradient_offset,
            parameter_gradients,
        );
    }
}

Finished windows. A window that runs past its episode's end counts for nothing from then on (zimrrl 9.5). On the kit the rollout keeps, in the activation buffer, a counting column for every step - 1 for a window still counting, 0 for a finished one - and every step's mean factor, both written by the host from the replay batch's flags (KitRollout.writeFinished). The loss kernels read them (RowMask): mse_bwd multiplies a row's gradient by its flag and the step's factor; the two-hot kernels multiply a row's two target shares by its flag, so a finished row's target is all zeros; the policy's distillation multiplies a row's weight by it. With every flag 1 and every factor 1 nothing changes, bit for bit.

The reward and value heads. At every step the reward head reads the dynamics head's wide row X_t itself, and each value head reads its first latent-width columns through the same stride: no copy. Because they read z_t, their input gradients carry more gradient at z_t, so each of their applications is registered with the rollout as a READER of its latent (KitRollout.addLatentReader), and the backward through time adds the latent columns of every reader's input gradient where it gathers z_t's. The heads' own backwards run first, so their input gradients are ready when the backward through time reaches them; each head's parameter gradients are summed over every dynamics head and step that applied it.

The value heads' applications drop out while they train (zimrrl 9.5): each has a mask region for its first layer, filled every update by the host from the same generator, split the same way, as the CPU agent's (zimrnum's own fillDropoutMask). Forward, mask_values multiplies the layer's linear outputs by it in place, before the norm; backward, mask_gradients multiplies the gradient at those outputs by it. A mask of all ones keeps every unit, and the update is the one without dropout, bit for bit.

   d z_t  =  consistency at t  +  the next step's input  +  the reward head at t  +  each value head at t
KitWorldModel.backward
/// The whole loss's backward (this type's head): every head application's two-hot gradient and its backward
/// - the reward head's and each value head's parameter gradients summed over every dynamics head and step -
/// then the rollout's, through time, with those heads' latent gradients merged in, scaled by the consistency
/// weight. Every network's parameter gradients are written over what grads held.
pub fn backward(world_model: Self, pipe: *Pipe) void {
    const rollout: Rollout = world_model.rollout;
    const options: LossOptions = world_model.loss_options;
    const horizon: u32 = rollout.options.horizon;
    const step_count: f32 = @floatFromInt(horizon);
    const dynamics_head_count: f32 = @floatFromInt(rollout.dynamics_heads.len);
    const value_head_count: f32 = @floatFromInt(world_model.value_networks.len);
    const wide_row_width: u32 = rollout.wideRowWidth();
    for (rollout.dynamics_heads, 0..) |dynamics_head, head_index| {
        for (dynamics_head.wide_row_offsets, 0..) |wide_row_offset, step| {
            // rho^t, as the rollout's own weights are made (`KitRollout.stepWeight`).
            const step_weight: f32 = Rollout.stepWeight(rollout.options.rho, step);
            const is_first_application: bool = head_index == 0 and step == 0;
            const parameter_gradients: ParameterGradients = if (is_first_application) .overwrite else .add;
            // The reward head: its share is rho^t / H, then over the dynamics heads, then its weight.
            const reward_share: f32 = step_weight / step_count;
            const reward_weight: f32 = options.reward_weight * (reward_share / dynamics_head_count);
            const reward_at_step: HeadApplication = world_model.reward_applications[head_index][step];
            const rewards_at_step: u32 = world_model.stepTargets(world_model.rewards_offset, step);
            world_model.headBackward(
                pipe,
                reward_at_step,
                rewards_at_step,
                step,
                reward_weight,
                wide_row_offset,
                wide_row_width,
                parameter_gradients,
            );
            // Each value head: rho^t / (H x value heads), then over the dynamics heads, then its weight.
            const value_share: f32 = step_weight / (step_count * value_head_count);
            const value_weight: f32 = options.value_weight * (value_share / dynamics_head_count);
            const value_targets_at_step: u32 = world_model.stepTargets(world_model.value_targets_offset, step);
            for (world_model.value_applications[head_index][step]) |value_at_step| {
                world_model.headBackward(
                    pipe,
                    value_at_step,
                    value_targets_at_step,
                    step,
                    value_weight,
                    wide_row_offset,
                    wide_row_width,
                    parameter_gradients,
                );
            }
        }
    }
    rollout.backward(pipe, options.consistency_weight);
}

The update. One clip of the world model's global gradient norm, then Adam, then the target value heads' follow (9.18 explains each). The world model's parameters - encoder, dynamics heads, reward head, value heads - are placed one after another, so they are one region the clip and Adam treat as a block, the target heads after them. The norm is two passes, because a GPU sums in parallel: each thread sums the squares of one chunk of the gradients, then one thread adds the chunks' totals and writes the factor, which Adam multiplies into each gradient as it reads it:

   grads   [ chunk 0 | chunk 1 | chunk 2 | ... ]       grad_square_partials: one thread per chunk
              |         |         |
              v         v         v
   acts    [ sum 0  |  sum 1  |  sum 2  | ... ]
                          |
                          v                          clip_factor: one thread
                 norm = sqrt(sum of the sums),  factor = 20 / norm if norm > 20, else exactly 1
                          |
                          v                          adam_clipped: one thread per parameter
                 Adam on gradient x factor           the encoder at 0.3 x the rate, the rest at the rate

The target heads follow by polyak, the same increment form zimrnum's polyakUpdate uses, so the host and the kit follow to the same bits.

KitWorldModel.update
/// One step of the optimiser after `backward` (this type's head, "the update"): the clip, Adam - the encoder
/// at its share of the rate - and the target value heads' follow. `update_count` counts the updates from 1, as
/// Adam's bias corrections need (`zimrnum.adamCorrectionMultipliers`).
pub fn update(
    world_model: Self,
    pipe: *Pipe,
    options: UpdateOptions,
    update_count: u32,
) void {
    // 1. The clip: each chunk's sum of squares, then the norm and the factor.
    const model_floats: u32 = world_model.model_params_end - world_model.model_params_start;
    const clip_chunk_floats: u32 = world_model.clip_chunk_floats;
    const chunk_count: u32 = (model_floats + clip_chunk_floats - 1) / clip_chunk_floats;
    pipe.params = .{
        .count = model_floats,
        .stride = clip_chunk_floats,
        .w_off = world_model.model_params_start,
        .y_off = world_model.clip_partials_offset,
    };
    pipe.run("grad_square_partials", chunk_count);
    pipe.params = .{
        .rows = chunk_count,
        .x_off = world_model.clip_partials_offset,
        .z_off = world_model.clip_norm_offset,
        .clip = options.gradient_clip,
    };
    pipe.run("clip_factor", 1);
    // 2. Adam on the clipped gradients: the encoder at its share of the rate, the rest at the rate.
    const corrections: zn.AdamCorrections(f32) = zn.adamCorrectionMultipliers(
        f32,
        options.beta1,
        options.beta2,
        update_count,
    );
    const encoder_rate: f32 = options.learning_rate * options.encoder_rate_scale;
    const clip_factor_offset: u32 = world_model.clip_norm_offset + 1;
    const encoder_floats: u32 = world_model.encoder_params_end - world_model.model_params_start;
    const rest_floats: u32 = world_model.model_params_end - world_model.encoder_params_end;
    const regions = [_]struct { start: u32, floats: u32, rate: f32 }{
        .{ .start = world_model.model_params_start, .floats = encoder_floats, .rate = encoder_rate },
        .{ .start = world_model.encoder_params_end, .floats = rest_floats, .rate = options.learning_rate },
    };
    for (regions) |region| {
        pipe.params = .{
            .count = region.floats,
            .w_off = region.start,
            .x_off = clip_factor_offset,
            .rate = region.rate,
            .beta1 = options.beta1,
            .beta2 = options.beta2,
            .epsilon = options.epsilon,
            .correction1 = corrections.first,
            .correction2 = corrections.second,
        };
        pipe.run("adam_clipped", region.floats);
    }
    // 3. The target value heads follow their online twins.
    for (world_model.target_value_networks, world_model.value_networks) |target_network, online_network| {
        const floats: u32 = target_network.paramsEnd() - target_network.paramsStart();
        pipe.params = .{
            .count = floats,
            .w_off = target_network.paramsStart(),
            .v_off = online_network.paramsStart(),
            .tau = options.target_follow,
        };
        pipe.run("polyak", floats);
    }
}

The value targets. A value head is trained toward what a stored step is worth by one step of the model, through every dynamics head (zimrrl 9.16). On the kit nothing is encoded again: the rollout's encoder pass already holds every stored step's true latent, its first H blocks. They are placed into wide rows, the policy draws an action beside each (policy_draw, the host's own draw), the reward head reads the wide rows, every dynamics head steps them, every target value head reads each head's next latents, and one thread per stored step adds it up in the host's order (value_target_combine), writing straight into the world model's value targets:

   encoder pass   [ z(o_0) | z(o_1) | ... | z(o_(H-1)) | z(o_H) ]      the first H blocks: every stored step
                     |
                     +--> the policy --> its draw --+
                     v                              v
   wide rows      Y = [ z | a ]  -- the reward head --> R(z, a), decoded
                        |
                        +-- dynamics head i --> f_i(z, a) -- target value head j --> V_ij, decoded

   target = R + gamma x (1 / heads) x sum over i of  mean over j of V_ij

The policy's distillation. The distillation loss's gradient has a closed form (9.14 derives it), so one thread per row writes the gradient at the policy network's raw outputs directly - the centre's and the spread's, each through its tanh - and beside it the row's divergence and entropy.

policy_distill_bwd
/// The policy's distillation loss, backward, ONE THREAD PER ROW (this section's head): for `rows` rows of `out_dim`
/// action dimensions -
///   reads  acts  `x_off`  the policy network's raw outputs [rows, 2 x dims]: raw centres, then raw spreads
///               `t_off`  the planner's means [rows, dims];  `u_off`  the logs of its spreads [rows, dims]
///               `v_off`  each row's weight [rows];  `e_off`  the scale's reciprocal (one value)
///   writes dacts `dy_off` the gradient at the raw outputs [rows, 2 x dims]
///          acts  `y_off`  each row's divergence, KL / dims [rows];  `z_off`  each row's entropy [rows]
/// The spread's bounds and the entropy's coefficient are `distill_log_std_low`, `_high`, `distill_entropy_coefficient`.
pub fn policy_distill_bwd(id: u32) void {
    if (id >= params.rows) {
        return;
    }
    distillRow(id, .divergence_and_gradients);
}

The running scale. BMPC moves the scale with the batch at hand before the policy's gradient divides by it, and divergences do not depend on the scale, so on the kit the order is three dispatches: the first step's divergences alone (policy_divergence); one thread that sorts them, reads their 5th and 95th percentiles and moves the scale - which stays in the activation buffer from one update to the next - and writes its reciprocal (running_scale_update); then the gradient, which reads the reciprocal. Any correct sort puts finite values in the same order, and the interpolation and the step are zimrmath's (quantileOfSorted, runningScaleStep), so the kit's scale is zimrnum's to the bit.

running_scale_update
/// BMPC's running scale, moved by one batch, ONE THREAD (`zimrnum.RunningScale.update`): the `count` values at acts
/// `x_off` - the first step's divergences, from `policy_divergence` - copied into acts `z_off` and sorted there, their
/// 5th and 95th percentiles (`zm.quantileOfSorted`, the host's own interpolation), and the scale at acts `v_off` -
/// which persists from update to update, 1 to start - moved a fraction `tau` toward their spread
/// (`zm.runningScaleStep`). Its reciprocal, what `policy_distill_bwd` multiplies by, goes to acts `e_off`.
///
/// The sort is an insertion sort in one thread: a batch is a few hundred values, and any correct sort puts finite
/// values in the same order, so the percentiles are the host's exactly.
pub fn running_scale_update(id: u32) void {
    if (id != 0) {
        return;
    }
    const count: u32 = params.count;
    var copy_index: u32 = 0;
    while (copy_index < count) : (copy_index += 1) {
        b_acts[params.z_off + copy_index] = b_acts[params.x_off + copy_index];
    }
    // Insertion sort: each value in turn slides left past every larger one.
    var sorted_end: u32 = 1;
    while (sorted_end < count) : (sorted_end += 1) {
        const inserted: f32 = b_acts[params.z_off + sorted_end];
        var position: u32 = sorted_end;
        while (position > 0 and b_acts[params.z_off + position - 1] > inserted) : (position -= 1) {
            b_acts[params.z_off + position] = b_acts[params.z_off + position - 1];
        }
        b_acts[params.z_off + position] = inserted;
    }
    const sorted: ActsRow = .{ .start = params.z_off };
    const fifth_percentile: f32 = zm.quantileOfSorted(f32, ActsRow, sorted, count, 0.05);
    const ninety_fifth_percentile: f32 = zm.quantileOfSorted(f32, ActsRow, sorted, count, 0.95);
    const spread: f32 = ninety_fifth_percentile - fifth_percentile;
    const scale: f32 = zm.runningScaleStep(f32, b_acts[params.v_off], params.tau, spread);
    b_acts[params.v_off] = scale;
    b_acts[params.e_off] = 1.0 / scale;
}

The policy's update. The policy learns on the rolled latents of every dynamics head, the heads' copies of a window stacked into one batch, every copy of a stored step pulled toward that step's one planner target. The latents are already in the rollout's wide rows, so the policy reads them where they are, once per step and head:

   the rollout's wide rows:     head 0:  X_0  X_1  X_2       head 1:  X_0  X_1  X_2
                                          |    |    |                  |    |    |
   the policy, per step and head:         P    P    P                  P    P    P     gradients summed
                                          |    |    |                  |    |    |
   the planner's targets:               step 0    1    2   (the same for every head's copy)

One update is five steps, and nothing in it reads back from the device: the policy forward on every head's latents at every step; the first step's divergences; the running scale moved by them; every row's gradient and the policy's backward, its gradients summed over every step and head; then the policy's own clip and its Adam step, with an epsilon of 1e-5 where the world model's is 1e-8 (BMPC's choice for the policy).

KitPolicyLearner.update
/// One update (this type's head, "one update"), after the world model's forward has filled the rollout's
/// wide rows. `update_count` counts the policy's updates from 1, for Adam's bias corrections.
pub fn update(learner: Self, pipe: *Pipe, update_count: u32) void {
    const rollout: Rollout = learner.rollout;
    const window_count: u32 = rollout.options.window_count;
    const wide_row_width: u32 = rollout.wideRowWidth();
    const head_count: u32 = @intCast(rollout.dynamics_heads.len);
    // 1. The policy on every head's latents at every step, read in the wide rows.
    for (learner.step_applications, 0..) |head_applications, step_index| {
        for (head_applications, rollout.dynamics_heads) |application, dynamics_head| {
            const wide_row_offset: u32 = dynamics_head.wide_row_offsets[step_index];
            application.forward(pipe, wide_row_offset, wide_row_width);
        }
    }
    // 2. The first step's divergences, every head's.
    for (0..head_count) |head_index| {
        pipe.params = learner.distillParams(0, head_index);
        pipe.run("policy_divergence", window_count);
    }
    // 3. The running scale, moved by them.
    pipe.params = .{
        .count = head_count * window_count,
        .x_off = learner.divergencesAt(0, 0),
        .z_off = learner.sort_scratch_offset,
        .v_off = learner.scale_offset,
        .e_off = learner.inverse_scale_offset,
        .tau = learner.options.scale_rate,
    };
    pipe.run("running_scale_update", 1);
    // 4. Every row's gradient, and the policy's backward: the first overwrites, every later one adds.
    for (learner.step_applications, 0..) |head_applications, step_index| {
        for (head_applications, rollout.dynamics_heads, 0..) |application, dynamics_head, head_index| {
            pipe.params = learner.distillParams(step_index, head_index);
            pipe.run("policy_distill_bwd", window_count);
            const is_first_application: bool = step_index == 0 and head_index == 0;
            const parameter_gradients: ParameterGradients = if (is_first_application) .overwrite else .add;
            const wide_row_offset: u32 = dynamics_head.wide_row_offsets[step_index];
            const raw_outputs_gradient: u32 = learner.gradient_offsets[step_index][head_index];
            application.backward(
                pipe,
                window_count,
                wide_row_offset,
                wide_row_width,
                raw_outputs_gradient,
                parameter_gradients,
            );
        }
    }
    // 5. The policy's own clip and Adam.
    learner.clipAndStep(pipe, update_count);
}

One update from the replay. KitLearner puts the pieces of this section together as the CPU agent's learner does: it samples a batch of windows from the replay with the same call, lays the windows out as the rollout reads them - the windows' first observations, then what followed each step; the actions, rewards and finished flags; the targets' noise and the value heads' dropout masks; the planner's stored targets for the policy, their spreads as logarithms - and uploads each region it wrote, and only those, since the rest of the activation buffer holds what the device keeps from one update to the next (the running scale, the planner's Gaussians). Then the world model's update, and the policy's unless the learner is pretraining. It keeps counters - each optimiser's steps, the real updates - so unlike its pieces it is used through a pointer.

KitLearner.update
/// One update (this type's head): sample, lay out, upload, the world model's update, then the policy's unless
/// `pretraining`. `dropout_rngs`: the value heads' mask generators, one per value application in the loss's
/// order - or null for the learner's own.
pub fn update(
    learner: *Self,
    pipe: *Pipe,
    replay: *Replay,
    rng: zn.Rng,
    update_index: u32,
    pretraining: bool,
    dropout_rngs: ?[]const zn.Rng,
) !void {
    const config: Tdmpc.Config = learner.config;
    // 1. The batch - the CPU learner's very call.
    try replay.sample(
        rng.split(0),
        update_index,
        config.horizon,
        learner.origins,
        learner.window_rows,
        learner.finished,
    );
    if (!pretraining) {
        learner.updates += 1;
    }
    // Reanalyze on every interval-th real update - the real updates counted from 1, so the 10th, the 20th.
    const reanalyze_interval: usize = config.reanalyze_interval;
    const interval_reached: bool = reanalyze_interval > 0 and learner.updates % reanalyze_interval == 0;
    if (!pretraining and interval_reached) {
        try learner.reanalyze(pipe, replay, rng.split(3));
    }
    // 2. Laid out, and uploaded region by region.
    learner.layOutBatch();
    learner.writeTargetNoise(rng.split(1));
    const mask_rngs: []const zn.Rng = dropout_rngs orelse learner.ownDropoutRngs(rng.split(2));
    const host_acts: []f32 = learner.host_acts;
    learner.rollout.writeWindow(host_acts, learner.observations, learner.actions);
    learner.rollout.writeFinished(host_acts, learner.finished);
    learner.world_model.writeTargets(host_acts, learner.rewards, learner.rewards);
    learner.value_targets.writeNoise(host_acts, learner.target_noise);
    try learner.world_model.writeValueDropoutMasksFrom(host_acts, mask_rngs);
    learner.rollout.uploadWindow(pipe, host_acts);
    learner.world_model.uploadTargets(pipe, host_acts);
    learner.value_targets.uploadNoise(pipe, host_acts);
    learner.world_model.uploadValueDropoutMasks(pipe, host_acts);
    // 3. The world model: its forward, the value targets its loss reads, its backward and its step.
    learner.world_model.forward(pipe);
    learner.value_targets.compute(pipe);
    learner.world_model.backward(pipe);
    learner.world_model_steps += 1;
    learner.world_model.update(pipe, .{
        .learning_rate = config.learning_rate,
        .encoder_rate_scale = config.encoder_rate_scale,
        .gradient_clip = config.gradient_clip,
        .target_follow = config.target_follow,
    }, learner.world_model_steps);
    // 4. The policy, on the rolled latents the world model's forward left in place - unless pretraining.
    if (!pretraining) {
        learner.policy_learner.writeTargets(host_acts, learner.target_means, learner.target_log_stds);
        learner.policy_learner.uploadTargets(pipe, host_acts);
        learner.policy_steps += 1;
        learner.policy_learner.update(pipe, learner.policy_steps);
    }
}

Reanalyze. Every tenth real update, the first windows of the batch are planned again (zimrrl 9.20): their stored states, from scratch, by a second planner on the same networks - the reanalyzing planner's settings, the policy's plans drawn with exploration's wider spread - before the world model learns. The new targets replace the batch's, so the policy learns from them, and are written back to the replay's stored rows. On the kit the second planner is one more KitPlanner, over the batch's stored states: the host writes their observations and the decision's noise, the kit decides, and the targets come back to the host for the replay. Reading them back is the one place an update waits for the device: the read is taken only once the readback reflects every dispatch made, never from an earlier one.

   the batch's rows   (step x W + window)          the planned states   (step x R + window)
     step 0  | w0 .. w(R-1) | wR .. w(W-1) |   -->     | w0 .. w(R-1) |
     step 1  | w0 .. w(R-1) | wR .. w(W-1) |   -->     | w0 .. w(R-1) |
   new targets back into the same rows, and into the replay

13.9 EfficientTDMPC's planner on the kit#

At every decision EfficientTDMPC searches: it proposes hundreds of candidate plans per state, has the model score them, and moves a Gaussian over plans toward the best (zimrrl 9.7 for the score, 9.8 for the search, 9.15 for the policy's place in it). On the kit the search is three pieces that share one layout - every state's block of candidates, their actions step by step, [horizon][state x candidate][action] - so each piece writes where the next one reads, and nothing goes back to the host between them:

   the policy's plans     -->  the first candidates of each state's block     KitPolicyPlans.fill
   the warm start         -->  each state's Gaussian: last plan shifted, or 0  KitMppi.begin
   each round:
     mppi_sample          -->  every other candidate, from its state's Gaussian
     the scorer           -->  every candidate's score                      KitPlanScorer.score
     mppi_elites, refit   -->  each state's Gaussian moved onto its elites     KitMppi.refit
   the choice             -->  one elite drawn by weight: target and spread   KitMppi.choose
   the action             -->  the target jittered, or the target itself      KitMppi.explore

KitPlanner.decide runs the whole decision in that order. Each state's Gaussian stays in the activation buffer from one decision to the next, which is what the warm start shifts.

Scoring plans. The planner proposes many candidate plans per state and the model scores them all (zimrrl 9.7 explains the score, and 9.8 the search it serves). A score needs no gradient, so on the kit nothing is kept for a backward: each network has one application over all the candidates' rows, overwritten at every step as the rollout moves on, and each dynamics head two wide rows it alternates between - the step's input and the next step's. The memory a plan takes does not grow with its length. Each state is encoded once and its latent copied into every candidate's row (broadcast_rows); at each step the actions are placed beside the latents, the reward head reads them, the dynamics head steps them into the other wide rows, and at the depths the objective weighs every value head reads where they lead. One thread per candidate then forms the score - the mean over every pair of a dynamics head and a value head, less beta standard deviations of their disagreement - in the host's order of arithmetic (plan_score_combine).

   each state's latent  --broadcast_rows-->  wide rows A    (every candidate's z columns)
   step t:   actions into the a columns;  reward head --> r(i, t);  dynamics head --> wide rows B
             at a weighted depth:  every value head --> V(i, t + 1, j)
   then A and B change places, and the next step reads B
KitPlanScorer.score
pub fn score(scorer: Self, pipe: *Pipe) void {
    // 1. Every state's latent, once - the encoder over the states, not over the candidates.
    scorer.encoder_pass.forward(pipe, scorer.observations_offset, 0);
    const state_latents: u32 = scorer.encoder_pass.outputsOffset();
    // 2. Every candidate rolled under every dynamics head: its rewards and the values it reaches.
    for (scorer.head_rollouts, 0..) |head_rollout, head_index| {
        scorer.rollHead(pipe, head_rollout, @intCast(head_index), state_latents);
    }
    // 3. Every candidate's score and variance, from every head's rewards and values.
    scorer.combineScores(pipe);
}

The policy's own plans. A few of every state's candidates are the policy's own plans (zimrrl 9.15): scored like every other candidate, never moved by the search, so a good policy makes planning start from good ground. On the kit, the plans roll through a pair of alternating wide rows: the policy reads the latent columns, its draw goes into the action columns beside them (policy_draw), the first dynamics head reads the whole row and its next latent goes into the other wide rows. Each step's actions are then carried into the scorer's candidate actions, each state's plans into the first rows of its block (copy_row_blocks).

   plan rows (state x plan)               candidate rows (state x candidate)
   state 0:  plan 0, plan 1, plan 2  -->   state 0:  0 1 2 | MPPI's samples 3 .. 5
   state 1:  plan 0, plan 1, plan 2  -->   state 1:  0 1 2 | MPPI's samples 3 .. 5
KitPolicyPlans.fill
/// Every state's plans drawn, rolled and written into the scorer's candidate actions (this type's head),
/// after the states' observations are in acts.
pub fn fill(policy_plans: Self, pipe: *Pipe) void {
    const scorer: Scorer = policy_plans.scorer;
    const options: Options = policy_plans.options;
    const states: u32 = scorer.options.states;
    const candidates: u32 = scorer.options.candidates;
    const row_count: u32 = states * options.plans;
    const candidate_rows: u32 = states * candidates;
    const latent_width: u32 = scorer.latent_width;
    const action_width: u32 = scorer.action_width;
    const wide_row_width: u32 = latent_width + action_width;
    // 1. Every state's latent, into each of its plans' first wide row.
    scorer.encoder_pass.forward(pipe, scorer.observations_offset, 0);
    pipe.params = .{
        .rows = states,
        .count = latent_width,
        .x_off = scorer.encoder_pass.outputsOffset(),
        .y_off = policy_plans.wide_rows_offsets[0],
        .stride = wide_row_width,
        .col = 0,
        .row_copies = options.plans,
    };
    pipe.run("broadcast_rows", row_count * latent_width);
    for (0..scorer.options.horizon) |step| {
        const step_index: u32 = @intCast(step);
        const current_rows: u32 = policy_plans.wide_rows_offsets[step % 2];
        const next_rows: u32 = policy_plans.wide_rows_offsets[(step + 1) % 2];
        // 2. The policy at the latents, and its draw beside them.
        policy_plans.policy_pass.forward(pipe, current_rows, wide_row_width);
        const step_noise: u32 = policy_plans.noise_offset + step_index * row_count * action_width;
        pipe.params = .{
            .rows = row_count,
            .out_dim = action_width,
            .x_off = policy_plans.policy_pass.outputsOffset(),
            .u_off = step_noise,
            .y_off = current_rows,
            .stride = wide_row_width,
            .col = latent_width,
            .distill_log_std_low = options.log_std_low,
            .distill_log_std_high = options.log_std_high,
        };
        pipe.run("policy_draw", row_count);
        // 3. The step's actions into each state's first candidates.
        const step_candidates: u32 = scorer.actions_offset + step_index * candidate_rows * action_width;
        pipe.params = .{
            .rows = row_count,
            .count = action_width,
            .x_off = current_rows,
            .y_off = step_candidates,
            .stride = wide_row_width,
            .col = latent_width,
            .plan_candidates = candidates,
            .plan_policy_plans = options.plans,
        };
        pipe.run("copy_row_blocks", row_count * action_width);
        // 4. The latents one step on - not after the last step.
        const is_last_step: bool = step + 1 == scorer.options.horizon;
        if (!is_last_step) {
            policy_plans.dynamics_pass.forward(pipe, current_rows, wide_row_width);
            placeColumns(M, pipe, .{
                .rows = row_count,
                .count = latent_width,
                .source_offset = policy_plans.dynamics_pass.outputsOffset(),
                .destination_offset = next_rows,
                .row_stride = wide_row_width,
                .first_column = 0,
            });
        }
    }
}

One round of the search. Each state keeps a Gaussian over plans - a mean and a spread per step and action dimension - in the activation buffer, from round to round (zimrrl 9.8). A round is three kernels around the scorer. mppi_sample draws every candidate past the policy's own from its state's Gaussian, one thread per value, straight into the scorer's candidate actions. mppi_elites gives each state one thread to pick its best candidates without sorting anything: each pick is the largest (score, candidate) pair strictly below the last one taken, which reproduces the host's stable sort read from the end - among equal scores the higher candidate first - and then the elites' weights, exp(temperature x (score - best)). mppi_refit moves each state's mean and spread to the elites' weighted mean and standard deviation, one thread per step and dimension.

   scores of one state:   0.1  0.2  0.25  0.9  0.9  0.9  -1  0.05       (candidates 0 .. 7)
   pick 1: the largest pair                      (0.9, 5)
   pick 2: the largest pair below (0.9, 5)       (0.9, 4)
   pick 3: the largest pair below (0.9, 4)       (0.9, 3)       elites 5, 4, 3 - weights 1/3 each
mppi_elites
/// Each state's elites and their weights, ONE THREAD PER STATE: of its `plan_candidates` scores at acts `x_off`
/// (made rankable, `zm.rankableScore`), the best `mppi_elites`, best first, in the host's order - the host sorts
/// ascending and stably and reads from the end, so among equal scores the higher candidate comes first. Each round
/// takes the largest (score, candidate) pair strictly below the last one taken, so nothing is sorted and nothing is
/// marked. Then each elite's weight, exp(`mppi_temperature` x (score - best)) - or, relative to the elites' spread
/// (`mppi_temperature_mode`, `MppiTemperature`), exp(`mppi_temperature` x (score - best) / (best - worst elite)) -
/// summed in rank order and each divided by the sum. Writes the elites' candidate numbers at acts `y_off` and their
/// weights at acts `z_off`, [states][elites].
pub fn mppi_elites(id: u32) void {
    if (id >= params.rows) {
        return;
    }
    // A candidate's number is stored as a float in the f32 buffer: exact, since every whole number below 2^24 is a
    // float, and a state has hundreds of candidates. `mppi_refit` reads it back with `@trunc`.
    //
    // Why rank by (score, candidate) PAIRS: the host sorts the scores ascending and stably - equal scores keep their
    // candidates' order - and reads the elites from the end, so among equal scores the HIGHER candidate is taken first.
    // Comparing pairs reproduces exactly that, and picking each time the largest pair below the last one taken needs
    // no sort and no record of which candidates were taken: a state's few hundred scores are read once per elite.
    const candidates: u32 = params.plan_candidates;
    const elite_count: u32 = params.mppi_elites;
    const scores_start: u32 = params.x_off + id * candidates;
    const elites_start: u32 = id * elite_count;
    var previous_score: f32 = 0;
    var previous_candidate: u32 = 0;
    var rank: u32 = 0;
    while (rank < elite_count) : (rank += 1) {
        var found: bool = false;
        var best_score: f32 = 0;
        var best_candidate: u32 = 0;
        var candidate: u32 = 0;
        while (candidate < candidates) : (candidate += 1) {
            const rankable: f32 = zm.rankableScore(f32, b_acts[scores_start + candidate]);
            const below_previous: bool = rank == 0 or rankable < previous_score or
                (rankable == previous_score and candidate < previous_candidate);
            const above_best: bool = !found or rankable > best_score or
                (rankable == best_score and candidate > best_candidate);
            if (below_previous and above_best) {
                found = true;
                best_score = rankable;
                best_candidate = candidate;
            }
        }
        b_acts[params.y_off + elites_start + rank] = float(best_candidate);
        previous_score = best_score;
        previous_candidate = best_candidate;
    }
    // The weights: the best weighs exactly 1 before normalising, so the sum is never zero.
    const best_elite: u32 = @trunc(b_acts[params.y_off + elites_start]);
    const best_rankable: f32 = zm.rankableScore(f32, b_acts[scores_start + best_elite]);
    // The scale a score difference is read in: 1 (absolute), or the elites' own spread - the best minus the worst
    // elite, the last one taken (relative). Elites all equal in score weigh alike.
    const worst_elite: u32 = @trunc(b_acts[params.y_off + elites_start + elite_count - 1]);
    const worst_rankable: f32 = zm.rankableScore(f32, b_acts[scores_start + worst_elite]);
    const elite_spread: f32 = best_rankable - worst_rankable;
    const is_relative: bool = params.mppi_temperature_mode == @backingInt(MppiTemperature.relative_to_elites);
    const per_score_unit: f32 = if (!is_relative) 1.0 else if (elite_spread > 0) 1.0 / elite_spread else 0.0;
    var weight_sum: f32 = 0;
    rank = 0;
    while (rank < elite_count) : (rank += 1) {
        const elite: u32 = @trunc(b_acts[params.y_off + elites_start + rank]);
        const rankable: f32 = zm.rankableScore(f32, b_acts[scores_start + elite]);
        const weight: f32 = @exp(params.mppi_temperature * (rankable - best_rankable) * per_score_unit);
        b_acts[params.z_off + elites_start + rank] = weight;
        weight_sum += weight;
    }
    rank = 0;
    while (rank < elite_count) : (rank += 1) {
        b_acts[params.z_off + elites_start + rank] /= weight_sum;
    }
}

Before and after the rounds. A decision begins by moving each state's Gaussian: where the state's episode goes on, its mean becomes its last plan shifted one step - that step has been taken, every later step moves up, the new last step starts at zero - and at an episode's start it is zero; every spread restarts at its ceiling, since last decision's certainty is not this one's (mppi_begin). One thread per state and action dimension walks up the steps, reading each before writing it, so the shift is done in place. After the rounds, one thread per state draws an elite by the refit's weights - a uniform draw against the weights' running sum, in rank order - and takes its first action as the decision's target, with the first step's spread (mppi_choose). While training, the action acted on is that target jittered by its spread and clamped (mppi_explore); when evaluating, the target itself.

   warm start, horizon 3:   last means [0.2, 0.5, -0.1]   -->   [0.5, -0.1, 0]
   the choice:              weights 0.441, 0.361, 0.198, draw 0.6   -->   running sums 0.441, 0.802: rank 1
   exploring:               target 0.6, spread 0.3, noise 1.5   -->   0.6 + 0.45 = 1.05   -->   1.0
KitPlanner.decide
/// One decision for every state (this type's head), after the decision's inputs are in acts.
pub fn decide(planner: Self, pipe: *Pipe, mode: Mode) void {
    planner.policy_plans.fill(pipe);
    // EfficientTDMPC decides every step: a warm plan has aged one step.
    planner.mppi.begin(pipe, 1);
    for (0..planner.mppi.options.rounds) |round| {
        planner.mppi.sample(pipe, @intCast(round));
        planner.scorer.score(pipe);
        planner.mppi.refit(pipe);
    }
    planner.mppi.choose(pipe);
    switch (mode) {
        .explore => planner.mppi.explore(pipe),
        .evaluate => planner.mppi.takeTargets(pipe),
    }
}

13.10 Training EfficientTDMPC on the kit#

KitTrainer trains the agent as the CPU agent's trainer does, frame by frame, with the kit doing all of the network work: the kit's planner acts for every environment, the host steps the environments and stores every step in the replay with the planner's target, and the kit's learner makes the schedule's updates. Every network lives once in the kit's parameter buffer, and the learner's pieces and both planners - the one that acts, and reanalyze's - read the same numbers.

   act       the kit's planner, exploring          (random actions while the schedule seeds the replay)
   step      every environment, on the host        the rows stored with the planner's targets
   advance   each environment's next observation, or a fresh episode where one ended
   learn     the schedule's updates                (KitLearner: world model, policy, reanalyze)

Forward-only applications. A network that only reads - to act, to plan or to make targets - never runs a backward, so its application reserves no gradient regions: a third of a layer's floats or more. The planners and the value targets use such applications; a backward through one is refused. The gradients a learner does keep grow with its batch - every activation of every application it learns from - so the activation gradients' buffer is sized on its own, apart from the parameters' buffers, which grow only with the networks.

Reanalyze in chunks. Reanalyze plans many stored states at once - three steps of twenty windows, each with as many candidates as acting - more activations than the kit's buffer holds. It plans them a few states at a time instead. Each state's search is its own - its own Gaussian, its candidates' scores, its noise drawn from its own number - so the chunks decide exactly as one decision over all of them would.

What the agent is sure of. After a decision, KitPlanner.readSignals reads back what the agent's own networks say about how sure they are at a state - all numbers the decision's forward passes already computed: the chosen plan's score and how much the heads disagree about it, how wide the reward and value heads' predicted distributions are, how evenly the encoder's SimNorm groups spread their mass, and how flat the encoder's first layer's outputs are for the observation. Along an episode in which the cartpole's pole falls:

   pole (deg)   score   disagreement   value width   inverse spread
        1.1      6.24         0.0013         1.04           79
       16.2      6.02         0.0022         0.81           47
       59.0      4.05         0.0126         0.61           16
      102.4      1.82         0.0054         0.36            8

14. Running it in a page#

examples/cartpole_duel puts the pieces on a page: one robot.zig cartpole model, a planner that knows the model (MPC) in front, and behind it a learner that does not — PPO, SAC or SuperTrack, switchable while it runs — each collecting on the CPU and training on the GPU. It is the pattern for running learning inside a frame.

14.1 Registering the kernels#

A page that dispatches the kit's kernels lists them for the pipeline, from the module's own kernels list, and the build registers the module so its WGSL is generated.

pipelineEntries
fn pipelineEntries(comptime M: type) [M.kernels.len]z.Compute(M).KernelWgsl {
    var table: [M.kernels.len]z.Compute(M).KernelWgsl = undefined;
    inline for (M.kernels, 0..) |name, i| {
        table[i] = .{ .name = name, .wgsl = @embedFile(name ++ "_wgsl") };
    }
    return table;
}

14.2 Budgeting the frame#

A frame has about 16 ms, shared by the renderer, the planner and the learner. Both processors are budgeted. The CPU's share is steered on the measured frame time: a frame that runs long cuts the budget sharply, a frame with room grows it slowly — additive increase, multiplicative decrease, the controller that converges instead of oscillating when what it measures is what it changes. Every frame still gets at least one collection tick, so learning never stalls. The GPU gets a new batch only when the previous one is back, so at most one is ever in flight and the device's queue never floods.

frame_target_ms
/// -- *** THE FRAME IS BUDGETED ON BOTH PROCESSORS --
///
/// A learner that issues GPU work faster than the device completes it floods the queue - and on
/// a phone the GPU is shared with the compositor, so a flooded queue stalls the whole device, not
/// just the page. So:
///   * CPU: the learner's collection budget is steered on the measured frame time (AIMD), within
///     [cpu_budget_min_ms, cpu_budget_max_ms];
///   * GPU: a new batch of minibatches is dispatched only once the last one is BACK -
///     `readGeneration().mirrored` has reached the `submitted` recorded after it - so at most one
///     batch is ever in flight, and its size (minibatches) is steered like the CPU budget.
const frame_target_ms: f32 = 1000.0 / 60.0;
cpu_budget_min_ms
const cpu_budget_min_ms: f32 = 0.25;
cpu_budget_max_ms
const cpu_budget_max_ms: f32 = 8.0;
planWithinFrame
/// -- *** THE BUDGET LOOP: PLAN A LITTLE, ALWAYS RETURN --
///
/// `mpc.optimize` with `iterations = n` does at most n improvement passes and returns. That is
/// the hook this whole demo hangs on: the planner is re-entrant across frames because its unit
/// of work is one iteration, and a frame simply stops asking.
///
/// -- ** THE BUDGET IS DRIVEN BY THE FRAME TIME, NOT BY A STOPWATCH --
///
/// A page has no wall clock of its own to time the planner with (`bridge.zig` imports none), and
/// needs none.
///
/// * `f.time.delta_time` measures the thing actually worth protecting - whether frames are
/// landing on time - rather than a proxy for it. Planning time is only one contributor; a device
/// struggling with the renderer needs the planner to back off just as much, and a stopwatch
/// around `optimize` cannot see that.
///
/// The target is 1/60 s. Overshooting costs a visible stutter, so back off fast; undershooting
/// only wastes headroom, so grow slowly. A symmetric controller oscillates here, because the
/// frame time it measures is the frame time it is changing.
fn planWithinFrame(s: *State, delta_time: f32) void {
    const target: f32 = 1.0 / 60.0;

    // -- *** PROFILING IS SUSPENDED ACROSS THE PLANNER, AND IT HAS TO BE --
    //
    // `robot.step` is instrumented, which is right for a frame that steps a robot a few times.
    // One planning frame here steps it **tens of thousands** of times - 250 knots x 6
    // finite-difference columns x up to 40 iterations - and every zone takes two timestamps,
    // which on wasm are two JS boundary crossings.
    //
    // Measured: at horizon 60 the smoke runner already saw 12 225 clock calls per frame. At
    // 250 it **exhausted Node's JS heap and the gate died** - and a browser would have been
    // paying the same crossings, tens of milliseconds a frame, for a profile nobody can read
    // (a flame graph of 60 000 identical `robot.step` zones is not a diagnostic).
    //
    // * THIS IS NOT PROFILER-BASHING. The instrument is priced for the workload it was built
    // for. A planner is a different workload, and the right move is to tell the instrument so.
    // Everything outside this call - rendering, UI, the physics the robot actually runs - is
    // still profiled normally.
    const was_frozen: bool = profiler.isFrozen();
    profiler.freeze();
    const iterations: u32 = @trunc(clamp(s.budget, 1.0, 40.0));
    const plan_start: f64 = z.wgpu.nowMs();
    const result: mpc.Result = mpc.optimize(&s.model, &s.data, &s.plan, costOf(s), .{
        .iterations = iterations,
    });
    if (result.iterations > 0) {
        const spent: f32 = @floatCast((z.wgpu.nowMs() - plan_start) / float(result.iterations));
        s.ms_per_iteration += (spent - s.ms_per_iteration) * 0.1;
    }
    if (!was_frozen) {
        profiler.unfreeze();
    }
    s.last_iterations = result.iterations;
    s.last_cost = result.cost;
    s.plan_iterations += result.iterations;
    if (s.first_cost == 0) {
        s.first_cost = result.initial_cost;
    }

    // -- *** "GOOD ENOUGH TO ACT ON" IS NOT "CONVERGED", AND WAITING FOR THE LATTER IS A BUG --
    //
    // This used to hold the robot still until `result.converged`, which on a phone - 4
    // iterations a frame, a cold plan starting from a 2.5 s free-fall rollout - meant staring
    // at a motionless cartpole under the word "planning" with no way to tell whether it was
    // making progress or wedged. That is a worse failure than a wrong answer, because the user
    // cannot distinguish it from a hang.
    //
    // * AND CONVERGENCE IS THE WRONG BAR ANYWAY. MPC re-solves every single tick; the plan
    // does not need to be optimal before the first step, it needs to be SANE. A budget of
    // iterations buys that, and everything after it is bought while the robot is already
    // moving, which is what the receding horizon is for.
    if (s.plan_iterations >= warmup_iterations or result.converged) {
        s.warming = false;
    }

    // Cost history, so "still planning" comes with evidence that it is working.
    if (s.cost_history_len < s.cost_history.len) {
        s.cost_history[s.cost_history_len] = result.cost;
        s.cost_history_len += 1;
    } else {
        copyForwards(f32, s.cost_history[0 .. s.cost_history.len - 1], s.cost_history[1..]);
        s.cost_history[s.cost_history.len - 1] = result.cost;
    }

    // A slow average, so one hitch - a texture upload, a GC pause - does not swing the budget.
    s.frame_ms += (delta_time * 1000.0 - s.frame_ms) * 0.1;
    // -- * A FAIR SHARE OF THE FRAME --
    // This rule was "add iterations only below 0.7 of the frame target" - which, on a display
    // locked to vsync, never happens once a learner fills the headroom: on Simon's phone MPC sat
    // at 1 iteration a frame. Now MPC's budget is MILLISECONDS, steered by the learners' own
    // AIMD (+0.1 ms on time, x0.7 when late), and turned into iterations with the measured cost
    // of one. Two AIMD flows with the same increase and decrease converge to EQUAL shares - the
    // classic TCP result - so neither can starve the other.
    const frame_ms: f32 = delta_time * 1000.0;
    if (frame_ms > frame_target_ms * 1.25) {
        s.mpc_budget_ms = @max(cpu_budget_min_ms, s.mpc_budget_ms * 0.7);
    } else if (frame_ms < frame_target_ms * 1.1) {
        s.mpc_budget_ms = @min(cpu_budget_max_ms, s.mpc_budget_ms + 0.1);
    }
    s.budget = clamp(s.mpc_budget_ms / @max(s.ms_per_iteration, 0.01), 1.0, 40.0);
    _ = target;
}

14.3 The learners, frame by frame#

Each learner has a tick — act and record one step of every cartpole — and a frame function that spends the budget on ticks and hands full batches to the GPU.

collectTick
/// One lockstep tick: every PPO cartpole acts on the CPU's weights and steps once.
fn collectTick(s: *State) void {
    const r: *Rollout = &s.rollouts[s.fill];
    for (0..n_envs) |e| {
        const row: usize = e * ppo_horizon + s.tick;
        const d: *rbt.Data = &s.envs[e];
        const obs: [4]f32 = observe(d);
        @memcpy(r.obs[row * 4 ..][0..4], &obs);
        var action: [1]f32 = undefined;
        r.logp[row] = s.learner.act(&obs, &action, s.rng.random());
        r.act[row] = action[0];
        r.value[row] = s.learner.value(&obs);
        d.ctrl[0] = clamp(action[0], -1.0, 1.0);
        rbt.step(&s.model, d);
        s.env_steps[e] += 1;
        const angle: f32 = d.pos[pole_hinge];
        const failed: bool = !isFinite(angle) or @abs(angle) > fail_angle or @abs(d.pos[cart_slide]) > fail_cart;
        const capped: bool = !failed and s.env_steps[e] >= episode_cap;
        r.reward[row] = if (failed) 0.0 else 1.0;
        r.terminal[row] = failed;
        r.truncated[row] = capped or (!failed and s.tick == ppo_horizon - 1);
        const next: [4]f32 = observe(d);
        r.next_value[row] = if (failed) 0.0 else s.learner.value(&next);
        if (failed or capped) {
            recordSurvival(s, s.env_steps[e]);
            resetEnv(s, e);
        }
    }
    s.tick += 1;
    s.total_samples += n_envs;
    s.window_samples += n_envs;
}
runPpo
/// PPO's share of the frame, budgeted on both processors (see `frame_target_ms`).
fn runPpo(s: *State, delta_time: f32) void {
    // -- Steer the budgets on the measured frame time: back off fast, creep up slowly. --
    const frame_ms: f32 = delta_time * 1000.0;
    const on_time: bool = frame_ms < frame_target_ms * 1.1;
    if (frame_ms > frame_target_ms * 1.25) {
        s.learner_budget_ms = @max(cpu_budget_min_ms, s.learner_budget_ms * 0.7);
        s.gpu_batches = @max(1, s.gpu_batches / 2);
    } else if (on_time) {
        s.learner_budget_ms = @min(cpu_budget_max_ms, s.learner_budget_ms + 0.1);
    }

    // -- GPU: new work only once the last batch is BACK (finished and mirrored). --
    //
    // ** POLL THE READBACK EVERY FRAME, FIRST. `readLatest` (inside `syncWeights`) both lands a
    // finished copy AND encodes the next one, and the mirrored generation only advances in it.
    // Calling it only once the GPU looked idle deadlocked: after the first batch nothing encoded
    // a copy, so `mirrored` never reached `gpu_wait` and training stopped for good. The stub GPU
    // reports 0/0 generations, so the smoke run could not see it. Taking the mirror every frame
    // is harmless: it only ever moves forward.
    _ = s.learner.syncWeights();
    const generation: z.Compute(zn_mlp).Generation = s.pipe.readGeneration();
    const gpu_idle: bool = generation.mirrored >= s.gpu_wait;
    if (gpu_idle) {
        if (!s.gpu_taken) {
            // The batch is back: the weights just taken are the ones it produced.
            s.synced += 1;
            s.gpu_taken = true;
        }
        if (s.training != null) {
            var issued: usize = 0;
            while (issued < s.gpu_batches and s.training != null) : (issued += 1) {
                trainSlice(s);
            }
            s.gpu_wait = s.pipe.readGeneration().submitted;
            s.gpu_taken = false;
            if (on_time) {
                s.gpu_batches = @min(gpu_batches_max, s.gpu_batches + 1);
            }
        }
    } else {
        s.busy_window += 1;
    }

    // -- CPU: collect within the budget; wait when the next rollout is full and the last is
    // still training. --
    // * AT LEAST ONE TICK A FRAME, then the budget: learning always progresses, even when the
    // frame's budget is spent (a tick is ~0.1 ms). The smoke runner's clock advances 16 ms a
    // CALL, so a budget-first loop exited before collecting anything - neither learner ever
    // trained headlessly, and the training paths went unexercised there.
    const start: f64 = z.wgpu.nowMs();
    var first: bool = true;
    while (first or z.wgpu.nowMs() - start < s.learner_budget_ms) {
        first = false;
        if (s.tick < ppo_horizon) {
            collectTick(s);
        } else if (s.training == null) {
            finishRollout(s) catch |err| {
                zm.assertUnreachable(@src(), "finishing a rollout failed: {t}", .{err});
            };
        } else {
            break;
        }
    }
    s.window_time += delta_time;
    if (s.window_time >= 1.0) {
        s.samples_per_second = float(s.window_samples) / s.window_time;
        s.gpu_busy_frames = s.busy_window;
        s.window_time = 0;
        s.window_samples = 0;
        s.busy_window = 0;
    }
}
runSac
/// SAC's share of the frame, budgeted exactly as PPO's: the CPU collects within the steered
/// budget; a batch of updates goes to the GPU only once the last one is back.
fn runSac(s: *State, delta_time: f32) void {
    const frame_ms: f32 = delta_time * 1000.0;
    const on_time: bool = frame_ms < frame_target_ms * 1.1;
    if (frame_ms > frame_target_ms * 1.25) {
        s.learner_budget_ms = @max(cpu_budget_min_ms, s.learner_budget_ms * 0.7);
        s.sac_batch = @max(1, s.sac_batch / 2);
    } else if (on_time) {
        s.learner_budget_ms = @min(cpu_budget_max_ms, s.learner_budget_ms + 0.1);
    }
    // Poll first: the readback only advances inside it (see runPpo).
    _ = s.sac.syncActor();
    const generation: z.Compute(zn_mlp).Generation = s.sac_pipe.readGeneration();
    if (generation.mirrored >= s.sac_wait) {
        if (!s.sac_taken) {
            const trip: f32 = @floatCast(z.wgpu.nowMs() - s.sac_issued_ms);
            s.sac_round_trip_ms += (trip - s.sac_round_trip_ms) * 0.2;
            s.synced += 1;
            s.sac_taken = true;
        }
        if (s.replay.len >= @max(sac_warmup, s.sac.options.batch)) {
            const issued: f64 = z.wgpu.nowMs();
            for (0..s.sac_batch) |_| {
                sacUpdate(s);
            }
            const per_update: f32 = @floatCast((z.wgpu.nowMs() - issued) / float(s.sac_batch));
            s.sac_submit_ms += (per_update - s.sac_submit_ms) * 0.2;
            s.sac_wait = s.sac_pipe.readGeneration().submitted;
            s.sac_taken = false;
            s.sac_issued_ms = issued;
            if (on_time) {
                s.sac_batch = @min(sac_batch_max, s.sac_batch + 1);
            }
        }
    } else {
        s.busy_window += 1;
    }
    // At least one tick a frame, then the budget (see runPpo).
    const start: f64 = z.wgpu.nowMs();
    sacTick(s);
    while (z.wgpu.nowMs() - start < s.learner_budget_ms) {
        sacTick(s);
    }
    s.window_time += delta_time;
    if (s.window_time >= 1.0) {
        s.samples_per_second = float(s.window_samples) / s.window_time;
        s.sac_updates_per_second = float(s.sac_updates_window) / s.window_time;
        s.gpu_busy_frames = s.busy_window;
        s.window_time = 0;
        s.window_samples = 0;
        s.sac_updates_window = 0;
        s.busy_window = 0;
    }
}
runSuperTrack
/// SuperTrack's share of the frame, budgeted as the others: the CPU collects within the steered
/// budget (at least one tick); a training iteration - the world step and the policy step, FUSED,
/// 8 dispatches in two submissions - goes to the GPU only once the last is back.
fn runSuperTrack(s: *State, delta_time: f32) void {
    const frame_ms: f32 = delta_time * 1000.0;
    if (frame_ms > frame_target_ms * 1.25) {
        s.learner_budget_ms = @max(cpu_budget_min_ms, s.learner_budget_ms * 0.7);
    } else if (frame_ms < frame_target_ms * 1.1) {
        s.learner_budget_ms = @min(cpu_budget_max_ms, s.learner_budget_ms + 0.1);
    }
    // Poll first: the readback only advances inside it; its weights become the acting policy.
    if (s.st_kit.readParams()) |weights| {
        s.st_host.loadPolicy(weights, s.st_kit.pol);
    }
    const generation: z.Compute(zn_mlp).Generation = s.st_pipe.readGeneration();
    if (generation.mirrored >= s.st_wait) {
        if (!s.st_taken) {
            const trip: f32 = @floatCast(z.wgpu.nowMs() - s.st_issued_ms);
            s.st_round_trip_ms += (trip - s.st_round_trip_ms) * 0.2;
            s.synced += 1;
            s.st_taken = true;
        }
        if (s.st_host.sampleWorldBatch() and s.st_host.samplePolicyBatch()) {
            const issued: f64 = z.wgpu.nowMs();
            s.st_kit.trainWorldFused(s.st_host.stage_states, s.st_host.stage_forces);
            s.st_kit.trainPolicyFused(s.st_host.stage_starts, s.st_host.stage_noise);
            const spent: f32 = @floatCast(z.wgpu.nowMs() - issued);
            s.st_submit_ms += (spent - s.st_submit_ms) * 0.2;
            s.st_wait = s.st_pipe.readGeneration().submitted;
            s.st_taken = false;
            s.st_issued_ms = issued;
            s.st_iterations += 1;
        }
    } else {
        s.busy_window += 1;
    }
    const start: f64 = z.wgpu.nowMs();
    stTick(s);
    while (z.wgpu.nowMs() - start < s.learner_budget_ms) {
        stTick(s);
    }
    s.window_time += delta_time;
    if (s.window_time >= 1.0) {
        s.samples_per_second = float(s.window_samples) / s.window_time;
        s.gpu_busy_frames = s.busy_window;
        s.window_time = 0;
        s.window_samples = 0;
        s.busy_window = 0;
    }
}
switchLearner
/// Swap the learner: the cartpoles restart and the survival record clears; each learner keeps
/// its own weights on its own pipe.
fn switchLearner(s: *State) void {
    s.kind = switch (s.kind) {
        .ppo => .sac,
        .sac => .supertrack,
        .supertrack => .ppo,
    };
    for (0..n_envs) |e| {
        resetEnv(s, e);
        s.st_steps[e] = 0;
        s.st_segments[e] = s.st_next_segment;
        s.st_next_segment += 1;
    }
    s.survival_len = 0;
    s.survival_at = 0;
    s.tick = 0;
}
update
fn update(f: *z.Frame, s: *State) void {
    const gl: *z.WgpuGl = f.gl;
    const u: ui.Ui = s.ui_host.begin(f);
    defer s.ui_host.render(f);
    const captured: bool = drawPanel(u, s, f.window.widthf(), f.window.heightf());

    // 1. PLAN - bounded, every frame, whether or not the physics advances.
    planWithinFrame(s, f.time.delta_time);
    switch (s.kind) {
        .ppo => runPpo(s, f.time.delta_time),
        .sac => runSac(s, f.time.delta_time),
        .supertrack => runSuperTrack(s, f.time.delta_time),
    }

    // 2. ACT - the simulation runs on its own clock, not the display's.
    //
    // * WHILE `warming`, THE ROBOT DOES NOT MOVE. A cold plan is nonsense for its first few
    // iterations, and applying it would flail the cart around for a quarter of a second before
    // the optimiser found anything. Holding still until the first solve converges makes the
    // ghost trajectory readable and the start honest: you are watching it think, then act.
    if (s.running and !s.warming) {
        s.accumulator += @min(f.time.delta_time, 0.1);
        while (s.accumulator >= sim_timestep) : (s.accumulator -= sim_timestep) {
            // * `feedbackControl` RATHER THAN `plan.ctrl[0]`, and the difference is the whole
            // reason MPC survives a slow solver. The plan in hand was linearised about a state
            // the robot has since left - up to two sim steps ago, because physics runs at 100 Hz
            // and planning at the display rate. `K_0*dx` is the backward pass's own answer to
            // being somewhere else.
            mpc.feedbackControl(&s.model, &s.data, &s.plan, s.applied);
            @memcpy(s.data.ctrl, s.applied);
            rbt.step(&s.model, &s.data);
            // ** SHIFT AFTER STEPPING, NOT BEFORE. The plan is indexed from "now"; once the
            // robot has advanced a tick, knot 1 is the new now. Shifting before the step
            // applies knot 1's control to knot 0's state - off by one, every tick, compounding.
            mpc.shift(&s.plan);
        }
    }

    z.clearViewport(f, bg);
    const aspect: f32 = f.window.widthf() / @max(1.0, f.window.heightf());
    // * FRAME THE RAIL, NOT THE CART. The plan spans the full 4.8 m of track and the ghost
    // trajectory is the thing worth seeing; a distance tuned to the robot alone crops it.
    s.cam.distance = clamp(5.2 / @max(0.35, aspect), 4.0, 11.0);
    const cam: Camera3D = s.cam.update(f, captured, .{ .min_distance = 1.2, .max_distance = 9.0 });
    z.beginMode3D(gl, cam);
    drawScene(s, gl);
    drawPpo(s, gl);
    z.endMode3D(gl);
}

15. Conventions and gotchas#

Every item here is a convention that, when broken, still produces smooth, plausible motion — just not the right motion. They are collected in one place because none of them announces itself.

15.1 Capture data#

  • Read each joint's own channel list. Channel counts and orders vary between exporters; the list says which numbers belong to the joint and in what order its rotations compose (Z Y X means Rz Ry Rx). Angles are in degrees.
  • End sites are joints with no channels. Skip them when walking a frame's numbers.
  • Only the root's position channels move anything. Every other joint sits at its OFFSET, turned by its parent's rotation.
  • The retarget needs the performer's rest pose. Zero rotations mean the skeleton's bind pose, which is not necessarily how anyone stands.

15.2 Frames and handedness#

  • Convert with a rotation, never a swizzle. Swapping two axes mirrors the performer. Use FrameConvert.rotate.
  • Positions convert by C; rotations by C q C−1.
  • Check handedness directly — the sign of a triple product of body directions, before and after conversion. How well the robot fits the capture will not reveal a mirror.
  • qmul(a, b) applies b first, as the Hamilton product does: rotating by qmul(a, b) is rotating by b, then by a.

15.3 The robot's coordinates#

  • Never subtract poses or add velocities to them. Use differentiatePos and integratePos; quaternions are part of a pose.
  • A ball's angular velocity, and the free root's, is in the joint's own frame, applied on the right. The free root's linear velocity is in world coordinates.
  • cvel is not a body's velocity. It lives in a shared frame; use bodyVelocity. Its angular part is in world axes.

15.4 Servoing#

  • Step the model at the clip's frame time. One simulator step per frame is what makes the reference and the simulation the same discrete trajectory.
  • Filter the clip before servoing it — in velocity space, at about 5 Hz (Clip.smoothed).
  • The velocity error is against the backward difference. Tracker does this; anything that replaces it must too, or fast motion is followed with a lag.
  • Inverse dynamics does not see passive forces. Limp the model (limpKeepArmature) or feed its springs and dampers forward.
  • A free root is not actuated. Its six rows can only come from the floor; split them with contactTorques or contactConsistentTorques.

15.5 The ragdoll#

  • Hinges only. Ball joints are refused, so humanoid_flex2 has no ragdoll.
  • Joints exist only below a root — a free body, or one welded to the world.
  • Its motors are position springs: no feedforward, a little overshoot, and slower settling in chains than a single spring.

15.6 The GPU#

  • Readback arrives a frame late. Act on the last weights you have.
  • Keep at most one batch in flight. Wait for readGeneration to show the last one back before dispatching the next.
  • Record an update as one submission (beginRecording … submitRecording).
  • Steps that share a buffer field in one frame upload disjoint ranges (uploadAt).

15.7 Learning#

  • A judged step is the policy alone. No exploration, no plan and no draw from the random stream: a judgement that consumed random numbers would change the run it measures (§11.14).
  • Every upload of a frame lands before any of its work. Two uses of one upload region in a frame leave only the second's numbers; the learner decides only at a round's last step, at most once per frame.
  • Hashed noises need streams of their own. Noise hashed from (seed, row, index) is the same number for the same row and index; the flow's noise and the exploration's take different seeds, or they are one noise.
  • A flow with no noise learns nothing from FlowDPG. Its step floor is the noise's length; give the flow a noise of its own (FlowSettings.noise_share).
  • A plan is corrections, not actions. Acting from one is the policy's reaction to the state reached, plus the plan's correction for the step (§11.14).

16. Recipes#

Short answers to "how do I…", each pointing at the code that does it.

16.1 Retarget a capture onto a humanoid#

Parse the capture and the performer's rest pose with codecs.bvh.parse, load a floating-base model, call retargetClip, then Clip.smoothed(m, 5.0). Check the result with Clip.residual and the joint ranges — the example in §6.9 does all of it.

16.2 Use a capture whose joints are named differently#

Add the other format's names to the match table's rows as alternatives; each row accepts them, in order, when its human_joint is absent. resolveMatchTable reports what it resolved to (§6.2).

16.3 Servo a clip#

Weld the root, limp the model, step at the clip's frame time, and each step feed three consecutive frames to Tracker.accelerations, then biasForce and inverseDynamics into applied_force. The program in §2.1 is exactly this.

16.4 Measure how closely a body follows#

Run forward kinematics on the reference pose and compare body rotations with worstBodyErrorDeg. For the ragdoll, read its bodies with robotBodyFrame first.

16.5 Check whether a floor can perform a clip#

Inverse dynamics of the clip on the floating model: the root's first three rows are the force the floor must supply, frame by frame. Compare its vertical part with zero and its horizontal part with friction (§8.2).

16.6 Put a humanoid in a scene as a ragdoll#

Use a hinge-only model, rmx.build it into a zimrphysics world, and drive it each step with driveToPose (§9.5).

16.7 Train on the GPU inside a page#

Instantiate the learner on the kit (GpuPpoOn, GpuSacOn or SuperTrackKitOn), register the kernels, record each update as one submission, keep one batch in flight, and budget the CPU on the frame time — §14 walks through a page that does.

16.8 Give the learner a flow and a planner#

Set robot_track_resident.Options.actor to .flow and Options.planning.enabled to true. The flow then corrects the policy and the planner searches for the characters in danger, each at its small default budget - Options.flow and Options.planning hold the numbers (§11.13, §11.14).

16.9 Stop a run and resume it#

exportState writes the learner's shape, options and counters, its networks' parameters, Adam's two moments and the feature normaliser as bytes; importState, into a learner built with the same options, carries training on from there. The replay is not kept: a resumed learner refills it by acting before its first update (§13.7).

16.10 Show another declaration in this document#

Add an empty block that names it — data-src for the file, data-decl for how its first line starts — and run zig build doc-folds. The block fills itself in from the source, and stays in step with it from then on.

17. Reference#

Every public declaration of the modules this document covers, with the first sentence of its doc comment. This table is generated from the source by zig build doc-folds (and by the gate), so it always lists what exists — a new public function appears here the moment it is written.
